source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. VII (Montreuil)

1.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI PRIMI : DILIGITE JUSTITIAM, QUI JUDICATIS TERRAM.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: Love justice, you that are the judges of the earth

paras.t: Locuturus auctor libri hujus de sapientia, exordium sumit a justitia, sine qua vera et salutaris sapientia non habetur. Diligite justitiam, qui judicatis terram. Quamvis enim justitia sit omnibus diligenda, præcipue tamen his qui præsident aliis, quibus ex officio incumbit terram, id est subditos suos in terra morantes, judicare. Nec enim digni sunt alios judicare, aut in solio judicii residere, nisi qui justi sunt et prudentes : quum et judicare sit actus justitiæ, tanquam virtutis et habitus inclinantis ad recte judicandum ; est quoque actus prudentiæ, tanquam ipsum actum elicientis, prout Thomas in secunda secundæ, quæstione 60, magis declarat. Prudentia autem, secundum Philosophum in Ethicis, non nisi virtuosis veraciter inest. Quemadmodum ergo vile et ridiculosum est, indoctum sedere in cathedra doctrinæ, et officium docendi assumere ; ita indignum, præsumptuosum et stultum est, injustum in solio judicii ad faciendum judicium apparere. Nam et talis agit contra ordinem caritatis, quæ incipit a se ipsa, et post Deum potissime amat proprium suum subjectum. Ipsa quoque requirit justitia, ut homo se ipsum in primis judicet, corripiat, et emendet. Propter quod ait Apostolus : Inexcusabilis es, o homo omnis qui judicas, alium judicas, te ipsum condemnas. Hinc Moyses filiis Israel ait : Date ex vobis viros sapientes et gnaros, quorum conversatio probata sit in tribubus vestris, et ponam eos vobis principes.
paras.en: Being about to speak of wisdom, the author of this book takes his beginning from justice, without which true and saving wisdom is not had. [[1:1|Love justice, you that are the judges of the earth|Diligite justitiam, qui judicatis terram]]. For although justice is to be loved by all, yet above all by those who are set over others, whose office it is to judge the earth, that is, their subjects dwelling on the earth. For none are worthy to judge others, or to sit on the throne of judgment, except those who are just and prudent: since to judge is an act of justice, as of the virtue and habit that inclines one to judge rightly; and it is also an act of prudence, as of that which elicits the act itself [that is, justice inclines the will to judge rightly, while prudence brings forth the judgment itself], as Thomas sets out more fully in the Secunda Secundæ, question 60. And prudence, according to the Philosopher in the Ethics, is truly present only in the virtuous. As, then, it is a mean and ridiculous thing for an unlearned man to sit in the chair of teaching and take upon himself the office of teaching, so it is unworthy, presumptuous and foolish for an unjust man to appear on the throne of judgment to give judgment. For such a man acts against the order of charity, which begins from oneself and, after God, loves above all its own subject [that is, the very person who loves]. Justice itself also requires that a man first of all judge, correct and amend himself. Wherefore the Apostle says: [[Rom 2:1|thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest|Inexcusabilis es, o homo omnis qui judicas]]: thou [[Rom 2:1|judgest another, thou condemnest thyself|alium judicas, te ipsum condemnas]]. Hence Moses says to the children of Israel: [[Deut 1:13|Let me have from among you wise and understanding men, and such whose conversation is approved among your tribes, that I may appoint them your rulers|Date ex vobis viros sapientes et gnaros, quorum conversatio probata sit in tribubus vestris, et ponam eos vobis principes]].

paras.t: Itaque, Diligite justitiam, id est virtutem et actum justitiæ, ita ut personaliter justi sitis, et toto affectu æquitatem ametis, unicuique quod suum est exhibendo, adjudicando, et conservando ; et nec cupiditate, nec amore, nec odio, nec timore, nec aliquo modo contra justitiam quid agatis aut judicetis. Judex enim debet esse quasi viva lex et animata justitia, ut semper esuriat sitiatque justitiam. Nihilo minus justitiæ debent esse admixtæ clementia atque discretio. Porro, secundum Ambrosium primo de Officiis : Justitia est virtus quæ unicuique quod suum est tribuit, alienum non vindicat, utilitatemque propriam negligit, quatenus communem custodiat æquitatem.
paras.en: So then, [[1:1|Love justice|Diligite justitiam]], that is, the virtue and the act of justice, so that you be just in your own persons and love equity with your whole affection, rendering, adjudging and preserving to each what is his own; and that neither from greed, nor love, nor hatred, nor fear, nor in any way, you do or judge anything against justice. For a judge ought to be as it were a living law and justice ensouled, so that he may ever [[Matt 5:6|hunger and thirst after justice|esuriat sitiatque justitiam]]. Nevertheless, justice ought to be mingled with clemency and discretion. Further, according to Ambrose in the first book On Duties: Justice is the virtue which renders to each what is his own, does not claim what is another's, and neglects its own advantage so as to guard the common equity.

paras.t: Sentite de Domino in bonitate, id est, bene sentite de Deo, quod scilicet universorum providentiam habeat, et male judicata rejudicabit. Ideo ejus justitiam sequi conemini, et ejus intuitu timeatis judicare injuste, ne ab eo damnemini. Vel : Sentite de Domino in bonitate, id est, per bonitatem et virtuositatem, atque connaturalitatem seu conformitatem vestri affectus ad Deum, judicate de eo sic, ut vester affectus sit divinæ et increatæ æquitati conformis : sicque sentiatis de eo, quod ipse sit omnium judex justissimus, non solum per nudam et informem, vestri intellectus notitiam, sed per ipsam voluntatis bonitatem, æquitatem ac sinceritatem.
paras.en: [[1:1|Think of the Lord in goodness|Sentite de Domino in bonitate]], that is, think well of God: namely, that he has providence over all things, and will judge again what has been judged ill. Therefore strive to follow his justice, and out of regard for him fear to judge unjustly, lest you be condemned by him. Or: [[1:1|Think of the Lord in goodness|Sentite de Domino in bonitate]], that is, through goodness and virtue, and the connaturality or conformity of your affection to God [*connaturalitas*: the kinship of a good will with its object, by which one judges of it as if by instinct], judge of him in such a way that your affection be conformed to the divine and uncreated equity: and so think of him that he is the most just judge of all, not only by the bare and unformed knowledge of your intellect [unformed: not quickened by charity], but by the very goodness, equity and sincerity of the will.

paras.t: Et in simplicitate cordis quærite illum : id est, corde simplici, non duplici, sine simulatione, fictione et perversa intentione, optate et studete Deo placere, conjungi, et in gratia, sapientia ac virtute proficere, omnia ordinando ad honorem gloriamque ipsius. Hinc enim in Ecclesiastico scriptum est : Ne accesseris ad Deum duplici corde. Christus quoque in Evangelio ait : Si oculus tuus nequam fuerit, id est, perversa intentio, totum corpus tuum tenebrosum erit. Et alibi ait Scriptura : Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei. Insuper, In simplicitate cordis quærite illum, id est, Deum cognoscere studeatis, per abstractionem et simplificationem intellectus vestri ab omni loco, tempore, corpulentia, imaginatione et materiali proprietate, ita ut sentiatis Deum simplicissimum esse, omnino immaterialem, indivisibilem, incircumscriptibilem, et infinite simpliciorem omni mente creata, angelica et humana.
paras.en: [[1:1|and seek him in simplicity of heart|Et in simplicitate cordis quærite illum]]: that is, with a simple heart, not a double one, without pretence, feigning and perverse intention, desire and strive to please God, to be joined to him, and to advance in grace, wisdom and virtue, ordering all things to his honour and glory. For hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 1:36|come not to him with a double heart|Ne accesseris ad Deum duplici corde]]. Christ too says in the Gospel: [[Matt 6:23|if thy eye be evil|Si oculus tuus nequam fuerit]], that is, a perverse intention, [[Matt 6:23|thy whole body shall be darksome|totum corpus tuum tenebrosum erit]]. And elsewhere Scripture says: [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei]]. Further, [[1:1|seek him in simplicity of heart|In simplicitate cordis quærite illum]]: that is, strive to know God by abstracting and simplifying your intellect from all place, time, bodiliness, imagination and material property, so that you perceive God to be most simple, wholly immaterial, indivisible, uncircumscribable, and infinitely simpler than every created mind, angelic and human.

paras.t: Quoniam invenitur ab his qui non tentant illum: quia tentare Deum, est species irreligiositatis, et contra illud : Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum. Porro, secundum Augustinum in libro contra Faustum, tentatio Dei consistit in hoc, quod homo ad evadendum aliquid mali, vel ad consequendum aliquid boni, prætermittit facere quod in se est. Idcirco, si quis omittat facere quod in se est ad obtinendam gratiam, opem seu illuminationem divinam, exspectans talia ex sola Dei provisione; Deum tentare censetur. Denique, tentare, est experimentum sumere de tentato : et ex ignorantia aut dubietate videtur procedere. Ideo aliquid agere vel postulare ad experiendum et explorandum providentiam seu omnipotentiam Dei, est Deum tentare, et contra reverentiam ejus. Idcirco sic quærens aut orans, non meretur exaudiri, sed magis repelli.
paras.en: [[1:2|For he is found by them that tempt him not|Quoniam invenitur ab his qui non tentant illum]]: because to tempt God is a species of irreligion, and is against that word: [[Deut 6:16|Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God|Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum]]. Further, according to Augustine in the book Against Faustus, the tempting of God consists in this, that a man, in order to escape some evil or to obtain some good, leaves undone what is in him to do [*facere quod in se est*, the schoolmen's phrase for doing all one can]. Therefore if anyone omits to do what is in him in order to obtain grace, help or divine enlightenment, expecting such things from God's providing alone, he is judged to tempt God. Lastly, to tempt is to make trial of the one tempted, and it seems to proceed from ignorance or doubt. Therefore to do or to ask something in order to try and probe the providence or the omnipotence of God is to tempt God, and is against the reverence due to him. Hence one who seeks or prays in this way does not deserve to be heard, but rather to be repelled.

paras.t: Apparet autem eis qui fidem habent in illum : id est, per exauditionis effectum, vel per secretorum revelationem, seu gratiosam illuminationem, ostendit suam benignitatem, providentiam ac potestatem, eis qui fide formata, id est per caritatem et actus virtuosos ornata, honorant, invocant, seu tendunt in ipsum. Hinc Salvator in Evangelio sæpius loquitur : Sicut credidisti, fiat tibi; et, Fides tua te salvam fecit; et, Omnia possibilia sunt credenti; itemque, Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis monti huic, Tolle te, et mittere in mare, et obediet vobis. Hinc scriptum est : Postulet in fide nihil hæsitans. Qui enim hæsitat, similis est fluctui maris, qui a vento movetur et circumfertur : non ergo æstimet homo ille, quod accipiat aliquid a Domino. Et alibi habetur : Ante orationem præpara animam tuam, et noli esse quasi homo tentans Deum.
paras.en: [[1:2|and he sheweth himself to them that have faith in him|Apparet autem eis qui fidem habent in illum]]: that is, through the effect of hearing their prayers, or through the revelation of secrets, or gracious enlightenment, he shows his kindness, providence and power to those who, with formed faith, that is, faith adorned with charity and virtuous acts, honour him, call upon him, or tend towards him. Hence the Saviour often says in the Gospel: [[Matt 8:13|as thou hast believed, so be it done to thee|Sicut credidisti, fiat tibi]] [the margin gives Matt. xviii, 13; the words are at Matt 8:13]; and, [[Matt 9:22|thy faith hath made thee whole|Fides tua te salvam fecit]]; and, [[Mark 9:22|all things are possible to him that believeth|Omnia possibilia sunt credenti]]; and again, [[Matt 17:19|if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain|Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis monti huic]], [[Mark 11:23|Be thou removed and be cast into the sea|Tolle te, et mittere in mare]][[Matt 21:21||]], and [[Luke 17:6|it would obey you|obediet vobis]] [Denis joins words from several Gospels here, as the margin's references show]. Hence it is written: [[Jas 1:6|let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea, which is moved and carried about by the wind|Postulet in fide nihil hæsitans. Qui enim hæsitat, similis est fluctui maris, qui a vento movetur et circumfertur]]: [[Jas 1:7|Therefore let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord|non ergo æstimet homo ille, quod accipiat aliquid a Domino]]. And elsewhere we have: [[Ecclus 18:23|Before prayer prepare thy soul: and be not as a man that tempteth God|Ante orationem præpara animam tuam, et noli esse quasi homo tentans Deum]].

paras.t: Perversæ enim cogitationes, videlicet dubitare de providentia Dei, et consimiles, quales sunt cogitationes tentantis Deum, separant, id est, mentem avertunt, a Deo : quia displicent ei, et veritati ac sapientiæ ejus contrariantur, sicque faciunt cogitantem a Deo distare, non loco sed dissimilitudine. Ideo scriptum est : Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter vos et Deum vestrum. Et alibi Dominus comminatur : Væ qui cogitatis inutile. Denuo et in Isaia hortatur : Auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum ab oculis meis.
paras.en: [[1:3|For perverse thoughts|Perversæ enim cogitationes]], namely, to doubt of God's providence, and the like, such as are the thoughts of one who tempts God, [[1:3|separate|separant]], that is, turn the mind away, [[1:3|from God|a Deo]]: because they displease him and are contrary to his truth and wisdom, and so make the one who thinks them to be far from God, not in place but by unlikeness. Therefore it is written: [[Is 59:2|your iniquities have divided between you and your God|Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter vos et Deum vestrum]]. And elsewhere the Lord threatens: [[Mich 2:1|Woe to you that devise that which is unprofitable|Væ qui cogitatis inutile]]. And again in Isaias he exhorts: [[Is 1:16|take away the evil of your devices from my eyes|Auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum ab oculis meis]] [*devise* and *devices* in these two places render *cogitatis* and *cogitationum*, the Latin of *thoughts* in the verse].

paras.t: Probata autem virtus corripit insipientes : id est, bene exercitata et approbata virtus, puta discretio, justitia, seu alia quævis, reddit hominem dignum ad increpandum imperitos, qui potius peccant ex ignorantia, aut infirmitate, seu vehementia passionis, quam ex proposito et habitu vitioso. Tales namque rationabili persuasione induci facilius possunt ad pœnitentiam et emendam : quia cessante passione, ignorantiave sublata, sæpe redeunt ad cor, seque emendant. Virtus quoque quanto perfectior, tanto plus inclinat ad caritativam et fraternam correptionem. Etenim quanto virtus fuerit major, tanto amplius vitia abhorret sibi contraria. Verumtamen hi qui ex habitu pravo, electione, et certa malitia peccant, aut vix, aut non, aut difficillime corriguntur. Ideo subditur :
paras.en: [[1:3|and his power, when it is tried, reproveth the unwise|Probata autem virtus corripit insipientes]] [Denis takes *virtus* as virtue, a good habit, and *probata* as proved, where the Douay-Rheims reads his power, when it is tried]: that is, virtue well exercised and approved, such as discretion, justice, or any other, makes a man worthy to rebuke the unskilled, who sin rather from ignorance, or weakness, or the vehemence of passion, than of set purpose and from a vicious habit. For such men can more easily be brought by reasonable persuasion to penance and amendment: because when the passion ceases, or the ignorance is taken away, they often return to their heart and amend themselves. Virtue too, the more perfect it is, the more it inclines to charitable and brotherly correction. For the greater virtue is, the more it abhors the vices contrary to it. But those who sin from a depraved habit, by choice and from certain malice [that is, knowingly and deliberately, not from ignorance or passion], are corrected scarcely, or not at all, or with the greatest difficulty. Therefore he adds:

paras.t: Quoniam in malevolam animam, cui placet ipsa malitia, et ex electione se vertit ad vitia, non introibit sapientia : illa præsertim quæ est donum Spiritus Sancti, et caritati inseparabiliter est conjuncta. Talis etiam anima non acquiescit salutari doctrinæ, neque correptionem admittit salubrem. Idcirco non eruditur, sed in suis manet perversitatibus atque erroribus. Ideo in Proverbiis dictum est : Qui diligit disciplinam, diligit scientiam; qui autem odit increpationes, insipiens est. Et alibi : Numquid non vestrum est scire judicium, qui odio habetis bonum?
paras.en: For [[1:4|into a malicious soul|in malevolam animam]], which takes pleasure in malice itself and by choice turns itself to vices, [[1:4|wisdom will not enter|non introibit sapientia]]: that wisdom above all which is a gift of the Holy Ghost and is inseparably joined to charity. Such a soul, too, does not assent to saving doctrine, nor does it admit wholesome correction. Therefore it is not taught, but remains in its perversities and errors. Hence it is said in the Proverbs: [[Prov 12:1|He that loveth correction, loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof, is foolish|Qui diligit disciplinam, diligit scientiam; qui autem odit increpationes, insipiens est]]. And elsewhere: [[Mich 3:1|Is it not your part to know judgment|Numquid non vestrum est scire judicium]], [[Mich 3:2|you that hate good|qui odio habetis bonum]]?

paras.t: Nec habitabit in corpore subdito peccatis, id est in homine vitioso, carnalibus inquinamentis concupiscentiisque subjecto, victo, oppresso. Talia quippe vitia præcipue mentem excæcant, et obtusum cor faciunt, hominemque assimilant brutis : imo fastidium pariunt divinorum, et causant acediam. Unde talis homo, nec a superiori potest illuminari ob suam superbiam, neque ab inferiori ob suam libidinem, nec ullum invenit in eo sapientia aditum. Hinc Dominus in Genesi contestatur : Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est. Nempe homo carnalis caro recte vocatur et corpus, sicut hoc loco : quia quæ carnis sunt sapit, non quæ Dei; et vilissima servitute subjectus est, servitque carni. Ideo loquitur Isaias : Quem docebit Dominus scientiam? Et respondet : Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere. Atque ut in Job asseritur : Sapientia non invenitur in terra suaviter viventium. Nam et Philosophus fatetur, quod vita carnalium sit brutalis. Unde et Rabanus : Frustra, inquit, sibi blandiuntur philosophi, et hæretici, ac falsi Christiani, quod sapientes existant. Soli enim mundi corde, sapientiam possunt accipere.
paras.en: [[1:4|nor dwell in a body subject to sins|Nec habitabit in corpore subdito peccatis]], that is, in a vicious man, subject to carnal defilements and lusts, overcome and oppressed by them. For such vices above all blind the mind and make the heart dull, and liken a man to the brutes: indeed they breed a distaste for divine things and cause acedia [that is, spiritual sloth, a sadness and weariness towards the things of God]. Hence such a man can neither be enlightened from above, because of his pride, nor from below, because of his lust, and wisdom finds no entrance in him. Hence the Lord solemnly declares in Genesis: [[Gen 6:3|My spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh|Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est]]. For the carnal man is rightly called flesh, and body, as in this place, because he is of those who [[Rom 8:5|mind the things that are of the flesh|quæ carnis sunt sapit]], not the things of God; and he is subject to the vilest servitude, and serves the flesh. Therefore Isaias says: [[Is 28:9|Whom shall he teach knowledge|Quem docebit Dominus scientiam]]? And he answers: [[Is 28:9|them that are weaned from the milk, that are drawn away from the breasts|Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere]]. And, as is asserted of wisdom in Job, [[Job 28:13|neither is it found in the land of them that live in delights|Sapientia non invenitur in terra suaviter viventium]]. For the Philosopher too acknowledges that the life of carnal men is brutish. Hence Rabanus too says: In vain do philosophers, heretics and false Christians flatter themselves that they are wise; for only the clean of heart can receive wisdom.

paras.t: Verumtamen attendendum, quod est quædam sapientia scholastica, acquisita, informis, et naturaliter adipiscibilis : quæ justis ac impiis est communis. Imo multi ambitiosi, libidinosi ac vitiosi, dicuntur et hoc modo sunt magni theologi et juristæ. Nec etiam prætacta sunt ita intelligenda, quasi iniqui pœnitere et converti nullatenus queant : sic enim esset desperandum de eis. Imo miseratione et gratiosa Omnipotentis (qui animarum optimus medicus est) præventione, possunt repente converti, ac taliter pœnitere ut ubi abundavit iniquitas, abundet et gratia : ita ut recte dicatur, Hæc mutatio dexteræ Excelsi. Verumtamen raro fit istud, et prædicta intelligenda sunt ad innuendum quam rara et difficilis sit talium vera conversio, ad naturales causas respiciendo. Juxta quem sensum scriptum est : Si potest Æthiops mutare pellem suam, et pardus varietates suas; et vos poteritis benefacere, quum didiceritis malum. Itaque vera et salutaris sapientia, quæ virtutibus est conjuncta, sine quibus nec prudentia esse valet, malevolam animam non introibit, quamdiu talis manet hujusmodi anima. Potest autem converti, sicque sapientiam veram sortiri. De qua Jacobus ait apostolus : Quæ desursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, deinde pacifica, modesta, suasibilis, bonis consentiens, plena misericordia et fructibus bonis.
paras.en: But it must be noted that there is a certain scholastic wisdom, acquired, unformed, and attainable by nature, which is common to the just and the wicked. Indeed many ambitious, lustful and vicious men are called great theologians and jurists, and in this way are so. Nor again is what was said above to be understood as though the wicked could in no way repent and be converted: for then one would have to despair of them. On the contrary, by the mercy and the gracious prevenience of the Almighty (who is the best physician of souls) [prevenience: grace going before and moving the will], they can be suddenly converted, and so repent that where iniquity abounded, grace too may abound[[Rom 5:20||]]: so that it may rightly be said, [[Ps 76:11|this is the change of the right hand of the most High|Hæc mutatio dexteræ Excelsi]]. Yet this happens rarely, and what was said above is to be understood as hinting how rare and difficult the true conversion of such men is, looking to natural causes. In which sense it is written: [[Jer 13:23|If the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots: you also may do well, when you have learned evil|Si potest Æthiops mutare pellem suam, et pardus varietates suas; et vos poteritis benefacere, quum didiceritis malum]]. And so true and saving wisdom, which is joined to the virtues, without which not even prudence can exist, [[1:4|will not enter into a malicious soul|malevolam animam non introibit]] as long as such a soul remains such. But it can be converted, and so obtain true wisdom; of which the apostle James says: [[Jas 3:17|the wisdom that is from above, first indeed is chaste, then peaceable, modest, easy to be persuaded, consenting to the good, full of mercy and good fruits|Quæ desursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, deinde pacifica, modesta, suasibilis, bonis consentiens, plena misericordia et fructibus bonis]].

paras.t: Denique, quod sapientia ista salubris infusa, non ingrediatur animam malitiosam sive malevolam, probat subdendo : Spiritus enim sanctus disciplinæ, id est Spiritus Sanctus, fons, causa, et doctor totius notitiæ disciplinalis, quæ dirigit, ordinat, seu reformat habentem. De quo Spiritu fertur in Psalmo : Verbo Domini cæli firmati sunt, et Spiritu oris ejus omnis virtus eorum ; et in libro Judicum sæpe, Factus est super eum Spiritus Domini ; et, Irruit in eum Spiritus Domini; in Job quoque, Spiritus Dei fecit me; itemque in Isaia, Et nunc Dominus misit me, et Spiritus ejus. In quibus utique verbis, inter Dominum et Spiritum ejus insinuatur distinctio, haud dubium quin personalis. Et quoniam ille qui perhibet ibi se missum, ad litteram intelligitur Christus, prout ex circumstantia textus probatur, in verbis illis tota superbeatissima innuitur Trinitas.
paras.en: Lastly, that this saving infused wisdom does not enter a malicious or malevolent soul, he proves by adding: [[1:5|For the Holy Spirit of discipline|Spiritus enim sanctus disciplinæ]], that is, the Holy Ghost, the fount, cause and teacher of all knowledge that disciplines [*disciplina*: teaching and the training it gives], which directs, orders or reforms the one who has it. Of which Spirit it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 32:6|By the word of the Lord the heavens were established; and all the power of them by the spirit of his mouth|Verbo Domini cæli firmati sunt, et Spiritu oris ejus omnis virtus eorum]]; and often in the book of Judges, [[Judg 11:29|the spirit of the Lord came upon|Factus est super eum Spiritus Domini]] him; and, [[Judg 14:19|the Spirit of the Lord came upon him|Irruit in eum Spiritus Domini]][[Judg 14:6||]][[Judg 15:14||]]; in Job too, [[Job 33:4|The spirit of God made me|Spiritus Dei fecit me]]; and again in Isaias, [[Is 48:16|and now the Lord God hath sent me, and his spirit|Et nunc Dominus misit me, et Spiritus ejus]]. In these words a distinction is certainly suggested between the Lord and his Spirit, and no doubt a personal one. And since he who there declares himself sent is understood literally to be Christ, as is proved from the context of the passage, in those words the whole most blessed Trinity is hinted at.

paras.t: Itaque, Spiritus sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum, id est, hominem simulatorem, hypocritam, versutum, duplicem corde inhabitare despiciet, quum ipse Spiritus Sanctus sit simplicissimus, sincerissimus, essentialiter sanctus, et Spiritus veritatis. Ideo fictus talis, est sibi omnino dissimilis, et præcipue displicens. Hinc Christus in Evangelio, contra hypocritas sæpissime atque acerrime sermocinatur; et de hypocrisi specialissime reprehendit Scribas et Pharisæos. Et maxime docet ut omnia pura agamus intentione, sinceroque animo, ad gloriam Dei, in vera humilitate, cupientes nesciri, quantum in nobis est, nisi ut præcepta publice impleamus ad Creatoris honorem, proximorumque ædificationem. Estque vitium istud tam grave, ut propter illud nec miserabilibus personis Dominus misereatur, juxta illud : Propter hoc super adolescentulis ejus non lætabitur Dominus, et pupillorum et viduarum ejus non miserebitur, quia omnis hypocrita est et nequam.
paras.en: So then, [[1:5|the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful|Spiritus sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum]], that is, will disdain to dwell in a man who is a dissembler, a hypocrite, crafty, double of heart; since the Holy Ghost himself is most simple, most sincere, holy by his essence, and the [[John 14:17|spirit of truth|Spiritus veritatis]][[John 15:26||]][[John 16:13||]]. Therefore such a feigner is wholly unlike him, and above all displeasing to him. Hence Christ in the Gospel speaks very often and very sharply against hypocrites[[Matt 6:1||]][[Matt 6:16||]][[Matt 7:3||]]; and most especially rebukes the Scribes and Pharisees for hypocrisy[[Matt 15:7||]][[Matt 22:18||]][[Matt 23:3||]][[Matt 23:13||]]. And above all he teaches that we do all things with a pure intention and a sincere mind, to the glory of God, in true humility, desiring to be unknown as far as lies in us, except that we fulfil the precepts publicly to the honour of the Creator and the edification of our neighbours[[Matt 6:1||]][[Matt 6:16||]][[Matt 23:8||]] [the margin cites whole passages in this paragraph: Matt. vi, 1–6, 16–18; vii, 3–5; xv, 7–8; xxii, 18–22; xxiii, 3–7, 13–36; and again vi, 1–6, 16–18; xxiii, 8–12; the first verse of each is marked]. And this vice is so grave that because of it the Lord does not have mercy even on pitiable persons, according to that word: [[Is 9:17|Therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men: neither shall he have mercy on their fatherless, and widows: for every one is a hypocrite and wicked|Propter hoc super adolescentulis ejus non lætabitur Dominus, et pupillorum et viduarum ejus non miserebitur, quia omnis hypocrita est et nequam]].

paras.t: Et auferet se a cogitationibus quæ sunt sine intellectu : id est, gratiam suam abstrahet ab habentibus cogitationes vanas, imperitas, et insensatas, quæ infinitæ Sapientiæ contrariantur, et displicent ei. Quæ protestatur : Ego Sapientia habito in consilio, et eruditis intersum cogitationibus. Quæ et in Evangelio ait quibusdam : Ut quid cogitatis mala in cordibus vestris?
paras.en: [[1:5|and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding|Et auferet se a cogitationibus quæ sunt sine intellectu]]: that is, he will withdraw his grace from those who have vain, unskilled and senseless thoughts, which are contrary to the infinite Wisdom and displease it. That Wisdom declares: [[Prov 8:12|I, wisdom, dwell in counsel, and am present in learned thoughts|Ego Sapientia habito in consilio, et eruditis intersum cogitationibus]]. The same Wisdom says to some in the Gospel: [[Matt 9:4|Why do you think evil in your hearts|Ut quid cogitatis mala in cordibus vestris]]?

paras.t: Et corripietur ipse fictus a superveniente iniquitate, id est, demerito suæ simulationis et duplicitatis permittetur in alia peccata incidere, secundum quod unum peccatum pondere suo trahit ad aliud. Sicque idem peccatum, est peccatum et pœna peccati, scilicet vitii præcedentis. Unde ait Apostolus : Propter quod tradidit illos Deus in passiones ignominiæ; et ipse Deus in Psalmo, Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum. Vel, Corripietur a superveniente iniquitate, id est, propter culpam sibi advenientem, debite punietur.
paras.en: [[1:5|and he shall not abide when iniquity cometh in|Et corripietur ipse fictus a superveniente iniquitate]] [Denis's text reads: *and the feigner himself shall be chastised by iniquity coming upon him*; the Douay-Rheims renders *corripietur* "he shall not abide"]: that is, for the demerit of his pretence and doubleness he will be allowed to fall into other sins, in that one sin by its own weight drags a man to another. And so the same sin is both a sin and the punishment of sin, namely of the vice that went before. Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 1:26|For this cause, God delivered them up to shameful affections|Propter quod tradidit illos Deus in passiones ignominiæ]]; and God himself in the Psalm: [[Ps 80:13|So I let them go according to the desires of their heart|Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum]]. Or: he shall be chastised [[1:5|when iniquity cometh in|a superveniente iniquitate]], that is, he will be duly punished for the guilt that comes upon him.

paras.t: Benignus est enim spiritus sapientiæ, id est Spiritus Sanctus dator et inspirator totius sapientiæ salutaris, sine quo nil possumus boni cogitare aut loqui, dicente Apostolo : Fiduciam talem habemus ad Deum, non quod simus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est; itemque, Nemo potest dicere, Dominus Jesus, nisi in Spiritu Sancto, id est cum attentione, ex caritatis affectu proferre. De quo scriptum est in Evangelio : Quum autem venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem. Qui etiam potest dici spiritus sapientiæ, id est Spiritus Christi, qui est virtus et Sapientia genita Dei Patris, a qua procedit sicut a Patre. Hic itaque spiritus sapientiæ benignus est, id est essentialiter pius et bonus, ignis æterni amoris, imo amor æternus.
paras.en: [[1:6|For the spirit of wisdom is benevolent|Benignus est enim spiritus sapientiæ]], that is, the Holy Ghost, the giver and inspirer of all saving wisdom, without whom we can think or speak nothing good, as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 3:4|such confidence we have|Fiduciam talem habemus]] [[2 Cor 3:4|towards God|ad Deum]]: [[2 Cor 3:5|Not that we are sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves: but our sufficiency is from God|non quod simus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est]]; and again, [[1 Cor 12:3|no man can say The Lord Jesus, but by the Holy Ghost|Nemo potest dicere, Dominus Jesus, nisi in Spiritu Sancto]], that is, utter it with attention, from the affection of charity. Of him it is written in the Gospel: [[John 16:13|when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will teach you all truth|Quum autem venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem]]. He can also be called the spirit of wisdom, that is, the Spirit of Christ, who is the power and the begotten Wisdom of God the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]], from whom he proceeds as from the Father. This spirit of wisdom, then, is benevolent, that is, by his essence kind and good, the fire of eternal love, nay, eternal Love itself.

paras.t: Et non liberabit maledicum a labiis suis, id est, hominem maledicum, detractorem, blasphemum, induratum, non eruet a vitiis suæ pestiferæ linguæ, nec a pœna æterna, quam pro ea meretur : quia communiter tales justo relinquit judicio. Unde et Christus in Evangelio asserit : Qui blasphemaverit in Spiritum Sanctum, non habet remissionem in hoc sæculo, neque in futuro. Sic enim quædam dicuntur irremissibilia crimina, quia raro et difficulter dimittuntur. Vel : Maledictum, id est culpa maledictionis prolatæ in aliquem, non liberabit a labiis suis, id est, non sinet hominem liberari a sententia damnationis labiorum Spiritus Sancti : quam proferet ipse Spiritus Sanctus contra maledicos, secundum illud Isaiæ : Labia Dei repleta sunt indignatione, Spiritus ejus velut torrens inundans ad perdendas gentes in nihilum; et rursus, Spiritu labiorum suorum interficiet impium.
paras.en: [[1:6|and will not acquit the evil speaker from his lips|Et non liberabit maledicum a labiis suis]], that is, he will not rescue the evil-speaking man, the detractor, the blasphemer, the hardened, from the vices of his pestilent tongue, nor from the eternal punishment which he deserves for it: because he commonly leaves such men to just judgment. Hence Christ too asserts in the Gospel: [[Mark 3:29|he that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost|Qui blasphemaverit in Spiritum Sanctum]] hath no forgiveness, [[Matt 12:32|neither in this world, nor in the world to come|in hoc sæculo, neque in futuro]]. For in this sense some crimes are called unforgivable, because they are rarely and with difficulty forgiven. Or: *the curse* [*maledictum*, read in place of *maledicum*, the evil speaker], that is, the guilt of a curse uttered against someone, [[1:6|will not acquit|non liberabit]] a man [[1:6|from his lips|a labiis suis]]: that is, it will not let a man be freed from the sentence of damnation of the lips of the Holy Ghost, which the Holy Ghost himself will pronounce against evil speakers, according to that saying of Isaias: [[Is 30:27|his lips are filled with indignation|Labia Dei repleta sunt indignatione]], [[Is 30:28|His breath as a torrent overflowing|Spiritus ejus velut torrens inundans]] [[Is 30:28|to destroy the nations unto nothing|ad perdendas gentes in nihilum]]; and again, [[Is 11:4|with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked|Spiritu labiorum suorum interficiet impium]] [*breath* in both places is *Spiritus* in the Latin].

paras.t: Quoniam renum illius, id est appetitionum sensualium ipsius maledicti, testis est Deus. Qui ait per Prophetam : Ego sum judex et testis. Ipse etenim omnia intuetur, et in judicio contra iniquum dat testimonium, ostendens se universa illius peccata conspexisse et nosse. Qui per alium Prophetam fatetur : Cognovi multa scelera vestra. Et cordis illius scrutator est verus, id est, Deus est infallibilis examinator et cognitor cogitationum affectionumque intellectualium hominis vitiosi. Qui, teste Apostolo, in futuro judicio revelabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium. Qui per Jeremiam loquitur : Pravum est cor hominis et inscrutabile : quis cognoscet illud? Ego Dominus scrutans cor, et probans renes, qui do unicuique juxta vias suas, et juxta fructum adinventionum suarum.
paras.en: For [[1:6|of his reins|renum illius]], that is, of the sensual appetites of that evil speaker, [[1:6|God is witness|testis est Deus]] [the reins, or kidneys, were held to be the seat of the desires]. He says by the Prophet: [[Jer 29:23|I am the judge and the witness|Ego sum judex et testis]]. For he beholds all things, and at the judgment gives testimony against the wicked man, showing that he has seen and known all his sins. He confesses by another Prophet: [[Amos 5:12|I know your manifold crimes|Cognovi multa scelera vestra]]. [[1:6|And he is a true searcher of his heart|Et cordis illius scrutator est verus]], that is, God is the unerring examiner and knower of the thoughts and intellectual affections of the vicious man. He, as the Apostle witnesses, at the judgment to come [[1 Cor 4:5|will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts|revelabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium]]. He says by Jeremias: [[Jer 17:9|The heart is perverse above all things, and unsearchable, who can know it|Pravum est cor hominis et inscrutabile : quis cognoscet illud]]? [[Jer 17:10|I am the Lord who search the heart, and prove the reins: who give to every one according to his way, and according to the fruit of his devices|Ego Dominus scrutans cor, et probans renes, qui do unicuique juxta vias suas, et juxta fructum adinventionum suarum]].

paras.t: Et linguæ ejus auditor, id est cognitor verborum maledicti præfati. Quemadmodum autem in nobis intellectus designatur nominibus sensuum exteriorum, ita in Deo, qui ait per Isaiam : Revelata sunt hæc in auribus meis (Domini exercituum). Et in Exodo dicitur : Clamor filiorum Israel venit ad me, et gemitum eorum audivi. Verumtamen, sicut Spiritus Sanctus dicitur corda scrutari ac investigare, non quasi ex ignorantia quadam rimando, aut quasi ardua ac difficilia sibi discutiendo et inquirendo, sicut homo dicitur Scripturas scrutari; sed quia omnia clarissime et profundissime ac diligentissime intuetur, juxta illud Apostoli, Spiritus scrutatur omnia, etiam profunda Dei : sic dicitur verba audire, non quasi ab extra percipiendo, sed intra æternaliter ac invariabiliter inspiciendo ac prænoscendo : nec mirum, quum ipse sit Deus. Ideo subditur :
paras.en: [[1:6|and a hearer of his tongue|Et linguæ ejus auditor]], that is, the knower of the words of the aforesaid evil speaker. Now just as in us the understanding is designated by the names of the outward senses, so too in God, who says by Isaias: [[Is 5:9|These things are in my ears|Revelata sunt hæc in auribus meis]] (the ears of the Lord of hosts) [the margin gives Is. v, 9; Denis's *revelata sunt*, "are revealed", is nearer Is 22:14, "the voice of the Lord of hosts was revealed in my ears"]. And in Exodus it is said: [[Ex 3:9|the cry of the children of Israel is come unto me|Clamor filiorum Israel venit ad me]], and [[Ex 6:5|I have heard the groaning|gemitum eorum audivi]] of them. Yet, just as the Holy Ghost is said to search and investigate hearts, not as though probing out of some ignorance, or as though examining and inquiring into things hard and difficult for him, as a man is said to search the Scriptures, but because he beholds all things most clearly, most deeply and most attentively, according to that saying of the Apostle, [[1 Cor 2:10|the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God|Spiritus scrutatur omnia, etiam profunda Dei]]: so he is said to hear words, not as though perceiving them from without, but by beholding and foreknowing them within, eternally and unchangeably; and no wonder, since he is God. Therefore he adds:

paras.t: Quoniam spiritus Domini replevit orbem terrarum. Sua etenim majestate incircumscripta implet ac penetrat omnia, juxta illud: Numquid non cœlum et terram ego impleo? dicit Dominus. Omnia quoque per ejus sapientiam sunt formata, secundum quod in Genesi legitur: Spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas; et alibi, Spiritus Domini ornavit cœlos. Rursus: Replevit orbem terrarum, id est mundum inferiorem, variis rebus, speciebus, animalibus mixtis, et necessariis vitæ, sicut fertur in Psalmo: Impleta est terra possessione tua. Etiam per alium Prophetam dicitur: Respexit terram, et implevit eam pecudibus. — Spiritualiter demum replevit orbem terrarum, id est habitantes ubique per gyrum terræ, seu Ecclesiam toto orbe terrarum diffusam, variis gratiæ donis, præsertim sub evangelica lege, cujus tempus dicitur tempus gratiæ. Unde ait Apostolus: Alii per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ, alii gratia sanitatum, alii operatio virtutum, alii genera linguarum, alii discretio spirituum, alii interpretatio sermonum: hæc omnia operatur unus atque idem Spiritus, dividens singulis prout vult. Hoc in beatissimis Apostolis et primitiva Ecclesia cœptum est fieri in Jerusalem, prout in Actis recitatur. Sed et bona naturæ, dona fortunæ, necessaria vitæ, sunt ab eo.
paras.en: [[1:7|For the Spirit of the Lord hath filled the whole world|Quoniam spiritus Domini replevit orbem terrarum]]. For by his uncircumscribed majesty he fills and penetrates all things, according to that: [[Jer 23:24|do not I fill heaven and earth, saith the Lord?|Numquid non cœlum et terram ego impleo? dicit Dominus]] All things too were formed through his wisdom, as we read in Genesis: [[Gen 1:2|the spirit of God moved over the waters|Spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas]]; and elsewhere: [[Job 26:13|His spirit hath adorned the heavens|Spiritus Domini ornavit cœlos]]. Again: [[1:7|hath filled the whole world|Replevit orbem terrarum]], that is, the lower world, with various things, species, animals and mixed bodies, and the necessaries of life, as is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 103:24|the earth is filled with thy riches|Impleta est terra possessione tua]]. By another Prophet too it is said: He looked upon the earth, and [[Bar 3:32|filled it with cattle|implevit eam pecudibus]] [the margin gives Baruch iii, 32, which has "filled it with cattle"; the words "he looked upon the earth" recall Ecclus 16:30, "God looked upon the earth, and filled it with his goods"]. — Spiritually, lastly, he [[1:7|hath filled the whole world|replevit orbem terrarum]], that is, those who dwell everywhere throughout the circle of the earth, or the Church spread throughout the whole world, with the various gifts of grace, especially under the law of the Gospel, whose time is called the time of grace. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 12:8|To one indeed, by the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom: and to another, the word of knowledge|Alii per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ]], [[1 Cor 12:9|to another, the grace of healing|alii gratia sanitatum]], [[1 Cor 12:10|To another the working of miracles|alii operatio virtutum]], [[1 Cor 12:10|to another, diverse kinds of tongues|alii genera linguarum]], [[1 Cor 12:10|to another, the discerning of spirits|alii discretio spirituum]], [[1 Cor 12:10|to another, interpretation of speeches|alii interpretatio sermonum]]: [[1 Cor 12:11|all these things, one and the same Spirit worketh, dividing to every one according as he will|hæc omnia operatur unus atque idem Spiritus, dividens singulis prout vult]]. This began to come about in the most blessed Apostles and the primitive Church at Jerusalem, as is related in the Acts. But the goods of nature too, the gifts of fortune, the necessaries of life, are from him.

paras.t: Et hoc quod continet omnia, id est, Spiritus Sanctus omnem in se perfectionem comprehendens, in quo omnia causaliter exemplariterque consistunt, relucent ac continentur tanquam in creatore, et quod cuncta conservat in esse, sine cujus manutenentia nec ad momentum possent durare, scientiam habet vocis, id est, omnia quæ proferuntur per linguam, agnoscit. Scientiam quoque linguarum confert, ut in Apostolis multisque aliis patuit: quibus repente concessit facultatem loquendi omnium linguis, notitiam etiam intelligendi idiomata cuncta. Qui et olim in ædificatione Babyloniæ turris linguas confudit, et ineffabiliter novas instituit. Vel: Hoc quod continet omnia, id est, homo habens aliquid commune cum omni creatura. Propter quod in Evangelio homo, omnis creatura vocatur, quum dicitur: Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ. Nempe cum Deo et angelis in intellectuali perfectione communicat; cum brutis, in sensitiva; cum terræ nascentibus, in vegetativa; cum elementis et mixtis inanimatis, in esse. Scientiam habet vocis, id est facultatem loquendi atque peritiam: et sicut jam tactum est, supernaturaliter a Spiritu Sancto accepit facultatem notitiamque linguarum, atque intelligentiam Scripturarum, quemadmodum Paulus fatetur: Gratias ago Deo, quod omnium vestrum linguis loquor.
paras.en: [[1:7|and that which containeth all things|Et hoc quod continet omnia]], that is, the Holy Ghost, who comprehends in himself every perfection, in whom all things consist, shine forth and are contained causally and exemplarily [that is, as in their cause and as in their pattern], as in their creator, and who preserves all things in being, without whose upholding they could not last even for a moment, [[1:7|hath knowledge of the voice|scientiam habet vocis]], that is, knows all things that are uttered by the tongue. He also confers the knowledge of tongues, as was plain in the Apostles and many others, to whom he suddenly granted the power of speaking in the tongues of all, and also the knowledge to understand every idiom[[Acts 2:4||]]. He it was who once, at the building of the tower of Babylon, confounded the tongues, and in a manner beyond words established new ones[[Gen 11:7||]]. Or: [[1:7|that which containeth all things|Hoc quod continet omnia]], that is, man, who has something in common with every creature. For this reason man is called every creature in the Gospel, where it is said: [[Mark 16:15|preach the gospel to every creature|Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ]]. For he shares with God and the angels in intellectual perfection; with the brutes, in the sensitive; with the things that spring from the earth, in the vegetative; with the elements and inanimate mixed bodies, in being. [[1:7|hath knowledge of the voice|Scientiam habet vocis]], that is, the faculty and skill of speaking: and, as was touched on already, he received supernaturally from the Holy Ghost the faculty and knowledge of tongues, and the understanding of the Scriptures, as Paul confesses: [[1 Cor 14:18|I thank my God I speak with all your tongues|Gratias ago Deo, quod omnium vestrum linguis loquor]].

paras.t: Propter hoc qui loquitur iniqua, non potest latere Deum omnia cognoscentem. Qui per Jeremiam prophetam ait: Putasne Deus e vicino ego sum, et non Deus de longe? Si occultabitur vir in absconditis, et ego non videbo eum? Nec præteriet illum corripiens judicium: id est, Deus districte omnia judicans, non deseret illum impunitum, quum et Christus in Evangelio protestetur: De omni verbo otioso quod locuti fuerint homines, reddent de eo rationem in die judicii. Et denuo: Ex verbis tuis, inquit, damnaberis. Unde et in Job asseritur: Deus inultum abire non patitur. Contra quod stulti in Isaia præsumunt, dicentes: Flagellum inundans quum transierit, non veniet super nos.
paras.en: [[1:8|Therefore he that speaketh unjust things, cannot be hid|Propter hoc qui loquitur iniqua, non potest latere]] from God, who knows all things; who says by Jeremias the prophet: [[Jer 23:23|Am I, think ye, a God at hand|Putasne Deus e vicino ego sum]], [[Jer 23:23|and not a God afar off?|et non Deus de longe?]] [[Jer 23:24|Shall a man be hid in secret places, and I not see him|Si occultabitur vir in absconditis, et ego non videbo eum?]]? [[1:8|neither shall the chastising judgment pass him by|Nec præteriet illum corripiens judicium]]: that is, God, who judges all things strictly, will not let him go unpunished; for Christ too declares in the Gospel: [[Matt 12:36|every idle word that men shall speak, they shall render an account for it in the day of judgment|De omni verbo otioso quod locuti fuerint homines, reddent de eo rationem in die judicii]]. And again: [[Matt 12:37|by thy words|Ex verbis tuis]], he says, [[Matt 12:37|thou shalt be condemned|damnaberis]]. Hence it is asserted in Job too: [[Job 24:12|God doth not suffer it to pass unrevenged|Deus inultum abire non patitur]]. Against which the foolish in Isaias presume, saying: [[Is 28:15|When the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come upon us|Flagellum inundans quum transierit, non veniet super nos]].

paras.t: In cogitationibus enim impii interrogatio erit: id est, cogitationes iniquorum Deus in judicio discutiet, judicabit, ac puniet: juxta illud, Dominus interrogat justum et impium; et rursus, Oculi Domini super facientes mala. Unde per Isaiam protestatur: Ego autem cogitationes eorum venio ut congregem. Sermonum autem illius auditio ad Deum veniet: id est, Deus per justam sententiam ac vindictam, ostendet se audisse et scire verba iniqui. Qui in Genesi locutus est: Clamor Sodomorum venit ad me. Atque ad Cain: Vox, inquit, sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me. Et ad correptionem iniquitatum illius, id est, auditio sermonum iniqui ad hoc ad Deum perveniet, ut ab eo debite puniatur cum vitiis sibi annexis. Vel sensus est, quod Deus suo justo judicio veniet ad iniquum, ad puniendum iniquitates ipsius, quemadmodum per Sophoniam disseruit: Disperdam eos qui avertuntur de post tergum Domini, et qui Dominum non exquisierunt.
paras.en: [[1:9|For inquisition shall be made into the thoughts of the ungodly|In cogitationibus enim impii interrogatio erit]]: that is, God in the judgment will examine, judge and punish the thoughts of the wicked; according to that: [[Ps 10:6|The Lord trieth the just and the wicked|Dominus interrogat justum et impium]] [the Latin has *interrogat*, "questions", answering to the *interrogatio*, "inquisition", of the text]; and again: [[Ps 33:17|the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things|Oculi Domini super facientes mala]] [Denis says "the eyes of the Lord", the words of Ps 33:16; the margin notes *Vultus*, "countenance", the reading of v. 17]. Hence he declares by Isaias: [[Is 66:18|But I know their works, and their thoughts: I come that I may gather them|Ego autem cogitationes eorum venio ut congregem]] [Denis leaves out "works"]. [[1:9|and the hearing of his words shall come to God|Sermonum autem illius auditio ad Deum veniet]]: that is, God, by his just sentence and vengeance, will show that he has heard and knows the words of the wicked man. He it is who spoke in Genesis: [[Gen 18:20|The cry of Sodom|Clamor Sodomorum]] [[Gen 18:21|is come to me|venit ad me]]. And to Cain: [[Gen 4:10|the voice|Vox]], he says, [[Gen 4:10|of thy brother's blood crieth to me|sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me]]. [[1:9|to the chastising of his iniquities|Et ad correptionem iniquitatum illius]]: that is, the hearing of the wicked man's words will reach God to this end, that he may be duly punished, together with the vices bound up with him. Or the sense is that God by his just judgment will come to the wicked man, to punish his iniquities, as he declared by Sophonias: I will destroy [[Soph 1:6|them that turn away from following after the Lord, and that have not sought the Lord|qui avertuntur de post tergum Domini, et qui Dominum non exquisierunt]].

paras.t: Quoniam auris zeli audit omnia, id est intellectus Dei zelantis, id est vehementer amantis animarum salutem, et contra vitia æmulantis, universa cognoscit. Hinc Deus vocatur zelotes, et amor, ac zelus: qui est essentialiter caritas est; et in quo idem sunt, zelans, ac zelus. Qui in Exodo fatetur: Ego sum Dominus Deus fortis, zelotes. Et tumultus, id est inquietudo, murmurationum non abscondetur: quia in judicio manifestabitur, ac graviter punietur, quantumcumque nunc occultetur.
paras.en: [[1:10|For the ear of jealousy heareth all things|Quoniam auris zeli audit omnia]], that is, the understanding of God, who is jealous [Latin *zelus*, both "jealousy" and "zeal"], that is, who vehemently loves the salvation of souls and is zealous against vices, knows all things. Hence God is called jealous[[Ex 34:14||]], and love[[1 John 4:8||]][[1 John 4:16||]], and zeal: for he is essentially charity, and in him the one who is zealous and zeal are the same. He confesses in Exodus: [[Ex 20:5|I am the Lord thy God, mighty, jealous|Ego sum Dominus Deus fortis, zelotes]]. [[1:10|and the tumult|Et tumultus]], that is, the disquiet, [[1:10|of murmuring shall not be hid|murmurationum non abscondetur]]: because in the judgment it will be made manifest and grievously punished, however hidden it may be now.

paras.t: Custodite ergo vos a murmuratione, id est, eam diligenter vitate, quæ nihil prodest. Imo et plurimum obest; atque tam grave peccatum est, ut asserat Augustinus quod populus Israel nullo peccato legitur Deum tam graviter offendisse ut murmurando. Ideo ait Apostolus: Neque murmuraveritis, sicut quidam illorum murmuraverunt, et a serpentibus perierunt. Christus quoque perversis in Evangelio loquens: Murmuratores, inquit, filii murmuratorum, implete mensuram patrum vestrorum. Nec solum enorme est contra Deum, sed etiam contra ejus vicarios ex impatientia murmurare, quum Moyses murmurantibus contra se et Aaron, dicat in Exodo: Non contra nos est murmur vestrum, sed contra Dominum. Et alibi legitur: Ortum est murmur populi, quasi dolentium pro labore: quod quum audisset Dominus, iratus est, et accensus est in eos ignis Domini. Si tam dire ac subito sunt plagati, qui itinere longo confecti ac lassi, murmuraverunt: quid damnationis imminet eis qui pro levi ac modica murmurant causa, imo frequenter pro non causa, hoc est omnino irrationabiliter, ex sua gulositate, elatione, impatientia? sicut de quibusdam in Psalmo fertur: Si vero non fuerint saturati, et murmurabunt. Advertant hi quod Dominus in libro Numerorum dixit: Omnes qui murmurastis contra me, non intrabitis terram super quam levavi manum meam, ut darem eam vobis.
paras.en: [[1:11|Keep yourselves, therefore, from murmuring|Custodite ergo vos a murmuratione]], that is, shun it carefully, [[1:11|which profiteth nothing|quæ nihil prodest]]. Nay, it does a great deal of harm; and it is so grave a sin that Augustine asserts that the people of Israel is not read to have offended God so grievously by any sin as by murmuring. Therefore the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 10:10|Neither do you murmur, as some of them murmured|Neque murmuraveritis, sicut quidam illorum murmuraverunt]], and perished by serpents[[Num 21:6||]] [these last words are from 1 Cor 10:9; v. 10 ends "were destroyed by the destroyer"]. Christ too, speaking to the perverse in the Gospel, says: Murmurers, sons of murmurers, [[Matt 23:32|Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers|implete mensuram patrum vestrorum]] [the words "murmurers, sons of murmurers" are not in the Gospel text; cf. Matt 23:31, "you are the sons of them that killed the prophets"]. Nor is it a monstrous thing to murmur against God only, but also against his vicars, out of impatience; for Moses says in Exodus to those who murmured against himself and Aaron: [[Ex 16:8|your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord|Non contra nos est murmur vestrum, sed contra Dominum]]. And elsewhere we read: [[Num 11:1|there arose a murmuring of the people|Ortum est murmur populi]], [[Num 11:1|as it were repining at their fatigue|quasi dolentium pro labore]]: [[Num 11:1|And when the Lord heard it he was angry|quod quum audisset Dominus, iratus est]], [[Num 11:1|And the fire of the Lord being kindled against them|et accensus est in eos ignis Domini]]. If those who murmured, worn out and weary from a long journey, were struck so dreadfully and so suddenly, what damnation hangs over those who murmur for a slight and trifling cause, nay often for no cause, that is, wholly unreasonably, out of their gluttony, pride, impatience? as is said of some in the Psalm: [[Ps 58:16|shall murmur if they be not filled|Si vero non fuerint saturati, et murmurabunt]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxvii, 16; the words are Ps 58:16]. Let these mark what the Lord said in the book of Numbers: [[Num 14:29|All you|Omnes]] that [[Num 14:29|have murmured against me|murmurastis contra me]], [[Num 14:30|Shall not enter into the land, over which I lifted up my hand|non intrabitis terram super quam levavi manum meam]] to give it you.

paras.t: Et a detractione parcite linguæ, id est, linguas vestras non polluatis, nec ad supplicia obligetis, obloquendo per eas. Per quæ enim quis peccat, per hæc et punitur. Unde hortatur et Apostolus, ut non exhibeamus membra nostra arma iniquitatis peccato. Verumtamen a detractione præsertim parcendum est animæ, ne æternaliter condemnetur. Est enim detractio valde enorme crimen, et gravius rapina ac furto. Atque, ut ait Bernardus, Lingua detractoris est gladius biceps, occidens non solum animam detrahentis, sed etiam audientis: imo et quantum in se est, animam quoque ejus cui obloquitur, cui dat occasionem invidiæ contra se, quum perceperit sibi esse detractum. Contra hoc pessimum virus, dicta sunt multa super Proverbia. In quibus inter cetera Salomon ait: Cum detractoribus ne commiscearis, quia repente consurget perditio eorum; et denuo, Qui detrahit alicui rei, ipse in futurum se obligat. Itaque qui detrahit, non parcit, sed crudelis est linguæ, quia abutitur ea, et ei injuriatur, sicut et is qui per alia membra peccat. Hinc apostolus Jacobus, ad probandum quam grave sit uti lingua perverse in maledicendo aut obloquendo, utitur exemplo naturæ, dicendo: Numquid fons ex eodem foramine emanat dulcem et amaram aquam? Numquid potest, fratres mei, ficus uvas facere, aut vitis ficus? Et iterum asserit: Qui detrahit fratri, detrahit legi.
paras.en: [[1:11|and refrain your tongue from detraction|Et a detractione parcite linguæ]] [literally "spare the tongue from detraction": Denis's gloss turns on this], that is, do not defile your tongues, nor bind them over to punishment, by speaking ill through them. For [[Wis 11:17|by what things a man sinneth, by the same also he is tormented|Per quæ enim quis peccat, per hæc et punitur]]. Hence the Apostle too exhorts us not to yield our members as instruments of iniquity unto sin[[Rom 6:13||]]. Yet from detraction it is above all the soul that must be spared, lest it be condemned eternally. For detraction is an exceedingly monstrous crime, and graver than robbery and theft. And, as Bernard says, the tongue of the detractor is a two-edged sword, killing not only the soul of the detractor but also that of the hearer; nay, as far as in it lies, the soul too of him who is spoken against, to whom it gives occasion of ill will against himself when he perceives that he has been detracted. Against this most evil poison much was said on Proverbs [that is, in Denis's commentary on Proverbs]. In which, among other things, Solomon says: [[Prov 24:21|have nothing to do with detractors|Cum detractoribus ne commiscearis]], [[Prov 24:22|For their destruction shall rise suddenly|quia repente consurget perditio eorum]]; and again: [[Prov 13:13|Whosoever speaketh ill of any thing, bindeth himself for the time to come|Qui detrahit alicui rei, ipse in futurum se obligat]]. So he who detracts does not spare his tongue, but is cruel to it, because he abuses it and wrongs it, just as he does who sins through his other members. Hence the apostle James, to prove how grave a thing it is to use the tongue perversely in cursing or speaking ill, uses an example from nature, saying: [[Jas 3:11|Doth a fountain send forth, out of the same hole, sweet and bitter water?|Numquid fons ex eodem foramine emanat dulcem et amaram aquam?]] [[Jas 3:12|Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear grapes? Or the vine, figs?|Numquid potest, fratres mei, ficus uvas facere, aut vitis ficus?]] And again he asserts: [[Jas 4:11|He that detracteth his brother|Qui detrahit fratri]], [[Jas 4:11|detracteth the law|detrahit legi]].

paras.t: Quoniam sermo obscurus, id est in occulto prolatus, ut est detractio; vel, Obscurus, id est vitiosus, utpote luce justitiæ veritateque carens; vel, Obscurus, id est sophisticus, et quodammodo veritatis colore opertus, quum sit fallax aut falsus; in vacuum non ibit, id est, sine pondere culpæ non profertur, nec carebit gravamine pœnæ. Os autem quod mentitur mendacio pernicioso, quod intentione nocendi pronuntiatur, occidit animam occisione peccati. De qua ait Salvator: Dimitte mortuos sepelire mortuos suos; atque Ezechiel, Mortificabant animas quæ non moriuntur. Hinc ait Psalmista: Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium. Et præsertim iniquum est mentiri in foro judicii, falsum testimonium perhibendo. Imo et reus mortaliter peccat, veritatem negando judici, a quo pro suo excessu est occidendus: ita quod nec timor mortis eum excusat a mortali peccato in tali mendacio. Quanto magis, qui extra talem casum mendaciter se excusant? Porro mendacium jocosum, et item officiosum, venialia sunt ex genere suo: quæ tamen cum tanta complacentia aut assuefactione possent proferri, quod essent mortalia. Præterea, quamvis dictum sit, Os quod mentitur, occidit animam; aptius tamen dici potest, quod anima per oris sui abusum ac mentitionem occidit se ipsam. Ipsa namque per rationem tenetur membra ac organa sui corporis refrenare ac gubernare.
paras.en: [[1:11|for an obscure speech|Quoniam sermo obscurus]], that is, one uttered in secret, as detraction is; or, *obscure*, that is, vicious, as lacking the light of justice and truth; or, *obscure*, that is, sophistical, and in some way covered with the colour of truth, though it is deceitful or false, [[1:11|shall not go for nought|in vacuum non ibit]] [literally "shall not go into the void"], that is, it is not uttered without the weight of guilt, nor will it lack the burden of punishment. [[1:11|and the mouth that belieth|Os autem quod mentitur]] with a pernicious lie [that is, a lie told to do harm], which is uttered with the intention of harming, [[1:11|killeth the soul|occidit animam]] with the killing of sin. Of which the Saviour says: [[Matt 8:22|let the dead bury their dead|Dimitte mortuos sepelire mortuos suos]]; and Ezechiel: [[Ezech 13:19|to kill souls which should not die|Mortificabant animas quæ non moriuntur]]. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 5:7|thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie|Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium]]. And it is especially wicked to lie in the court of justice, by bearing false witness. Nay, even the accused sins mortally by denying the truth to the judge by whom he is to be put to death for his offence: so that not even the fear of death excuses him from mortal sin in such a lie. How much more those who excuse themselves by lying outside such a case? Moreover, the jocose lie [that is, one told in jest], and likewise the officious lie [that is, a lie told to help someone or avert harm, not a malicious one], are venial of their kind; yet they could be uttered with such complacency or habit that they would be mortal. Further, though it is said, [[1:11|the mouth that belieth, killeth the soul|Os quod mentitur, occidit animam]], it can more aptly be said that the soul, by the abuse and lying of its mouth, kills itself. For it is bound by reason to bridle and govern the members and organs of its body.

paras.t: Nolite zelare mortem in errore vitæ vestræ: id est, non ametis mortem culpæ vivendo erronee; nec etiam desideretis aut vobis ipsis inferatis mortem corporalem ex impatientia propter vitæ præsentis adversa, aut ex irrationabili tædio vitæ, aut quasi putantes per mortem corporalem pœnas vitare, quasi anima sit mortalis, quum post vitam præsentem sequantur multo graviora supplicia, maxime eos qui sibi ipsis sacrilegas injiciunt manus. Neque acquiratis perditionem in operibus manuum vestrarum, id est, nolite damnationem mereri per opera vitiosa. Et per manus, intelligenda sunt cetera membra operativa, seu potius operativæ potentiæ. Similiter per opera, subintelligendæ sunt omissiones operandorum.
paras.en: [[1:12|Seek not death in the error of your life|Nolite zelare mortem in errore vitæ vestræ]] [Latin *zelare*, "to be zealous for", "to love eagerly"]: that is, do not love the death of guilt by living in error; nor yet desire or inflict on yourselves bodily death, out of impatience at the adversities of the present life, or from an unreasonable weariness of life, or as if thinking to escape punishments through bodily death, as though the soul were mortal; since after the present life far graver torments follow, above all for those who lay sacrilegious hands on themselves. [[1:12|neither procure ye destruction by the works of your hands|Neque acquiratis perditionem in operibus manuum vestrarum]], that is, do not merit damnation by sinful works. And by *hands* are to be understood the other members that work, or rather the operative powers. Likewise by *works* are to be understood also the omissions of things that ought to be done.

paras.t: Quoniam Deus mortem non fecit. Certum est quod mortem culpæ Deus non fecit: quæ mors est formaliter ipsum peccatum, quod non est aliquid positivum, quantum ad suam deformitatem, nec est a Deo, sed a voluntate perversa. Voluntas namque creata et libera, in quantum ex nihilo, habet ut possit deficere et peccare. Mortem vero corporalem (quæ non est nisi privatio seu terminus vitæ, aut separatio animæ a corpore) Deus non fecit directe, sed potius concomitanter, quia per accidens sequitur vitam in mixtis: nec est proprie aliquid positivum, sed quædam destructio aut expulsio formæ. Unde mors aliquo modo a Deo est, quum in Ecclesiastico scriptum sit: Mors et vita a Deo est. Verumtamen, in quantum mors est pœna peccati, directe a Deo est, qui testatur: Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam. Respiciendo autem ad primam hominis institutionem, qua Deus instituit eum taliter immortalem, quod nisi peccaret, non moreretur, Deus mortem directe non fecit, quum scriptum sit: Deus creavit hominem inexterminabilem. Mortem vero damnationis æternæ (quæ est malum pœnale) Deus fecit et infert, sicut et cetera mala pure pœnalia, quum per Prophetam affirmet: Ego Dominus faciens pacem, et creans malum. Unde et alius ait Propheta: Si erit malum in civitate quod Dominus non fecerit? Et apud Jonam dicitur: Misertus est Dominus super malitiam quam locutus fuerat ut faceret eis, et non fecit.
paras.en: [[1:13|For God made not death|Quoniam Deus mortem non fecit]]. It is certain that God did not make the death of guilt, which death is formally sin itself; and sin is not anything positive as regards its deformity, nor is it from God, but from a perverse will. For a created and free will, inasmuch as it is from nothing, has it in it that it can fail and sin. Bodily death (which is nothing but the privation or end of life, or the separation of the soul from the body) God did not make directly, but rather concomitantly [that is, as something that comes along with what he does make], because it follows life by accident in mixed bodies [that is, bodies compounded of the elements]; nor is it properly anything positive, but a certain destruction or expulsion of the form. Hence death is in some way from God, since it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 11:14|life and death|Mors et vita]] [[Ecclus 11:14|are from God|a Deo est]]. Yet inasmuch as death is the punishment of sin, it is directly from God, who testifies: [[Deut 32:39|I will kill and I will make to live|Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam]]. But looking to the first institution of man, in which God made him immortal in such a way that, unless he sinned, he would not die, God did not make death directly, since it is written: [[Wis 2:23|God created man incorruptible|Deus creavit hominem inexterminabilem]]. But the death of eternal damnation (which is an evil of punishment) God made and inflicts, as he does the other evils that are purely penal, since he affirms by the Prophet: [[Is 45:7|I the Lord|Ego Dominus]], [[Is 45:7|I make peace, and create evil|faciens pacem, et creans malum]]. Hence another Prophet too says: [[Amos 3:6|Shall there be evil in a city, which the Lord hath not done?|Si erit malum in civitate quod Dominus non fecerit?]] And in Jonas it is said: [[Jon 3:10|God had mercy with regard to the evil which he had said that he would do to them, and he did it not|Misertus est Dominus super malitiam quam locutus fuerat ut faceret eis, et non fecit]].

paras.t: Nec lætatur in perditione vivorum, id est in morte seu damnatione viventium, in quantum sunt viventes, seu homines salutis capaces, et creaturæ ipsius. Imo sic vult omnes homines salvos fieri. Et per Ezechielem locutus est: Numquid voluntatis meæ est mors impii, et non magis ut convertatur, et vivat? Verumtamen, in quantum vivi sunt impii, obstinati ac reprobi, sic Deus zelo justitiæ lætatur in eorum perditione, sicut et justus lætabitur quum viderit vindictam. Propter quod in Proverbiis ait: Ego quoque in interitu vestro ridebo, et subsannabo, quum vobis quod timebatis, evenerit; et alibi, Complebo furorem meum in eis, et consolabor.
paras.en: [[1:13|neither hath he pleasure in the destruction of the living|Nec lætatur in perditione vivorum]], that is, in the death or damnation of the living, inasmuch as they are living, that is, men capable of salvation, and his creatures. Nay, in this sense he [[1 Tim 2:4|will have all men to be saved|vult omnes homines salvos fieri]]. And by Ezechiel he spoke: [[Ezech 18:23|Is it my will that a sinner should die|Numquid voluntatis meæ est mors impii]], [[Ezech 18:23|and not that he should be converted from his ways, and live?|et non magis ut convertatur, et vivat?]] Yet inasmuch as the living are wicked, obstinate and reprobate, in this sense God, out of zeal for justice, takes pleasure in their destruction, even as [[Ps 57:11|the just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge|justus lætabitur quum viderit vindictam]]. For which reason he says in Proverbs: [[Prov 1:26|I also will laugh in your destruction, and will mock when that shall come to you which you feared|Ego quoque in interitu vestro ridebo, et subsannabo, quum vobis quod timebatis, evenerit]]; and elsewhere: [[Ezech 5:13|I will accomplish my fury|Complebo furorem meum]] in them, [[Ezech 5:13|and I will be comforted|et consolabor]].

paras.t: Creavit enim, ut essent, omnia: id est, cuncta originaliter produxit ex nihilo, ut unumquodque esset et permaneret juxta cursum suæ periodi, sicut de homine sanctus Job loquitur Deo: Constituisti terminos ejus, qui præteriri non poterunt. Quædam vero produxit incorruptibilia et immortalia, ut angelos ac animas rationales, atque cœlestia corpora, ac elementa: ita quod, quoad se tota, corrumpi non valent. Mixta vero fecit ut essent, directa intentione; sed corruptio concomitatur conditionem eorum. Et quæ in se ipsis perpetuari non queunt, voluit per successionem perpetuum esse sortiri: ut sic omnia aliquo modo divinum esse participent, ut etiam docet Philosophus.
paras.en: [[1:14|For he created all things that they might be|Creavit enim, ut essent, omnia]]: that is, he brought forth all things in their origin out of nothing, that each might be and endure according to the course of its period; as holy Job says to God of man: [[Job 14:5|thou hast appointed his bounds which cannot be passed|Constituisti terminos ejus, qui præteriri non poterunt]]. Some things indeed he brought forth incorruptible and immortal, as the angels and rational souls, and the heavenly bodies, and the elements: so that, taken as wholes, they cannot be corrupted. Mixed bodies he made that they might be, by direct intention; but corruption accompanies their condition. And those that cannot be perpetuated in themselves he willed to obtain perpetual being by succession, so that in this way all things might in some manner share in the divine being, as the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle] also teaches.

paras.t: Et sanabiles fecit nationes orbis terrarum: id est, omnes homines atque progenies fecit salutis capaces, et per rationem liberumque arbitrium pœnitere ac reformari potentes, auxiliante gratia Dei; multa quoque concessit naturalia remedia contra morbos. Non enim est in illis medicamentum exterminii, id est remedium contra mortem. Quasi dicat: Nationes possunt in hac vita sanari et reformari, non autem mortem corporalem omnino evadere: juxta illud, Quis est homo qui vivet, et non videbit mortem? Vel, Non est in illis medicamentum exterminii, id est, interimendo se ipsos non medentur suis doloribus, sed graviores incurrunt, ut patuit. Nec inferorum regnum in terra: id est, dæmones non possunt hominibus in hoc mundo ad suum libitum dominari, neque nocere, nisi homines sponte illorum tentaminis consentiant, aut Deus permittat. Rursus, Regnum inferorum non est in terra, quia et his, puta iniquis, quibus diaboli dominantur, non ita dominantur sicut damnatis, quum isti valeant pœnitere, et dæmonum manus evadere, illi nequaquam. Imo isti pœnitendo possunt in æternum salvari. Propter quod subditur:
paras.en: [[1:14|and he made the nations of the earth for health|Et sanabiles fecit nationes orbis terrarum]] [literally "he made the nations of the world healable"], that is, he made all men and their offspring capable of salvation, and able, through reason and free will, to repent and be reformed, with the help of God's grace; he also granted many natural remedies against diseases. [[1:14|there is no poison of destruction in them|Non enim est in illis medicamentum exterminii]], that is, no remedy against death [Denis takes *medicamentum*, which the Douay-Rheims renders "poison", in its other sense of "remedy"]. As if he said: The nations can be healed and reformed in this life, but cannot wholly escape bodily death; according to that: [[Ps 88:49|Who is the man that shall live, and not see death|Quis est homo qui vivet, et non videbit mortem?]] Or: [[1:14|there is no poison of destruction in them|Non est in illis medicamentum exterminii]], that is, by killing themselves they do not cure their pains, but incur graver ones, as was shown. [[1:14|nor kingdom of hell upon the earth|Nec inferorum regnum in terra]]: that is, the demons cannot lord it over men in this world at their pleasure, nor harm them, unless men freely consent to their temptations, or God permits it. Again, the kingdom of hell is not upon the earth, because even those, namely the wicked, over whom the devils rule, they do not rule as they rule the damned; for these can repent and escape the hands of the demons, those in no way. Nay, these by repenting can be saved for ever. For which reason it is added:

paras.t: Justitia enim perpetua est et immortalis. Hanc autem acquirit homo veraciter pœnitendo. Non tamen est sic intelligendum, quod justus non possit peccando justitiam perdere, sed quod justitia ex sua natura potest perpetua permanere, quum ejus subjectum sit immortalis voluntas, et in patria perseveret, quantum ad actus suos perfectos, quemadmodum caritas, quæ (Apostolo teste) non excidit; et etiam quoniam justus habet propositum jugiter adhærendi justitiæ, et permanendi in ea, sine quo proposito nemo est justus. Hinc a viris perfectis sic definitur justitia: Justitia est constans et perpetua voluntas, jus suum unicuique tribuens. Et sumitur ibi voluntas, pro actu seu habitu voluntatis. Nam et secundo Ethicorum Aristoteles docet: Ad hoc quod actus sit virtuosus, tria exiguntur: primo, ut aliquis agat sciens; secundo, ut agat eligens et propter debitum finem; tertio, quod immobiliter operetur: non quod actus incessabiliter exerceatur, sed quoad agentis firmum et rectum propositum, prout in secunda secundæ, quæstione 58, Thomas plenius hæc declarat. Insuper justitia immortalis atque perpetua perhibetur, quoniam liberat a morte peccati, et deducit ad regnum æternum, juxta quod ait Salvator: Fulgebunt justi sicut sol in regno Patris eorum.
paras.en: [[1:15|For justice is perpetual and immortal|Justitia enim perpetua est et immortalis]]. This a man acquires by truly repenting. Yet it is not to be understood as if the just man could not lose justice by sinning, but that justice of its nature can remain perpetual, since its subject is the immortal will, and it persists in the homeland [that is, in heaven] as to its perfect acts, as charity does, which (as the Apostle testifies) never falls away[[1 Cor 13:8||]] [the margin gives only 1 Cor. xiii; the words are in v. 8]; and also because the just man has the purpose of cleaving to justice continually and of remaining in it, without which purpose no one is just. Hence justice is thus defined by accomplished men: Justice is the constant and perpetual will that gives to each his right [the definition of the Roman law, in Justinian's Institutes]. And *will* is taken there for an act or habit of the will. For Aristotle too teaches in the second book of the Ethics: For an act to be virtuous three things are required: first, that a man act knowingly; secondly, that he act choosing, and for the due end; thirdly, that he work unwaveringly: not that the act be exercised without ceasing, but as regards the firm and right purpose of the agent; as Thomas declares these things more fully in the Secunda Secundæ, question 58. Further, justice is said to be immortal and perpetual because it frees from the death of sin and leads to the eternal kingdom, according to what the Saviour says: [[Matt 13:43|shall the just shine as the sun, in the kingdom of their Father|Fulgebunt justi sicut sol in regno Patris eorum]].

paras.t: Injustitia autem, mortis est acquisitio, id est, æternam damnationem meretur: quemadmodum enim ex suo genere est mortale quidquid caritati contrariatur, ita et quidquid repugnat justitiæ. Et potest hoc loco per injustitiam, intelligi omne peccatum mortale, hoc est omnis transgressio legis divinæ: quæ injustitia contrariatur justitiæ quæ est virtus communis. Injustitia autem quæ opponitur justitiæ, prout est virtus specialis ac cardinalis, est speciale, et ex suo genere peccatum mortale.
paras.en: *But injustice is the acquiring of death* [these words follow v. 15 in the Latin text Denis comments on; they are not in the Clementine Vulgate or the Douay-Rheims], that is, it merits eternal damnation: for as whatever is contrary to charity is mortal of its kind, so too is whatever is opposed to justice. And by *injustice* in this place may be understood every mortal sin, that is, every transgression of the divine law: which injustice is contrary to justice as it is a general virtue [Latin *communis*: justice taken broadly, as embracing all virtue]. But the injustice that is opposed to justice as it is a special and cardinal virtue is a special sin, and mortal of its kind.
