paras.en: [[4:17|For they shall see the end of the wise man|Videbunt enim finem sapientis]], that is, the unjust will behold the just man overtaken by death, and the end of his life; [[4:17|and it shall not understand what God hath designed for him|et non intelligent quid cogitaverit de illo Deus]], that is, why he decreed to take him away thus, and how great a glory he wills to bestow on him; [[4:17|and why the Lord hath set him in safety|et quare minuerit illum Dominus]] [Denis reads *minuerit*, "hath lessened", where the Vulgate has *munierit*, "hath set in safety"], that is, for what cause he shortened his days.

paras.t: Videbunt justum sic mortuum, et contemnent eum, quasi inaniter vixerit juste, quia tam cito beneficio vitæ privatus est, nec ab injustis videtur distinctus in morte. Hinc et in Job legitur : Deridetur justi simplicitas, lampas contempta apud cogitationes divitum, usque ad tempus præfinitum. Unde Dominus per Prophetam talibus contemptoribus loquitur : Invaluerunt super me verba vestra, et dixistis : Vanus est qui servit Domino : ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes, siquidem ædificati sunt. Idcirco subjungitur : Illos autem justorum contemptores Dominus irridebit : sicut in Psalmo habetur, Qui habitat in cœlis irridebit eos.
paras.en: [[4:18|They shall see|Videbunt]] the just man thus dead, [[4:18|and shall despise him|et contemnent eum]], as if he had lived justly in vain, since he was so soon deprived of the gift of life and seems not to be distinguished from the unjust in death. Hence we read in Job too: [[Job 12:4|the simplicity of the just man is laughed to scorn|Deridetur justi simplicitas]], [[Job 12:5|The lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich, is ready for the time appointed|lampas contempta apud cogitationes divitum, usque ad tempus præfinitum]]. Hence the Lord speaks to such despisers through the Prophet: [[Mal 3:13|Your words have been unsufferable to me|Invaluerunt super me verba vestra]], and you have said: [[Mal 3:14|He laboureth in vain that serveth God|Vanus est qui servit Domino]]: [[Mal 3:15|Wherefore now we call the proud people happy, for they that work wickedness are built up|ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes, siquidem ædificati sunt]]. Therefore he adds: But as for those despisers of the just, [[4:18|the Lord shall laugh them to scorn|Illos autem justorum contemptores Dominus irridebit]]; as we have in the Psalm: [[Ps 2:4|He that dwelleth in heaven shall laugh at them|Qui habitat in cœlis irridebit eos]].

paras.t: Et erunt post hæc decedentes sine honore : nam quamvis in medio propinquorum exspirent, et magnifice sepeliantur, tamen eorum animæ confusibilissime tractabuntur; et in contumelia inter mortuos in perpetuum, id est, sine fine in suis opprobriis inter reprobos permanebunt. De quibus dicitur in Psalmo : Sicut vulnerati dormientes in sepulcris, quorum non es memor amplius. Hinc etiam fertur de divite vitioso : Mortuus est dives, et sepultus est in inferno. Econtra autem de Lazaro justo dicitur : Factum est ut moreretur mendicus, et portaretur ab angelis in sinum Abrahæ.
paras.en: [[4:19|And they shall fall after this without honour|Et erunt post hæc decedentes sine honore]] [the text prints *decedentes*, "departing"; a note in the margin gives *decidentes*, "falling", as in the Vulgate]: for though they breathe their last amid their kinsfolk and are buried magnificently, yet their souls will be dealt with in the utmost confusion; [[4:19|and be a reproach among the dead for ever|et in contumelia inter mortuos in perpetuum]], that is, they will remain without end in their disgrace among the reprobate. Of whom it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:6|Like the slain sleeping in the sepulchres, whom thou rememberest no more|Sicut vulnerati dormientes in sepulcris, quorum non es memor amplius]]. Hence too it is said of the vicious rich man: [[Luke 16:22|And the rich man also died: and he was buried in hell|Mortuus est dives, et sepultus est in inferno]]. But on the other hand it is said of Lazarus the just: [[Luke 16:22|And it came to pass that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom|Factum est ut moreretur mendicus, et portaretur ab angelis in sinum Abrahæ]].

paras.t: Quoniam disrumpet illos inflatos : id est, Deus avellet animas eorum a suis corporibus omnino discruciatis et intus corruptis. Sic quippe per Osee loquitur de iniquis : Occurram eis ut ursa raptis catulis; dirumpam interiora eorum, et consumam eos ut leo (qui erant inflati superbia). Et hoc faciet Dominus sine voce : quoniam impii in fine vitæ præ debilitate nequeunt loqui; et in judicio respondere non valent Deo, nec vocem excusationis emittere : quia, ut ait Apostolus, inexcusabiles sunt, qui quum cognovissent Deum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt. Et commovebit illos a fundamentis, id est, funditus agitabit et auferet, et ab omnibus rebus, quibus quasi fundamentis innitebantur, tollet eos ac dividet; et usque ad supremum, id est maxime, desolabuntur, tam in morte, quam in æterna damnatione : sicut cantatur in Psalmo, Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Et erunt gementes in pœnis, nec consolationem invenient, ut constat de divite, qui nec guttam aquæ potuit impetrare in tormentorum suorum incendio. In quibus illud Jeremiæ maxime adimplebitur : Dabo eos in vexationem, et maledictionem, et stuporem, et sibilum, et opprobrium sempiternum, eo quod non audierint verba mea. Et memoria eorum peribit : juxta illud in Job, Memoria vestra comparabitur cineri; et item, Laus impiorum brevis est; ac alibi, Nomen impiorum putrescet.
paras.en: [[4:19|for he shall burst them puffed up|Quoniam disrumpet illos inflatos]]: that is, God will tear their souls away from their bodies, utterly tormented and corrupted within. For thus he speaks of the wicked through Osee: [[Osee 13:8|I will meet them as a bear that is robbed of her whelps, and I will rend the inner parts of their liver: and I will devour them there as a lion|Occurram eis ut ursa raptis catulis; dirumpam interiora eorum, et consumam eos ut leo]] (them, that is, who were puffed up with pride). And the Lord will do this while they are [[4:19|speechless|sine voce]]: for the wicked at the end of life cannot speak for weakness; and at the judgment they are not able to answer God or utter a word of excuse, because, as the Apostle says, [[Rom 1:20|they are inexcusable|inexcusabiles sunt]], who, [[Rom 1:21|when they knew God, they have not glorified him as God|quum cognovissent Deum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt]]. [[4:19|and shall shake them from the foundations|Et commovebit illos a fundamentis]], that is, he will shake them and carry them off from the ground up, and will take them away and part them from all the things on which they leaned as on foundations; [[4:19|and they shall be utterly|et usque ad supremum]], that is, to the utmost, [[4:19|laid waste|desolabuntur]], both in death and in eternal damnation, as is sung in the Psalm: [[Ps 72:19|How are they brought to desolation?|Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem?]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxii, 19] [[4:19|they shall be in sorrow|Et erunt gementes]] in their punishments, and will find no consolation, as is plain from the rich man, who could not obtain a drop of water in the burning of his torments[[Luke 16:24||]]. In them that word of Jeremias will above all be fulfilled: [[Jer 29:18|I will give them up unto affliction|Dabo eos in vexationem]], to be [[Jer 29:18|a curse, and an astonishment, and a hissing, and a reproach|et maledictionem, et stuporem, et sibilum, et opprobrium]] everlasting, [[Jer 29:19|Because they have not hearkened to my words|eo quod non audierint verba mea]] [the margin gives Jer. xxiv, 18, 19; the words are from Jer 29:18–19]. [[4:19|and their memory shall perish|Et memoria eorum peribit]]: according to that in Job, [[Job 13:12|Your remembrance shall be compared to ashes|Memoria vestra comparabitur cineri]]; and again, [[Job 20:5|the praise of the wicked is short|Laus impiorum brevis est]]; and elsewhere, [[Prov 10:7|the name of the wicked shall rot|Nomen impiorum putrescet]].

paras.t: Venient in cogitatione peccatorum suorum timidi, id est, ex remorsu conscientiæ et consideratione suorum excessuum, cum inæstimabili timore divino præsentabuntur judicio. Juxta quod in Job legitur : Angustia vallabit impium, sicut regem qui paratur ad prælium; et rursus ibidem, Sonitus terroris in auribus impii. Et traducent illos ex adverso iniquitates ipsorum : id est, propter peccata sua abducentur seorsum a societate Sanctorum, et constituentur ad judicantis sinistram, atque in ignem projicientur æternum. Quod totum eos promeruisse, protestabuntur eorum facinora : quorum sibi conscii erunt, et accusabuntur a conscientia propria. Sicque justis in sublime scandentibus, ipsi deprimentur in ima.
paras.en: [[4:20|They shall come with fear at the thought of their sins|Venient in cogitatione peccatorum suorum timidi]], that is, out of the remorse of conscience and the consideration of their excesses, they will be brought before the judgment of God with a fear past reckoning. According to what we read in Job: [[Job 15:24|distress shall surround him, as a king that is prepared for the battle|Angustia vallabit impium, sicut regem qui paratur ad prælium]]; and again in the same place, [[Job 15:21|The sound of dread is always in his ears|Sonitus terroris in auribus impii]]. [[4:20|and their iniquities shall stand against them to convict them|Et traducent illos ex adverso iniquitates ipsorum]]: that is, because of their sins they will be led apart from the company of the saints, and set at the left hand of the Judge[[Matt 25:33||]], and cast into everlasting fire[[Matt 25:41||]][[Matt 25:46||]]. That they have deserved all this their crimes will bear witness, of which they will be conscious, and they will be accused by their own conscience. And so, while the just mount on high, they will be thrust down to the depths.

5.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI QUINTI : TUNC STABUNT JUSTI IN MAGNA CONSTANTIA.
5.title_en: Exposition of the fifth chapter: Then shall the just stand with great constancy

paras.t: Quam diversimode justus Deus post hanc vitam tractet justos et impios, hic narratur.
paras.en: How differently the just God deals with the just and with the wicked after this life is told here.

paras.t: Tunc, scilicet in futuro generali ac finali judicio: de quo in fine præcedentis fertur capituli, Venient in cogitatione peccatorum suorum timidi; stabunt justi ad dexteram Judicis elevati in aere, in magna constantia, id est in immobili securitate, ac insuperabili fortitudine, adversus eos qui se angustiaverunt, id est contra suos persecutores, a quibus fuerunt oppressi atque afflicti. Contra quos movebunt zelo justitiæ, zelantes pro Judice, et pro divinæ majestatis honore, ut satisfiat Deo per condemnationem iniquorum, pro injuriis et offensis ipsius; non autem zelo invidiæ aut vindictæ, nisi in quantum vindicta est effectus justitiæ. Juxta quem modum, vindicta esse pars justitiæ perhibetur. Et qui abstulerunt labores eorum, id est, bona eorum opera impediverunt pro posse, et virtuosos eorum labores ac patientias in adversis, atque certamina pro Deo et fide, reputaverunt cassos et vanos, nulla mercede beata remunerandos. Laboraverunt quoque justi convertere proximos, quorum conversionem impii impediebant pro viribus. Interdum etiam sumitur labor pro temporali possessione, quæ laboribus congregatur et colitur, sicut in Psalmo: Dedit illis regiones gentium, et labores populorum possederunt. Tales autem labores abstulerunt impii justis, præsertim martyribus, juxta id ad Hebræos: Rapinam bonorum vestrorum cum gaudio suscepistis.
paras.en: [[5:1|Then|Tunc]], that is, at the future general and final judgment, of which it was said at the end of the preceding chapter: [[Wis 4:20|They shall come with fear at the thought of their sins|Venient in cogitatione peccatorum suorum timidi]]; [[5:1|shall the just stand|stabunt justi]] at the right hand of the Judge[[Matt 25:33||]], raised up into the air, [[5:1|with great constancy|in magna constantia]], that is, in unshakeable security and unconquerable fortitude, [[5:1|against those that have afflicted them|adversus eos qui se angustiaverunt]], that is, against their persecutors, by whom they were oppressed and afflicted. Against these they will be moved by zeal for justice, zealous for the Judge and for the honour of the divine majesty, that satisfaction may be made to God for the injuries and offences done to him, through the condemnation of the wicked; not, however, by the zeal of envy or of revenge, except insofar as revenge is an effect of justice; in which sense revenge is said to be a part of justice. [[5:1|And taken away their labours|Et qui abstulerunt labores eorum]], that is, who hindered their good works as far as they could, and reckoned their virtuous labours and their patience in adversity, and their struggles for God and the faith, empty and vain, to be rewarded with no blessed recompense. The just also laboured to convert their neighbours, whose conversion the wicked hindered with all their might. Sometimes, too, *labour* is taken for temporal possessions, which are gathered and tilled by labour, as in the Psalm: [[Ps 104:44|And he gave them the lands of the Gentiles: and they possessed the labours of the people|Dedit illis regiones gentium, et labores populorum possederunt]]. And such labours the wicked took away from the just, especially from the martyrs, according to that of the Epistle to the Hebrews: You [[Heb 10:34|took with joy the being stripped of your own goods|Rapinam bonorum vestrorum cum gaudio suscepistis]].

paras.t: Videntes turbabuntur timore horribili. Nec mirum, quia horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis. Videntes, inquam, Judicem omnipotentem iratum: quem offenderunt, blasphemaverunt, spreverunt. Qui in Apocalypsi ita describitur: Vidi vestitum podere, et oculi ejus ut flamma ignis, et pedes ejus similes aurichalco, sicut in camino ardenti, et vox illius tanquam vox aquarum multarum, et de ore ejus gladius ex utraque parte acutus exibat, et facies ejus sicut sol lucet in virtute sua. Quibus verbis adjecit Joannes: Et quum vidissem eum, cecidi ad pedes ejus tanquam mortuus.
paras.en: [[5:2|These seeing it, shall be troubled with terrible fear|Videntes turbabuntur timore horribili]]. And no wonder, for [[Heb 10:31|it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God|horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis]]. Seeing, I say, the almighty Judge in anger, whom they offended, blasphemed and despised; who is described thus in the Apocalypse: I saw[[Apoc 1:12||]] one [[Apoc 1:13|clothed with a garment down to the feet|vestitum podere]], [[Apoc 1:14|and his eyes were as a flame of fire|et oculi ejus ut flamma ignis]], [[Apoc 1:15|and his feet like unto fine brass, as in a burning furnace. And his voice as the sound of many waters|et pedes ejus similes aurichalco, sicut in camino ardenti, et vox illius tanquam vox aquarum multarum]], [[Apoc 1:16|and from his mouth came out a sharp two-edged sword. And his face was as the sun shineth in his power|et de ore ejus gladius ex utraque parte acutus exibat, et facies ejus sicut sol lucet in virtute sua]]. To which words John added: [[Apoc 1:17|And when I had seen him, I fell at his feet as dead|Et quum vidissem eum, cecidi ad pedes ejus tanquam mortuus]].

paras.t: Si ergo imaginaria visio judicis hujus fuit ita terribilis etiam S. Joanni, quod ex ejus horrore cecidit tantus Apostolus tanquam mortuus: quid mirum, si iniqui et reprobi in die judicii, ex reali et sensitiva judicis hujus visione turbabuntur timore horribili? Turbabuntur quoque tam horribiliter ex magnifica apparitione et inspectione justorum, quos pro nihilo reputaverunt et angustiaverunt. Tertio, turbabuntur ex sui ipsorum inspectione: quia deformiora et horribiliora erunt eorum corpora, quam fuerunt quando in monumentis erant pro media parte a vermibus serpentibusque corrosa. Quarto, ineffabiliter turbabuntur præ horrore sententiæ contra se proferendæ, atque imminentis damnationis æternæ.
paras.en: If, then, an imaginary vision [that is, a vision seen in the imagination, not with the bodily eye] of this Judge was so terrible even to St John that so great an Apostle fell as dead for dread of it, what wonder if the wicked and reprobate on the day of judgment, at a real vision of this Judge seen with the senses, [[5:2|shall be troubled with terrible fear|turbabuntur timore horribili]]? They will also be so terribly troubled at the magnificent appearance and sight of the just, whom they reckoned as nothing and afflicted. Thirdly, they will be troubled at the sight of themselves, because their bodies will be more misshapen and more horrible than they were when they lay in the tombs half eaten away by worms and serpents. Fourthly, they will be troubled beyond words for dread of the sentence about to be pronounced against them, and of the eternal damnation hanging over them.

paras.t: Et mirabuntur in subitatione insperatæ salutis, id est de hoc, quod electi et justi tam repente et improvise eis apparent in gloria tanta, et tantam salutem sunt consecuti, quam reprobi nequaquam putaverunt eos consecuturos. Tunc, ut sanctus testatur Hieronymus, judicaturo Domino lugubre mundus immugiet, et tribus ad tribum pectora feriet; potentissimi quondam reges nudo latere palpitabunt. Tunc Aristotelis argumenta non proderunt, quum venerit filius illius pauperculæ quæstuariæ judicare fines terræ.
paras.en: [[5:2|And shall be amazed at the suddenness of their unexpected salvation|Et mirabuntur in subitatione insperatæ salutis]], that is, at this, that the elect and the just appear to them so suddenly and unforeseen in such great glory, and have attained so great a salvation, which the reprobate never thought they would attain. Then, as St Jerome testifies, when the Lord comes to judge, the world will bellow in mourning, and tribe by tribe will beat their breasts; kings once most mighty will tremble with naked sides. Then the arguments of Aristotle will be of no avail, when the son of that poor working woman comes to judge the ends of the earth [quæstuaria, a woman who works for hire: in Jerome's letter to Heliodorus these are the scornful words of the unbelievers about Christ].

paras.t: Gementes præ angustia spiritus: juxta illud Isaiæ: Ecce servi mei laudabunt præ exsultatione cordis, et vos clamabitis præ dolore cordis, et præ contritione spiritus ululabitis. Hinc ait et Apostolus: Repentinus eis superveniet interitus, sicut dolor in utero habentis. Verum, juxta Ezechielis oraculum, Gement gemitibus incircumcisorum: quia non erit gemitus pœnitentiæ salutaris, de quo loquitur Dominus, In quacumque hora peccator ingemuerit pro peccatis suis, omnium iniquitatum ejus non recordabor; sed erit gemitus desolationis extremæ, procedens ex servili dolore et desperante mœrore.
paras.en: [[5:3|Groaning for anguish of spirit|Gementes præ angustia spiritus]]: according to that of Isaias: Behold [[Is 65:14|my servants shall praise for joyfulness of heart, and you shall cry for sorrow of heart, and shall howl for grief of spirit|servi mei laudabunt præ exsultatione cordis, et vos clamabitis præ dolore cordis, et præ contritione spiritus ululabitis]]. Hence the Apostle also says: [[1 Thess 5:3|then shall sudden destruction come upon them, as the pains upon her that is with child|Repentinus eis superveniet interitus, sicut dolor in utero habentis]]. But, according to the oracle of Ezechiel, [[Ezech 30:24|they shall groan bitterly|Gement gemitibus]], with the groans of the uncircumcised [the margin gives Ezech. xxx, 24, where the Vulgate has gement gemitibus interfecti, 'they shall groan with the groans of the slain'; 'the uncircumcised' are joined with the slain in Ezech 32]: for it will not be the groaning of saving penance, of which the Lord speaks: At whatever hour the sinner shall groan for his sins[[Ezech 18:21||]], [[Ezech 18:22|I will not remember all his iniquities|omnium iniquitatum ejus non recordabor]] [the margin gives Ezech. xviii, 21, 22; the first words are the saying as commonly quoted, not the Vulgate's]; but it will be the groaning of utter desolation, coming from servile sorrow and despairing grief.

paras.t: Unde subjungitur: dicent intra se, id est cogitabunt, pœnitentiam agentes, id est, dolorem habentes de suis peccatis, non utique ex caritate, nec zelo justitiæ, nec virtutis seu boni honesti amore; sed ex servili tantarum pœnarum timore, et ex amore privato ac improbo sui, quo adversa refugient. Pœnitebunt igitur se peccasse, non in quantum peccata sunt offensiva inhonorativaque Dei, et sinceritati virtutum contraria, sed in quantum sunt eis tantæ miseriæ causa. Talis fuit pœnitentia vitiosi Antiochi, de quo fertur, quod orabat scelestus Dominum, a quo non erat misericordiam consecuturus; pœnitentia quoque Esau, de quo scriptum est ad Hebræos, Non invenit pœnitentiæ locum, quanquam cum lacrimis inquisisset eam. Hoc modo solent miseri pœnitere in magna infirmitate, instantique morte, qui tempore juventutis ac sanitatis nolunt a vitiis abstinere, dicentes cum Balaam, Moriatur (id est, a corpore separetur) anima mea morte justorum; vitam vero justorum renuunt sequi, dicentes cum pravis discipulis, Durus est hic sermo. Et præ angustia, id est desolatione, tristitia et pressura, spiritus, id est animæ suæ, gementes interiori dictione, ut tactum est.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[5:3|Saying within themselves|dicent intra se]] [the margin gives the reading dicentes, 'saying', as in the Vulgate; the text has dicent, 'they shall say'], that is, they shall think, [[5:3|repenting|pœnitentiam agentes]], that is, having sorrow for their sins: not, to be sure, out of charity, nor from zeal for justice, nor from love of virtue or of the honest good [that is, the good loved for its own worth, not for pleasure or profit], but from servile fear of such great pains, and from a private and wicked love of self, by which they will shrink from adversity. They will repent, then, of having sinned, not insofar as sins offend and dishonour God and are contrary to the purity of the virtues, but insofar as they are to them the cause of so great misery. Such was the penance of the wicked Antiochus, of whom it is recorded that [[2 Mach 9:13|this wicked man prayed to the Lord, of whom he was not like to obtain mercy|orabat scelestus Dominum, a quo non erat misericordiam consecuturus]]; and the penance of Esau, of whom it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:17|he found no place of repentance, although with tears he had sought it|Non invenit pœnitentiæ locum, quanquam cum lacrimis inquisisset eam]]. In this way the wretched are wont to repent in great sickness and with death at hand, who in the time of youth and health will not abstain from vices, saying with Balaam: [[Num 23:10|Let my soul die|Moriatur]] (that is, be separated from the body) [[Num 23:10|the death of the just|anima mea morte justorum]]; but they refuse to follow the life of the just, saying with the wicked disciples: [[John 6:61|This saying is hard|Durus est hic sermo]]. [[5:3|For anguish|præ angustia]], that is, in desolation, sadness and distress, [[5:3|of spirit|spiritus]], that is, of their soul, [[5:3|groaning|gementes]] with inward speech, as has been touched on.

paras.t: Hi sunt quos aliquando habuimus in derisum. Quemadmodum quarto Regum leguntur principes dixisse ad Jehu de filio prophetarum misso ab Eliseo: Quid venit insanus iste ad te? Nam carnalis homo non sapit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, sed stultitia est illi, quod pertinet ad salutem.
paras.en: [[5:3|These are they, whom we had sometime in derision|Hi sunt quos aliquando habuimus in derisum]]: as in the fourth book of Kings the captains are read to have said to Jehu of the son of the prophets sent by Eliseus: [[4 Kings 9:11|why came this madman to thee?|Quid venit insanus iste ad te?]] For [[1 Cor 2:14|the sensual man perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God|carnalis homo non sapit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei]]; rather, what pertains to salvation, [[1 Cor 2:14|it is foolishness to him|stultitia est illi]].

paras.t: Hinc vitiis obtenebrati, transitoria et sensibilia toto cupientes affectu, eos despiciunt et irrident quos vident talia aspernari. Hinc justi in Psalmo dicunt: Posuisti nos in similitudinem gentibus, commotionem capitis in populis, subsannationem et derisum his qui sunt in circuitu nostro. Et in similitudinem, id est proverbium, improperii: id est, tantum contempsimus eos velut miserrimos, quod volentes alicui maledicere, formam sumpsimus maledicendi ex eis, dicendo: Accidat tibi sicut Laurentio aut Vincentio.
paras.en: Hence those darkened by vices, desiring transitory and sensible things with all their affection, despise and mock those whom they see spurning such things. Hence the just say in the Psalm: [[Ps 43:15|Thou hast made us a byword among the Gentiles: a shaking of the head among the people|Posuisti nos in similitudinem gentibus, commotionem capitis in populis]], [[Ps 43:14|a scoff and derision to them that are round about us|subsannationem et derisum his qui sunt in circuitu nostro]]. [[5:3|And for a parable|Et in similitudinem]], that is, a proverb, [[5:3|of reproach|improperii]]: that is, we so despised them as most wretched that, when we wished to curse anyone, we took our form of cursing from them, saying: May it befall thee as it befell Laurence or Vincent [the martyrs St Laurence and St Vincent, both burnt on the gridiron].

paras.t: Nos insensati, id est vera et salutari sapientia destituti, utpote carnalia, non divina ac spiritualia, sapientes, gustantes, amantes, vitam illorum æstimabamus insaniam. Ideo dixit Ezechiel insanis filiis Israel: Ego portentum vestrum. Paulus quoque Corinthiis scribens: Tanquam purgamenta, inquit, hujus mundi facti sumus, omnium peripsema usque adhuc. Et finem illorum sine honore: id est, æstimabamus quod mortem eorum nullus honor, nulla gloria consequeretur. Ideo scriptum est in Isaia: Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet; et viri misericordiæ tolluntur, et non est qui intelligat. In Threnis etiam Israel ait: Posuit me in proverbium vulgi, et factus sum quasi vas inutile.
paras.en: [[5:4|We fools|Nos insensati]], that is, destitute of true and saving wisdom, as those who savoured, tasted and loved carnal things, not divine and spiritual ones, [[5:4|esteemed their life madness|vitam illorum æstimabamus insaniam]]. Therefore Ezechiel said to the mad children of Israel: [[Ezech 12:11|I am a sign of things to come to you|Ego portentum vestrum]] [portentum, a portent or prodigy: a thing to be stared at]. Paul also, writing to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 4:13|We are made as the refuse|Tanquam purgamenta]], he says, [[1 Cor 4:13|of this world, the offscouring of all, even until now|hujus mundi facti sumus, omnium peripsema usque adhuc]]. [[5:4|And their end without honour|Et finem illorum sine honore]]: that is, we esteemed that no honour, no glory, would follow their death. Therefore it is written in Isaias: [[Is 57:1|The just perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart, and men of mercy are taken away, because there is none that understandeth|Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet; et viri misericordiæ tolluntur, et non est qui intelligat]]. In Lamentations also Israel says: [[Job 17:6|He hath made me as it were a byword of the people|Posuit me in proverbium vulgi]], and I am become as a useless vessel [the print marks 'Lamentations' as doubtful, and the margin gives Job xvii, 6, where the first half stands; for the second half compare Ps 30:13 and Jer 48:38].

paras.t: Quomodo computati sunt inter filios Dei, id est inter electos et Sanctos, et inter angelos Dei? De quibus Deus loquitur ad Job: Ubi eras, quum me laudarent simul astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei? Et inter Sanctos sors, id est hereditaria portio, illorum est: quia cum Sanctis æternam beatitudinem sunt sortiti, prout primo Regum in cantico Anna fatetur: Suscitat Dominus de pulvere egenum, et de stercore elevat pauperem, ut sedeat cum principibus, et solium gloriæ teneat.
paras.en: [[5:5|How they are numbered among the children of God|Quomodo computati sunt inter filios Dei]], that is, among the elect and the saints, and among the angels of God! Of whom God speaks to Job: [[Job 38:4|Where wast thou|Ubi eras]], [[Job 38:7|when the morning stars praised me together, and all the sons of God made a joyful melody?|quum me laudarent simul astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei?]] [[5:5|And their lot|Et inter Sanctos sors]], that is, their hereditary portion, [[5:5|is among the saints|illorum est]]: for they have obtained by lot eternal beatitude with the saints, as Anna confesses in her canticle in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 2:8|He raiseth up the needy from the dust, and lifteth up the poor from the dunghill: that he may sit with princes, and hold the throne of glory|Suscitat Dominus de pulvere egenum, et de stercore elevat pauperem, ut sedeat cum principibus, et solium gloriæ teneat]].

paras.t: Ergo erravimus, id est, ex isto perpendimus nos errasse, a via veritatis, id est a notitia et tenore veritatis vitæ, veritatis doctrinæ, et veritatis justitiæ; et justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis: id est, ab increata luce, a qua omnis procedit justitia, illustrati non sumus lumine supernaturali gratiæ ac virtutum, quia posuimus obicem illuminationi ipsius, qui quantum in se est, omnibus præsto est, imo aversos invitat ad se; naturali tamen ingenio universos illustrat: de quo accipi potest illud Psalmistæ, Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine; et illud B. Joannis, Erat lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum.
paras.en: [[5:6|Therefore we have erred|Ergo erravimus]], that is, from this we perceive that we have erred, [[5:6|from the way of truth|a via veritatis]], that is, from the knowledge and keeping of the truth of life, the truth of doctrine and the truth of justice; [[5:6|and the light of justice hath not shined unto us|et justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis]]: that is, we have not been enlightened by the uncreated light, from which all justice proceeds, with the supernatural light of grace and of the virtues, because we put an obstacle in the way of his enlightening, who for his part is at hand to all, nay, invites to himself those who have turned away; yet he enlightens all men with natural understanding, of which may be taken that saying of the Psalmist, [[Ps 4:7|The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us|Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine]], and that of blessed John, [[John 1:9|That was the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world.|Erat lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum]]

paras.t: Et Sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis, id est, Christus evangelicæ legis dator, non se infudit cordibus nostris. Unde et ad Corinthios scribit Apostolus: Deus hujus sæculi excæcavit mentes infidelium, ut non fulgeat eis Evangelium gloriæ Christi.
paras.en: [[5:6|And the sun of understanding hath not risen upon us|Et Sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis]], that is, Christ, the giver of the Gospel law, has not poured himself into our hearts. Hence the Apostle also writes to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 4:4|the god of this world hath blinded the minds of unbelievers|Deus hujus sæculi excæcavit mentes infidelium]], [[2 Cor 4:4|that the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ|Evangelium gloriæ Christi]] [[2 Cor 4:4|should not shine unto them|ut non fulgeat eis]].

paras.t: Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, id est in operibus, curis et occupationibus vitiorum, quibus annexæ sunt multæ angustiæ, afflictiones ac tædia. Propter quod dicitur in Ecclesiaste: Homini bono dedit Deus sapientiam et scientiam et lætitiam, peccatori autem afflictionem et curam superfluam. Aliqua etiam vitia in se ipsis afflictione, molestia atque periculis plena sunt: ut ira, invidia, amaritudo, indignatio, impatientia, furtum, rapina; sed et ipsas voluptates gustus ac tactus concomitantur multa incommoda.
paras.en: [[5:7|We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction|Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis]], that is, in the works, cares and business of the vices, to which many distresses, afflictions and wearinesses are joined. Wherefore it is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 2:26|God hath given to a man that is good in his sight, wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he hath given vexation, and superfluous care|Homini bono dedit Deus sapientiam et scientiam et lætitiam, peccatori autem afflictionem et curam superfluam]]. Some vices, too, are in themselves full of affliction, trouble and dangers, such as anger, envy, bitterness, indignation, impatience, theft, robbery; and even the pleasures of taste and touch themselves are accompanied by many discomforts.

paras.t: Et ambulavimus vias difficiles. O quam difficiles ac molestas vias, occupationes, labores, incedunt ambitiosi et lubrici; quot resistentias patiuntur; quoties cassatur eorum conatus, et frustratur fine intento! Quam multi e regione contra eos incedunt, a quibus multoties opprimuntur, ita quod recte in libro Job dictum est: Involutæ sunt semitæ gressuum eorum.
paras.en: [[5:7|And have walked through hard ways|Et ambulavimus vias difficiles]]. O what hard and troublesome ways, occupations and labours the ambitious and the lustful tread! How much resistance they suffer! How often their efforts are brought to nothing and cheated of the end they intended! How many come against them from the opposite side, by whom they are often overthrown, so that it is rightly said in the book of Job: [[Job 6:18|The paths of their steps are entangled|Involutæ sunt semitæ gressuum eorum]].

paras.t: Viam autem Domini, id est arctam viam salutis, conversationem pœnitentialem, observantiam præceptorum, id est evangelicæ legis doctrinam, et Christum, qui ait, Ego sum via, veritas, et vita, ignoravimus, id est, formatam practicamque notitiam non habuimus rerum illarum, sed informem ac nudam notitiam. Non tamen per hoc excusantur, quoniam juris, quod quis scire tenetur, ignorantia non excusat; sicut nec ignorantia crassa seu affectata.
paras.en: [[5:7|But the way of the Lord|Viam autem Domini]], that is, the narrow way of salvation, a life of penance, the keeping of the commandments, that is, the teaching of the Gospel law, and Christ, who says, [[John 14:6|I am the way, and the truth, and the life|Ego sum via, veritas, et vita]], [[5:7|we have not known|ignoravimus]]: that is, we had no formed and practical knowledge of those things, but only an unformed and bare knowledge [formed knowledge: knowledge given life by charity and put into practice]. Yet they are not excused by this, since ignorance of a law that one is bound to know does not excuse; nor does crass or affected ignorance [affected ignorance: ignorance deliberately cultivated, so as to sin more freely].

paras.t: Quid nobis profuit superbia? aut divitiarum jactantia quid contulit nobis? quasi dicant: Nil profuit nobis ad salutem, imo plurimum impedivit et nocuit, nostrasque animas spiritualiter interemit. Quod consequenter per multas similitudines pandunt.
paras.en: [[5:8|What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?|Quid nobis profuit superbia? aut divitiarum jactantia quid contulit nobis?]] As if they said: It profited us nothing for salvation; nay, it hindered and harmed us very greatly, and killed our souls spiritually. This they go on to set out by many likenesses.

paras.t: Transierunt omnia illa tanquam umbra, id est velocissime, instar umbræ. Nam et vita præsens est cursus ad mortem, et instabilissima valde, ita ut dicat apostolus Jacobus: Quæ est vita vestra? Vapor est ad modicum parens, deinceps exterminabitur.
paras.en: [[5:9|All those things are passed away like a shadow|Transierunt omnia illa tanquam umbra]], that is, most swiftly, as a shadow does. For the present life too is a race towards death, and exceedingly unstable, so that the apostle James says: [[Jas 4:15|what is your life? It is a vapour which appeareth for a little while and afterwards shall vanish away|Quæ est vita vestra? Vapor est ad modicum parens, deinceps exterminabitur]].

paras.t: Et tanquam nuntius præcurrens. Unde Job asserit: Dies mei velociores fuerunt cursore; transierunt quasi naves poma portantes.
paras.en: [[5:9|And like a post that runneth on|Et tanquam nuntius præcurrens]] [a post: a courier, a running messenger]. Hence Job declares: [[Job 9:25|My days have been swifter than a post|Dies mei velociores fuerunt cursore]]; [[Job 9:26|they have passed by as ships carrying fruits|transierunt quasi naves poma portantes]].

paras.t: Hinc sequitur: et tanquam navis quæ pertransit fluctuantem, id est inundantem, aquam: cujus, quum præterierit, non est vestigium invenire, id est impressionem aut signum transitus ejus, neque semitam carinæ illius in fluctibus. Carina, vocatur venter navis, scindens et deprimens aquam, non tamen relinquens in ea stabilem impressuram.
paras.en: Hence there follows: [[5:10|And as a ship, that passeth through the waves|et tanquam navis quæ pertransit fluctuantem]] [Latin fluctuantem aquam, 'the billowing water'], that is, through the overflowing water: [[5:10|whereof when it is gone by, the trace cannot be found|cujus, quum præterierit, non est vestigium invenire]], that is, the impression or sign of its passing, [[5:10|nor the path of its keel in the waters|neque semitam carinæ illius in fluctibus]]. The keel is the name for the belly of the ship, which cuts and presses down the water, yet leaves no lasting impression in it.

paras.t: Aut avis quæ transvolat in aere: cujus nullum invenitur argumentum itineris illius, id est indicium sui volatus, sed tantum sonitus alarum verberans levem ventum: et scindens per vim itineris aerem, commotis alis transvolavit; et post hoc nullum signum invenitur itineris illius.
paras.en: [[5:11|Or as when a bird flieth through the air|Aut avis quæ transvolat in aere]], [[5:11|of the passage of which no mark can be found|cujus nullum invenitur argumentum itineris illius]], that is, no indication of its flight, [[5:11|but only the sound of the wings beating the light air, and parting it by the force of her flight: she moved her wings, and hath flown through, and there is no mark found afterwards of her way|sed tantum sonitus alarum verberans levem ventum: et scindens per vim itineris aerem, commotis alis transvolavit; et post hoc nullum signum invenitur itineris illius]].

paras.t: Aut tanquam sagitta emissa in locum destinatum, id est intentum, divisus aer ex sagitta volante in eo: quia duo corpora non possunt naturaliter esse in uno loco, ideo unum alteri cedit, et mollius duriori; continuo, id est statim, in se reclusus est, ut ignoretur transitus illius: aer enim est maxime fluxibilis, mollis, et refluens in se.
paras.en: [[5:12|Or as when an arrow is shot at a mark|Aut tanquam sagitta emissa in locum destinatum]], that is, the place aimed at, [[5:12|the divided air|divisus aer]] by the arrow flying through it (for since two bodies cannot by nature be in one place, the one gives way to the other, and the softer to the harder), [[5:12|quickly|continuo]], that is, at once, [[5:12|cometh together again, so that the passage thereof is not known|in se reclusus est, ut ignoretur transitus illius]]: for air is exceedingly fluid and soft, and flows back into itself.

paras.t: Sic et nos nati, continuo desivimus esse: id est, ab exordio quo cœpimus esse, cœpimus et deficere ac corrumpi, eo quod sumus ex contrariis compositi, in quibus unum corruptive seu læsive agit in aliud, scilicet calidum naturale, in humidum radicale: et quanto plus protenditur vita, tanto plus breviatur. Quidquid enim præteriit, jam ex ea deperiit, et ei abscissum est. Sicque vitæ istius decursus, instar prædictarum volubilium rerum, omnino instabilis est, et incerta ejus duratio. Unde in Job legitur de iniquo: Velut somnium avolans non invenietur; transiet quasi visio nocturna. Et de se ipso sanctus Job loquitur: Dies mei velocius transierunt, quam a texente tela succiditur. Hinc loquitur et Isaias: Omnis caro fœnum, et omnis gloria ejus quasi flos agri. Horum ergo consideratione discamus transitoria aspernari, et spiritualia ac divina toto corde amplecti; et ibi sint fixa desideria nostra, ubi poterimus beatitudine adimpleri æterna.
paras.en: [[5:13|So we also being born, forthwith ceased to be|Sic et nos nati, continuo desivimus esse]]: that is, from the very beginning in which we began to be, we began also to fail and to decay, because we are made up of contraries, of which one acts upon the other so as to corrupt or injure it, namely the natural heat upon the radical moisture [in the medicine of the time, the body's vital heat slowly consumes its innate moisture]: and the more life is prolonged, the more it is shortened. For whatever of it has passed has already perished out of it and been cut off from it. And so the course of this life, like the fleeting things just mentioned, is altogether unstable, and its duration uncertain. Hence we read in Job of the wicked man: [[Job 20:8|As a dream that fleeth away he shall not be found, he shall pass as a vision of the night|Velut somnium avolans non invenietur; transiet quasi visio nocturna]]. And holy Job speaks of himself: [[Job 7:6|My days have passed more swiftly than the web is cut by the weaver|Dies mei velocius transierunt, quam a texente tela succiditur]]. Hence Isaias too says: [[Is 40:6|All flesh is grass, and all the glory thereof as the flower of the field|Omnis caro fœnum, et omnis gloria ejus quasi flos agri]]. By considering these things, then, let us learn to despise transitory things and to embrace spiritual and divine things with all our heart; and let our desires be fixed there where we shall be able to be filled with eternal beatitude.

paras.t: Et virtutis quidem nullum signum valuimus ostendere, id est nullum opus habitus virtuosi: quia jugiter eramus malis intenti, ita quod affectiva vis nostra erat quasi immobilitata in vitiis, et sic non valuimus, id est, vix aut difficulter potuimus, aliquid boni efficere, aut virtutem habere. Juxta quem sensum Christus in Evangelio loquitur: Quomodo potestis loqui bona, quum sitis mali? Philosophus quoque affirmat, quod incontinens vult continere, sed non potest. Vel, Nullum signum virtutis, id est firmæ stabilitatis, juxta illud Job: Homo quasi flos egreditur et conteritur, et fugit velut umbra, et nunquam in eodem statu permanet. In malignitate autem nostra, id est vitiositate habituata, qua ex igne seu ferventi affectu, et forti inclinatione habituum pravorum peccavimus, non ex ignorantia aut infirmitate duntaxat, consumpti sumus, id est corrupti, defuncti, et finem vitæ sortiti; spiritualiter quoque annihilati, et mortui corde.
paras.en: [[5:13|And have been able to shew no mark of virtue|Et virtutis quidem nullum signum valuimus ostendere]], that is, no work of a virtuous habit: because we were continually bent on evil, so that our affective power was as it were made fast in vices; and so we were not able, that is, we could hardly or only with difficulty, do anything good or have virtue. In this sense Christ says in the Gospel: [[Matt 12:34|How can you speak good things, whereas you are evil?|Quomodo potestis loqui bona, quum sitis mali?]] The Philosopher too affirms that the incontinent man wishes to contain himself but cannot. Or, [[5:13|no mark of virtue|Nullum signum virtutis]], that is, of firm stability, according to that of Job: Man [[Job 14:2|who cometh forth like a flower, and is destroyed, and fleeth as a shadow, and never continueth in the same state|Homo quasi flos egreditur et conteritur, et fugit velut umbra, et nunquam in eodem statu permanet]]. But [[5:13|in our wickedness|In malignitate autem nostra]], that is, in vice become habitual, by which we sinned from the fire, or fervent affection, and strong inclination of evil habits, not merely from ignorance or weakness, we [[5:13|are consumed|consumpti sumus]], that is, corrupted, dead, and come to the end of life; and spiritually, too, brought to nothing and dead in heart.

paras.t: Talia dixerunt in inferno hi qui peccaverunt. Jam dictum est, quod in die judicii ista dicturi sint, quando justi stabunt in magna constantia contra eos: quomodo ergo nunc dicitur, quod in inferno dixerunt hæc? Præterea, qualiter potuerunt in inferno ita prudenter loqui, et statum suum tam rationabiliter considerare, quum in Ecclesiaste legatur, Quodcumque potest manus tua, instanter operare, quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia, erunt apud inferos? Respondetur, quod damnati in inferno locati, possunt hæc dicere etiam ante diem judicii. Vel infernus vocatur omnis locus punitionis damnatorum. Ad aliud respondetur, quod damnati considerare queunt ea quæ augmentativa sunt calamitatis eorum, non ea quæ possent relevare eamdem, prout plenius super Ecclesiasten fuit expositum.
paras.en: [[5:14|Such things as these the sinners said in hell|Talia dixerunt in inferno hi qui peccaverunt]]. It has already been said that they will say these things on the day of judgment, when the just shall stand with great constancy against them: how then is it now said that they said these things in hell? Moreover, how could they speak so wisely in hell and consider their state so reasonably, when we read in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 9:10|Whatsoever thy hand is able to do, do it earnestly: for neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge shall be in hell|Quodcumque potest manus tua, instanter operare, quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia, erunt apud inferos?]]? The answer is that the damned, once placed in hell, can say these things even before the day of judgment. Or else every place where the damned are punished is called hell. To the other question the answer is that the damned can consider the things that increase their calamity, not those that could relieve it, as was set out more fully on Ecclesiastes[[Eccles 9:10||]].

paras.t: Et merito ista dixerunt, quoniam spes impii tanquam lanugo est, quæ a vento tollitur, id est vana, fallax, et facillime periens, quia in rebus transitoriis et caducis figit spem suam. Contra quem loquitur Jeremias: Maledictus homo qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium suum, et a Domino recedit cor ejus. Porro lanugo est flos tribuli: qui desiccatus, levi motu fertur in aerem et dissipatur, quemadmodum spuma ac fumus, atque memoria hospitis, una tantum nocte alicubi hospitati. De quibus mox additur: et tanquam spuma gracilis ex inundatione aquæ consurgens, quæ a procella, id est tempestate, dispergitur; et tanquam fumus qui a vento diffusus est, id est hinc inde fusus ac dissipatus: unde ait Psalmista, Defecerunt sicut fumus dies mei; et tanquam memoria hospitis unius diei prætereuntis.
paras.en: And rightly did they say these things, [[5:15|for the hope of the wicked is as dust, which is blown away with the wind|quoniam spes impii tanquam lanugo est, quæ a vento tollitur]] [Latin lanugo, 'down', where the Douay-Rheims has 'dust'], that is, vain, deceitful and very easily perishing, because he fixes his hope on transitory and perishable things. Against such a man Jeremias speaks: [[Jer 17:5|Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord|Maledictus homo qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium suum, et a Domino recedit cor ejus]]. Now *lanugo* is the flower of the thistle, which, when it has dried, is carried into the air by a light breath and scattered, like froth and smoke, and like the memory of a guest who has lodged somewhere for one night only. Of these it is added straight away: [[5:15|and as a thin froth|et tanquam spuma gracilis]] rising from the flood of water, [[5:15|which is dispersed by the storm|quæ a procella]], that is, the tempest; [[5:15|and a smoke that is scattered abroad by the wind|et tanquam fumus qui a vento diffusus est]], that is, poured out hither and thither and scattered: whence the Psalmist says, [[Ps 101:4|My days are vanished like smoke|Defecerunt sicut fumus dies mei]]; [[5:15|and as the remembrance of a guest of one day that passeth by|et tanquam memoria hospitis unius diei prætereuntis]].

paras.t: Præterea, reproborum vanitate, instabilitate et ærumna descriptis, ut opposita juxta se posita lucidius patent, subditur de electorum proprietate, felicitate et gloria: Justi autem in perpetuum vivent: quia in sæculo isto vivunt per caritatem, quæ nunquam excidit, et in futuro per beatam fruitionem. Et ita hic vivunt vita gratiæ, de qua transferuntur ad vitam gloriæ. Quod si ad tempus in purgatorio detineantur, manent ibidem in caritate et gratia, et vehementissime adspirant ad gloriam, cujus dilatio eis ineffabiliter est pœnosa. Hinc in Evangelio asserit Christus: Qui credit in me, non morietur in æternum; itemque, Si quis sermonem meum servaverit, non gustabit mortem in æternum.
paras.en: Further, the vanity, instability and misery of the reprobate having been described, there is added, so that opposites set side by side may show more clearly, the character, happiness and glory of the elect: [[5:16|But the just shall live for evermore|Justi autem in perpetuum vivent]]: for in this world they live by charity, which [[1 Cor 13:8|never falleth away|nunquam excidit]], and in the world to come by blessed enjoyment [of God]. And so here they live the life of grace, from which they are carried over to the life of glory. And if for a time they are held back in purgatory, they remain there in charity and grace, and long most vehemently for glory, whose delay is painful to them beyond words. Hence Christ declares in the Gospel: He that [[John 11:26|believeth in me shall not die for ever|Qui credit in me, non morietur in æternum]]; and again, [[John 8:52|If any man keep my word, he shall not taste death for ever|Si quis sermonem meum servaverit, non gustabit mortem in æternum]].

paras.t: Et apud Dominum est merces eorum: id est, tota eorum salus ac præmium essentiale consistit in Deo, videlicet in immediata, clara, faciali ac fruitiva visione ipsius. Accidentale autem præmium consistit in rebus et objectis creatis, ad Deum relatis: præsertim in Christi humanitate, deinde in gloriosissimæ Virginis intuitione, ac deinceps in omnium supernorum civium mutua contuitione, societate, dilectione, communione. Hinc ait in prima sua Canonica Joannes apostolus: Nunc filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit quid erimus. Scimus quoniam quum apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est. Paulus quoque: Videmus, inquit, nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciem.
paras.en: [[5:16|And their reward is with the Lord|Et apud Dominum est merces eorum]]: that is, their whole salvation and essential reward consists in God, namely in the immediate, clear, face-to-face and enjoying vision of him. The accidental reward [that is, the joy added to the essential reward, which is the vision of God itself] consists in created things and objects referred to God: above all in the humanity of Christ, then in beholding the most glorious Virgin, and after that in the mutual beholding, fellowship, love and communion of all the citizens on high. Hence John the apostle says in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 3:2|we are now the sons of God: and it hath not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he shall appear we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is|Nunc filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit quid erimus. Scimus quoniam quum apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est]]. Paul also: [[1 Cor 13:12|We see now|Videmus]], he says, [[1 Cor 13:12|through a glass in a dark manner: but then face to face|nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciem]].

paras.t: Et cogitatio illorum apud Altissimum. In hac etenim vita conantur cogitationes suas stabilire in Deo, juxta illud, Jacta cogitatum tuum in Dominum; et tota eorum intentio fertur in Deum, ad cujus honorem ac gloriam ordinant se et omnia sua. Porro in patria cogitatio eorum est immobilitata in Deo, nec ibi sunt cogitationes volubiles sicut modo. Nulla vero potest ibi evagatio cordis consistere: quoniam quidquid aliud cogitant quam Deum, indeviabiliter referunt in eum.
paras.en: [[5:16|And the care of them with the most High|Et cogitatio illorum apud Altissimum]] [Latin cogitatio, 'thought', where the Douay-Rheims has 'care': Denis takes it of their thoughts]. For in this life they strive to make their thoughts steadfast in God, according to that saying, [[Ps 54:23|Cast thy care upon the Lord|Jacta cogitatum tuum in Dominum]] [Denis has cogitatum, 'thy thought', for the Vulgate's curam]; and their whole intention is borne towards God, to whose honour and glory they order themselves and all that is theirs. But in the fatherland their thought is made fast in God, and there are no shifting thoughts there as now. No wandering of the heart can exist there, for whatever else than God they think of, they refer to him without turning aside.

paras.t: Ideo accipient regnum decoris de manu Domini, id est splendidissimum illud regnum cœleste, de omnipotenti liberalitate Salvatoris: qui dicet, Venite, benedicti Patris mei, percipite regnum quod vobis paratum est ab origine mundi. De quo ait Propheta: Domine, dilexi decorem domus tuæ, et locum habitationis gloriæ tuæ; et Isaias: Non erit tibi sol amplius ad lucendum per diem, nec splendor lunæ illuminabit te; sed erit tibi Dominus in lucem sempiternam, et Deus tuus in gloriam tuam.
paras.en: [[5:17|Therefore shall they receive a kingdom of glory|Ideo accipient regnum decoris]] [decoris, 'of beauty', where the Douay-Rheims has 'of glory'; hence the psalm verse below on the beauty, decorem, of God's house] [[5:17|at the hand of the Lord|de manu Domini]], that is, that most splendid heavenly kingdom, from the almighty bounty of the Saviour, who will say: [[Matt 25:34|Come, ye blessed of my Father, possess you the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world|Venite, benedicti Patris mei, percipite regnum quod vobis paratum est ab origine mundi]]. Of which the Prophet says: [[Ps 25:8|I have loved, O Lord, the beauty of thy house; and the place where thy glory dwelleth.|Domine, dilexi decorem domus tuæ, et locum habitationis gloriæ tuæ]] And Isaias: [[Is 60:19|Thou shalt no more have the sun for thy light by day, neither shall the brightness of the moon enlighten thee: but the Lord shall be unto thee for an everlasting light, and thy God for thy glory.|Non erit tibi sol amplius ad lucendum per diem, nec splendor lunæ illuminabit te; sed erit tibi Dominus in lucem sempiternam, et Deus tuus in gloriam tuam]]

paras.t: Et diadema speciei de manu Domini, id est coronam pulchritudinis gloriosæ, quæ est aurea, scilicet præmium essentiale. De qua fertur in Psalmo: Posuisti in capite ejus coronam de lapide pretioso; itemque, Gloria et honore coronasti eum, Domine.
paras.en: [[5:17|And a crown of beauty at the hand of the Lord|Et diadema speciei de manu Domini]], that is, the crown of glorious beauty which is the *aurea*, namely the essential reward [the aurea, 'golden crown', is the schoolmen's name for the essential reward of the blessed, as distinct from the aureola, the lesser crown added for particular victories]. Of which it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 20:4|thou hast set on his head a crown of precious stones|Posuisti in capite ejus coronam de lapide pretioso]]; and again, [[Ps 8:6|thou hast crowned him with glory and honour|Gloria et honore coronasti eum]], O Lord.

paras.t: Quoniam dextera sua teget eos, id est, per virtutem gratiosæ suæ præsentiæ hic eos operiet, eisque obumbrabit contra æstum tentationum et impugnationes concupiscentiarum; et brachio suo defendet illos, id est, virtute et omnipotentia sua atque per dona gratiæ suæ contra invisibiles ac visibiles hostes eos tuebitur: non ut non impugnentur, sed ne finaliter ac spiritualiter superentur, sed magis prævaleant: quemadmodum scriptum est, Dominus fortitudo plebis suæ, et protector salvationum Christi sui est. Ideo exoramus: Custodi me, Domine, ut pupillam oculi; sub umbra alarum tuarum protege me. Hinc hortatur Apostolus: Confortamini in Domino, et in potentia virtutis ejus. Et apud Isaiam inducitur: Super omnem gloriam protectio erit in umbraculum diei ab æstu, et in securitatem et absconsionem a turbine et a pluvia. Hoc est quod promittitur in Psalmo: Scapulis suis obumbrabit tibi, et sub pennis ejus sperabis; scuto circumdabit te veritas ejus.
paras.en: [[5:17|For with his right hand he will cover them|Quoniam dextera sua teget eos]], that is, by the power of his gracious presence he will cover them here, and overshadow them against the heat of temptations and the assaults of the concupiscences; [[5:17|and with his holy arm he will defend them|et brachio suo defendet illos]], that is, by his power and almightiness, and through the gifts of his grace, he will protect them against enemies invisible and visible: not so that they are not attacked, but so that they are not in the end and spiritually overcome, and rather prevail; as it is written: [[Ps 27:8|The Lord is the strength of his people, and the protector of the salvation of his anointed.|Dominus fortitudo plebis suæ, et protector salvationum Christi sui est]] Therefore we pray: [[Ps 16:8|keep me, as the apple of thy eye. Protect me under the shadow of thy wings|Custodi me, Domine, ut pupillam oculi; sub umbra alarum tuarum protege me]]. Hence the Apostle exhorts: [[Eph 6:10|be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his power|Confortamini in Domino, et in potentia virtutis ejus]]. And in Isaias it is set down: [[Is 4:5|Over all the glory shall be a protection|Super omnem gloriam protectio]] [[Is 4:6|for a shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a security and covert from the whirlwind, and from rain|erit in umbraculum diei ab æstu, et in securitatem et absconsionem a turbine et a pluvia]]. This is what is promised in the Psalm: [[Ps 90:4|He will overshadow thee with his shoulders: and under his wings thou shalt trust.|Scapulis suis obumbrabit tibi, et sub pennis ejus sperabis]] [[Ps 90:5|His truth shall compass thee with a shield|scuto circumdabit te veritas ejus]].

paras.t: Consequenter describitur impiorum punitio, magis quam ante in speciali: et loquitur de Deo quasi de homine judicante, irato, seque armante, et alios in adjutorium assumente adversus reos. Frequenter equidem loquitur Scriptura de Deo more humano, ut humanæ mentis imbecillitas amplius informetur, ac fortius compungatur.
paras.en: Next the punishment of the wicked is described, more in particular than before; and it speaks of God as of a man who judges, is angry, arms himself and takes others to help him against the guilty. Scripture indeed often speaks of God in human fashion, so that the weakness of the human mind may be the better instructed and the more strongly pricked to compunction.

paras.t: Et accipiet armaturam zelus illius: id est, amor Dei ad justitiam, et zelatio ejus contra iniquitatem, per modum armantis se procedet contra iniquos. Porro arma Dei sunt, omnipotentia, justitia, veritas ejus: quæ dicitur accipere, quando per ea procedit in actum, juxta illud in Apocalypsi: Gratias agimus tibi, Domine Deus omnipotens, qui accepisti virtutem tuam magnam. Unde orat vir sanctus: Apprehende arma et scutum, et exsurge in adjutorium mihi. Sic homo dicitur pedem suum accipere, quando cum eo aliquem trudit.
paras.en: [[5:18|And his zeal will take armour|Et accipiet armaturam zelus illius]]: that is, God's love for justice and his zeal against iniquity will go forth against the wicked after the manner of one arming himself. Now the arms of God are his almightiness, his justice and his truth, which he is said to take when he goes forth into act by them, according to that in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 11:17|We give thee thanks, O Lord God Almighty|Gratias agimus tibi, Domine Deus omnipotens]], [[Apoc 11:17|because thou hast taken to thee thy great power|qui accepisti virtutem tuam magnam]]. Hence the holy man prays: [[Ps 34:2|Take hold of arms and shield: and rise up to help me.|Apprehende arma et scutum, et exsurge in adjutorium mihi]] So a man is said to take up his foot when he thrusts at someone with it.

paras.t: Et armabit, id est, expeditam efficacemque faciet, creaturam ad ultionem inimicorum, id est, ad puniendum per creaturam subjectorum vitia iniquorum, qui sunt adversarii Dei: quos Deo jubente ignis succendet, et cetera elementa affligent, impressionesque aeris perterrebunt, sicut Christus prædixit: Erunt signa in sole et luna et stellis, et in terra pressura gentium præ confusione sonitus maris et fluctuum.
paras.en: [[5:18|And he will arm|Et armabit]], that is, will make ready and effective, [[5:18|the creature for the revenge of his enemies|creaturam ad ultionem inimicorum]], that is, to punish through the creature the vices of the wicked subject to it, who are the adversaries of God: whom, at God's command, fire will burn, the other elements will afflict, and the disturbances of the air [that is, storms, lightning and the like] will terrify, as Christ foretold: [[Luke 21:25|there shall be signs in the sun and in the moon and in the stars; and upon the earth distress of nations, by reason of the confusion of the roaring of the sea, and of the waves|Erunt signa in sole et luna et stellis, et in terra pressura gentium præ confusione sonitus maris et fluctuum]].

paras.t: Induet pro thorace justitiam, id est, propria justitia utetur pro forti lorica; et accipiet pro galea judicium certum: id est, tam evidenter justum exercebit judicium, quod nullus poterit reclamare, omnesque scient rectissimum ejus esse judicium.
paras.en: [[5:19|He will put on justice as a breastplate|Induet pro thorace justitiam]], that is, he will use his own justice as a strong coat of mail; [[5:19|and will take true judgment instead of a helmet|et accipiet pro galea judicium certum]]: that is, he will exercise a judgment so evidently just that no one will be able to protest against it, and all will know his judgment to be most right.

paras.t: Sumet scutum inexpugnabile, æquitatem: id est, æquitate sua pietati contemperata, pro invincibili et imperforabili scuto utetur.
paras.en: [[5:20|He will take equity for an invincible shield|Sumet scutum inexpugnabile, æquitatem]]: that is, he will use his equity, tempered with mercy, as an invincible shield that cannot be pierced.

paras.t: Acuet autem diram iram in lanceam: id est, severa ultione tanquam lancea punget reos; et pugnabit cum illo orbis terrarum contra insensatos: id est, terra, et contenta in ea, Deo jubente, impiorum angebunt tormenta, et creaturæ Creatoris sui ulciscentur injuriam. Nam et maximi erunt tunc terræ motus, caligo, et tempestates.
paras.en: [[5:21|And he will sharpen his severe wrath for a spear|Acuet autem diram iram in lanceam]]: that is, he will pierce the guilty with severe vengeance as with a spear; [[5:21|and the whole world shall fight with him against the unwise|et pugnabit cum illo orbis terrarum contra insensatos]]: that is, the earth and what it contains, at God's command, will heighten the torments of the wicked, and the creatures will avenge the wrong done to their Creator. For then there will be very great earthquakes, darkness and storms.

paras.t: Ibunt directe emissiones fulgurum: id est, coruscationes terribiles dirigentur in impios, et horrenda tunc fient tonitrua, multo majora quam olim in Ægypto; et tanquam a bene curvato arcu nubium exterminabuntur: id est, sicut lineæ quæ apparent in iride, quando sunt nubes in aere, cito disparent et dissolvuntur; sic impii expellentur a superficie terræ, et ab electorum cohabitatione; et ad certum locum insilient, id est, in profunda inferorum projicientur, terra os suum aperiente, eosque absorbente: et ibi, juxta Isaiam, claudentur in carcere.
paras.en: [[5:22|Then shafts of lightning shall go directly|Ibunt directe emissiones fulgurum]]: that is, terrible flashes will be aimed at the wicked, and dreadful thunders will then be made, far greater than those once in Egypt; [[5:22|from the clouds, as from a bow well bent, they shall be shot out|et tanquam a bene curvato arcu nubium exterminabuntur]] [Denis takes exterminabuntur, 'they shall be shot out', of the wicked: 'they shall be driven out']: that is, as the bands that appear in the rainbow when there are clouds in the air quickly vanish and dissolve, so the wicked will be driven from the face of the earth and from dwelling with the elect; [[5:22|and shall fly to the mark|et ad certum locum insilient]] [literally 'shall leap to a fixed place'], that is, they will be cast into the depths of hell, the earth opening its mouth and swallowing them up; and there, according to Isaias, [[Is 24:22|they shall be shut up there in prison|claudentur in carcere]].

paras.t: Et a petrosa ira plenæ mittentur grandines, id est, ab ira et rigorositate Dei, instar petrarum acuta ac dura, emittentur grandines maximæ, velut saxa, super iniquos. De his in Apocalypsi multa dicuntur. Figuraque horum fuerunt quæ sub Moyse in Ægypto fiebant: ubi ignis, grando et fulgura pariter ferebantur. Unde in Psalmo: Pluet super peccatores laqueos; ignis, sulfur et spiritus procellarum, pars calicis (id est pœnæ) eorum. Excandescet in illos aqua maris: id est, mare sua elevatione, turbatione ac sonitu, quasi iratum se monstrabit adversus malignos; et flumina concurrent duriter, id est, terribiliter confluent, quasi furentia, et exuntia sua loca.
paras.en: [[5:23|And thick hail shall be cast upon them from the stone casting wrath|Et a petrosa ira plenæ mittentur grandines]]: that is, from the wrath and rigour of God, sharp and hard like stones, very great hailstones like rocks will be sent forth upon the wicked. Of these many things are said in the Apocalypse[[Apoc 8:7||]][[Apoc 11:19||]][[Apoc 16:21||]]. And a figure of these were the things done under Moses in Egypt, where fire, hail and lightning were borne along together[[Ex 9:24||]][[Ex 9:23||]]. Hence in the Psalm: [[Ps 10:7|He shall rain snares upon sinners: fire and brimstone, and storms of winds, shall be the portion of their cup|Pluet super peccatores laqueos; ignis, sulfur et spiritus procellarum, pars calicis]] (that is, of their punishment). [[5:23|The water of the sea shall rage against them|Excandescet in illos aqua maris]]: that is, the sea, by its rising, its tossing and its roar, will show itself as it were angry against the wicked; [[5:23|and the rivers shall run together in a terrible manner|et flumina concurrent duriter]], that is, they will flow together terribly, as if raging, and going out of their places.

paras.t: Contra illos stabit spiritus virtutis, id est ventus fortis, vel angelica virtus maledictos accusans, et ministeria exhibens in miraculosa prædictorum productione; et tanquam turbo venti dividet illos ab electis, sicut in Evangelio legitur: Exibunt angeli, et separabunt malos de medio justorum, et mittent illos in caminum ignis.
paras.en: [[5:24|A mighty wind shall stand up against them|Contra illos stabit spiritus virtutis]] [spiritus virtutis, literally 'a spirit of power': hence Denis's two readings], that is, a strong wind, or an angelic power accusing the accursed and doing service in the miraculous bringing about of the things foretold; [[5:24|and as a whirlwind shall divide them|et tanquam turbo venti dividet illos]] from the elect, as we read in the Gospel: [[Matt 13:49|The angels shall go out, and shall separate the wicked from among the just|Exibunt angeli, et separabunt malos de medio justorum]], [[Matt 13:50|and shall cast them into the furnace of fire|et mittent illos in caminum ignis]].

paras.t: Inde subditur: et ad eremum perducet omnem terram iniquitatis illorum, id est, terrenam et carnalem congregationem impiorum impellet ad locum infernalem: quæ est terra desolatissima, infructuosa, terra famis et sitis, atque imago mortis. De qua sanctus Job loquitur: Dimitte me antequam vadam, et non revertar, ad terram tenebrosam et opertam mortis caligine, terram miseriæ et tenebrarum; ubi umbra mortis, et nullus ordo, sed sempiternus horror inhabitat.
paras.en: Then is added: [[5:24|and their iniquity shall bring all the earth to a desert|et ad eremum perducet omnem terram iniquitatis illorum]] [Denis reads iniquitatis, 'he shall bring the whole land of their iniquity to a desert', where the Vulgate has iniquitas, 'their iniquity']: that is, he will drive the earthly and carnal congregation of the wicked to the place of hell, which is a land most desolate and fruitless, a land of hunger and thirst, and the image of death. Of which holy Job speaks: [[Job 10:20|Suffer me|Dimitte me]] [[Job 10:21|before I go and return no more, to a land that is dark and covered with the mist of death|antequam vadam, et non revertar, ad terram tenebrosam et opertam mortis caligine]], [[Job 10:22|a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death, and no order, but everlasting horror dwelleth|terram miseriæ et tenebrarum; ubi umbra mortis, et nullus ordo, sed sempiternus horror inhabitat]]

paras.t: Et malignitas evertet sedes potentium: id est, impietas et abusus potentium erunt causa, quod ipsi cum sua potestate dejicientur ac disperibunt. De quibus sequenti capitulo legitur: Potentes potenter tormenta patientur.
paras.en: [[5:24|And wickedness shall overthrow the thrones of the mighty|Et malignitas evertet sedes potentium]]: that is, the impiety and abuse of power of the mighty will be the cause of their being cast down and perishing together with their power. Of whom we read in the following chapter: [[Wis 6:7|The mighty shall be mightily tormented|Potentes potenter tormenta patientur]].

paras.t: Quum ergo hæc ita se habeant, Melior, id est virtuosior atque salubrior, est sapientia, per quam Deo adhæretur ac deservitur, et præfata mala horribilia evadentur, quam vires corporales potentium; et vir prudens, qui discrete se habet, et vitiis spretis, inhæret virtutibus, rationabile obsequium exhibens Deo, melior est quam fortis corpore, secundum quod talis. De quo Amos propheta testatur: Peribit fuga a veloce, et fortis non salvabit animam suam. Juxta hunc modum et Salomon dixit: Melior est patiens viro forti; et qui dominatur animo suo, expugnatore urbium.
paras.en: Since, then, these things are so, [[Wis 6:1|Wisdom|est sapientia]], by which God is cleaved to and served and the aforesaid horrible evils are escaped, [[Wis 6:1|is better|Melior]], that is, more virtuous and more wholesome, [[Wis 6:1|than strength|quam vires]], the bodily strength of the mighty; [[Wis 6:1|and a wise man|et vir prudens]], who bears himself with discretion and, spurning vices, cleaves to virtues, offering God a reasonable service, is better [[Wis 6:1|than a strong man|quam fortis]] in body, as such. Of whom Amos the prophet testifies: [[Amos 2:14|Flight shall perish from the swift|Peribit fuga a veloce]], [[Amos 2:14|neither shall the strong save his life|et fortis non salvabit animam suam]]. In the same way Solomon also said: [[Prov 16:32|The patient man is better than the valiant: and he that ruleth his spirit, than he that taketh cities.|Melior est patiens viro forti; et qui dominatur animo suo, expugnatore urbium]]

paras.t: Ecce quam terribiliter descripta sunt hic futurum judicium, supplicia reproborum, et consummatio mundi. Merito ergo dixit S. Hieronymus: Sive comedo, sive bibo, sive aliud quid ago, semper videtur mihi tuba illa sonare in auribus meis: Surgite, mortui, venite ad judicium. Si Sanctus ille ita expavit, qualiter nos formidare oportet, ac vivere timorate? Præsertim quum et beatissimus princeps dicat Apostolorum: Adveniet autem dies Domini tanquam fur: in quo cœli magno impetu transient, elementa vero calore solventur, terra autem et quæ in ipsa sunt opera, exurentur. Quum ergo hæc omnia dissolvenda sint, quales oportet nos esse in sanctis conversationibus et pietatibus, exspectantes et properantes in adventum diei Domini, per quem cœli ardentes solventur, et elementa ignis ardore tabescent?
paras.en: See how terribly the judgment to come, the punishments of the reprobate and the consummation of the world are described here. Rightly, then, did St Jerome say: Whether I eat, or drink, or do anything else, that trumpet always seems to me to be sounding in my ears: Arise, ye dead, come to judgment. If that holy man was so afraid, how ought we to fear, and to live in the fear of God? Above all since the most blessed prince of the Apostles also says: [[2 Pet 3:10|But the day of the Lord shall come as a thief, in which the heavens shall pass away with great violence and the elements shall be melted with heat and the earth and the works which are in it shall be burnt up.|Adveniet autem dies Domini tanquam fur: in quo cœli magno impetu transient, elementa vero calore solventur, terra autem et quæ in ipsa sunt opera, exurentur]] [[2 Pet 3:11|Seeing then that all these things are to be dissolved, what manner of people ought you to be in holy conversation and godliness?|Quum ergo hæc omnia dissolvenda sint, quales oportet nos esse in sanctis conversationibus et pietatibus]] [Denis reads *nos*, “we”, for *vos*, “you”], [[2 Pet 3:12|Looking for and hasting unto the coming of the day of the Lord, by which the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with the burning heat?|exspectantes et properantes in adventum diei Domini, per quem cœli ardentes solventur, et elementa ignis ardore tabescent?]]

paras.t: Postremo et id sciendum, quia quod dictum est hic de armatura Dei, consonat ei, vel sumptum videtur ex eo, quod apud Isaiam scriptum est: Indutus est Dominus justitia ut lorica, et galea salutis in capite ejus; indutus est vestimentis ultionis, et opertus est quasi pallio zeli, sicut ad vindictam, quasi ad retributionem indignationis hostibus suis, et vicissitudinem inimicis.
paras.en: Lastly, this too is to be known: that what is said here of the armour of God agrees with, or seems to be taken from, what is written in Isaias: [[Is 59:17|He put on justice as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation upon his head: he put on the garments of vengeance, and was clad with zeal as with a cloak.|Indutus est Dominus justitia ut lorica, et galea salutis in capite ejus; indutus est vestimentis ultionis, et opertus est quasi pallio zeli]] [Denis adds *Dominus*, “the Lord”, as subject], [[Is 59:18|As unto revenge, as it were to repay wrath to his adversaries, and a reward to his enemies|sicut ad vindictam, quasi ad retributionem indignationis hostibus suis, et vicissitudinem inimicis]].

8.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI OCTAVI : ATTINGIT ERGO A FINE USQUE AD FINEM FORTITER.
8.title_en: Explanation of the eighth chapter: She reacheth therefore from end to end mightily

paras.t: Adhuc de excellentia et effectibus increatæ Sapientiæ, et qualiter se ad eam habuerit, et quid fructus ex ea sit consecutus, prosequitur auctor in isto capitulo.
paras.en: In this chapter the author continues on the excellence and the effects of the uncreated Wisdom, and on how he stood towards her, and what fruit he obtained from her.

paras.t: Attingit ergo a fine usque ad finem fortiter. Hæc etenim Sapientia quum sit incircumscriptibilis, ubique est præsens, et omnia penetrat, ipsisque essentiis rerum illabitur. Idcirco ab uno fine universi usque ad alium ejus finem, seu de uno extremo mundi ad aliud ejus extremum, attingit, nec infra hos limites terminatur. Hinc in Ecclesiastico protestatur: Gyrum cœli circuivi sola, et profundum abyssi penetravi. Insuper, quum Sapientia ista sit vere æterna, attingit a fine, id est a termino in quo mundus incepit, usque ad terminum in quo mundus sensibilis iste deficiet. Propter quod in Proverbiis fatetur: Quando præparabat cœlos, aderam; quando certa lege et gyro vallabat abyssos. Rursus, Attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter: quia sicut per eam omnia facta sunt potenter, sic per eam gubernantur omnia sapienter. Unde subjungitur: et disponit omnia suaviter, id est, cuncta regit et ordinat convenienter, secundum naturam uniuscujusque eorum, per media apta ad finem congruum sibi, ad quem unicuique inclinationem indidit naturalem. Nam etsi hominem ad supernaturalem condidit finem, nihilo minus impressit ei naturalem inclinationem ad felicitatem: et supernaturalis illa beatitudo, est homini incomparabiliter melior ac delectabilior quam naturalis felicitas. Hinc et in Job asseritur: Universorum finem considerat, et omnia quæ sub cælo sunt, respicit. Istud Christus sapientia Patris in Evangelio compendiosissime docet, prohibens sollicitudinem temporalium immoderatam, volens nos in Deo tanquam in providissimo, piissimo ac fidelissimo patre confidere, et declarans etiam irrationalia et inanimata a divina providentia procurari: Respicite, inquiens, volatilia cœli, quoniam non seminant neque metunt; et Pater vester cœlestis pascit ea.
paras.en: [[8:1|She reacheth, therefore, from end to end mightily|Attingit ergo a fine usque ad finem fortiter]]. For since this Wisdom is uncircumscribable [that is, not contained within any bounds of place], she is present everywhere, and penetrates all things, and flows into the very essences of things. Therefore she reaches from one end of the universe to its other end, or from one extremity of the world to its other extremity, and is not bounded within these limits. Hence she declares in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 24:8|I alone have compassed the circuit of heaven, and have penetrated into the bottom of the deep|Gyrum cœli circuivi sola, et profundum abyssi penetravi]]. Moreover, since this Wisdom is truly eternal, she reaches from the end, that is, from the term at which the world began, to the term at which this sensible world shall fail. For this reason she confesses in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:27|When he prepared the heavens, I was present: when with a certain law, and compass, he enclosed the depths|Quando præparabat cœlos, aderam; quando certa lege et gyro vallabat abyssos]]. Again, [[8:1|She reacheth, therefore, from end to end mightily|Attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter]]: because as all things were made mightily through her, so all things are governed wisely through her. Hence it is added: [[8:1|and ordereth all things sweetly|et disponit omnia suaviter]], that is, she rules and orders all things fittingly, according to the nature of each of them, by means suited to the end proper to it, towards which she has given each a natural inclination. For although she created man for a supernatural end, she nonetheless impressed on him a natural inclination to happiness; and that supernatural beatitude is incomparably better and more delightful for man than natural happiness. Hence it is also said in Job: [[Job 28:3|the end of all things he considereth|Universorum finem considerat]], [[Job 28:24|and looketh on all things that are under heaven|et omnia quæ sub cælo sunt, respicit]]. Christ, the wisdom of the Father, teaches this most concisely in the Gospel, forbidding immoderate anxiety about temporal things, wishing us to trust in God as in a most provident, most loving and most faithful father, and declaring that even irrational and inanimate things are cared for by divine providence: [[Matt 6:26|Behold|Respicite]], he says, [[Matt 6:26|the birds of the air, for they neither sow, nor do they reap|volatilia cœli, quoniam non seminant neque metunt]]; [[Matt 6:26|and your heavenly Father feedeth them|et Pater vester cœlestis pascit ea]].

paras.t: Denique subtiliores ac meliores philosophi, ex consideratione decentissimi ordinis rerum, et propria uniuscujusque adornatione, proprietate, eventu, dixerunt hæc omnia sub divina providentia cadere.
