Unde decimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus: Plotinus Platonicus de Providentia disputans, eam a summo Deo usque ad hæc terrena et ima pertingere, flosculorum ac foliorum pulchritudine comprobat: quæ omnia quasi abjecta ac velocissime pereuntia, decentissimos formarum suarum numeros habere non posse affirmat, nisi inde formentur, ubi forma intelligibilis et incommutabilis simul habens omnia, perseverat. Propter hoc, quinto de Civitate Dei rursus disseruit Augustinus: Deus nec exigui et contemptibilis animantis viscera, nec herbæ flosculum, nec arboris folium sine suarum convenientia partium et quadam veluti pace reliquit. Idcirco et in libro de Causis pulchre probatur, quod causa prima regit res omnes per finem decoris, id est cum summo decore. Siquidem inferiora regit per superiora, irrationalia per intellectualia, homines per angelos, sed et per se ipsam aliqua agit in rebus. Et quamvis in se et per se universa disponit, providentiam tamen per causas secundas in multis exsequitur.
paras.en: Finally, the subtler and better philosophers, from considering the most seemly order of things, and the proper adornment, property and outcome of each, said that all these things fall under divine providence. Hence Augustine says in the tenth book of the City of God: Plotinus the Platonist, disputing on Providence, proves from the beauty of little flowers and leaves that it reaches from the highest God down to these earthly and lowest things: all of which, being as it were cast off and perishing very swiftly, he affirms could not have the most seemly proportions [Latin *numeros*, "numbers", that is, measured harmonies] of their forms unless they were formed from that place where the intelligible and unchangeable form, having all things together, abides. For this reason Augustine again discoursed in the fifth book of the City of God: God has left neither the entrails of a small and contemptible animal, nor the little flower of a herb, nor the leaf of a tree, without the agreement of its parts and a kind of peace. Therefore it is also finely proved in the Book of Causes that the first cause rules all things through the end of comeliness, that is, with the highest comeliness. For it rules lower things through higher, irrational things through intellectual ones, men through angels; but it also does some things in creatures by itself. And although in itself and by itself it disposes all things, yet in many things it carries out its providence through secondary causes.

paras.t: Præterea, quamvis in rerum regimine multa videantur indecentia et injusta, ut quod justi ab impiis opprimuntur, ac consimilia; tamen in ordine ad providentiam Dei cuncta congruentissime disponuntur. Et frequenter quod esse videtur pœna, est medicina; et quod reputatur injuria, est corona. Sed in talibus occulta sunt et latent nos divina judicia.
paras.en: Moreover, although in the governing of things many things seem unseemly and unjust, as that the just are oppressed by the wicked, and the like, yet in relation to the providence of God all things are most fittingly ordered. And often what seems to be a punishment is a medicine, and what is reckoned an injury is a crown. But in such matters the divine judgements are hidden and concealed from us.

paras.t: Hanc, scilicet increatam Sapientiam, et etiam infusam sapientiam quæ est donum, amavi, et exquisivi, id est, obtinere multipliciter laboravi, a juventute mea, in qua non concupiscentiæ, sed sapientiæ studui: quoniam ipsa locuta est: Ego diligentes me diligo; et qui mane vigilaverit ad me, inveniet me. Unde rursus Sapiens exhortatur: Fili, a juventute tua excipe doctrinam, et usque ad canos invenies sapientiam. Et quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere: id est, studui ei amorose ac familiariter adhærere, eamque brachiis caritatis amplecti, atque ex unione cum ea fructum actuum virtuosorum producere: quod totum tam de Sapientia increata, quam de sapientia infusa, suo potest modo intelligi. Porro in Canticis canticorum Sapientia ista increata ac genita, non sponsa, ut hic, sed sub nomine fratris et regis ac dilecti, sponsus vocatur. Cujus triplex, ut ibi expositum fuit, est sponsa: videlicet generalis, quæ est universalis Ecclesia, et etiam sponsa particularis, videlicet anima justi, sponsaque singularis, quæ est beatissima et incomparabilis Virgo Maria. Ipsa etenim sapientia dicitur sponsa, propter rationes jam tactas. Unde et in Proverbiis legitur: Dic sapientiæ, Soror mea es; et prudentiam voca amicam. Est itaque sponsa, quia amator sincerus, homo justus, seu spiritus rationalis mundus et sanctus, suscipit eam, et brachiis eam stringit amoris, et conjungit se ei, atque ex unione cum ea parit fructum virtutum. Est quoque sponsus, quoniam mentem creatam applicat sibi, et sancta succendit dilectione, spiritualiterque fecundat, atque ex ea et per eam producit opera bona, juxta illud in Isaia: Omnia opera nostra operatus es in nobis. Unde dixit Apostolus: Deus est qui operatur in nobis velle et perficere.
paras.en: [[8:2|Her|Hanc]], namely the uncreated Wisdom, and also the infused wisdom which is a gift, [[8:2|have I loved, and have sought her out|amavi, et exquisivi]], that is, I laboured in many ways to obtain her, [[8:2|from my youth|a juventute mea]], in which I applied myself not to concupiscence but to wisdom: for she herself has said: [[Prov 8:17|I love them that love me: and they that in the morning early watch for me, shall find me|Ego diligentes me diligo; et qui mane vigilaverit ad me, inveniet me]]. Hence the Wise Man exhorts again: [[Ecclus 6:18|My son, from thy youth up receive instruction, and even to thy grey hairs thou shalt find wisdom|Fili, a juventute tua excipe doctrinam, et usque ad canos invenies sapientiam]]. [[8:2|and have desired to take for my spouse|Et quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere]]: that is, I strove to cleave to her lovingly and familiarly, and to embrace her with the arms of charity, and from union with her to bring forth the fruit of virtuous acts: all of which can be understood in its own way both of the uncreated Wisdom and of infused wisdom. Further, in the Canticle of Canticles this uncreated and begotten Wisdom is called not the bride, as here, but the Bridegroom, under the name of brother[[Cant 8:1||]] and king[[Cant 1:3||]][[Cant 1:11||]] and beloved[[Cant 2:8||]] [the margin gives Cant. viii, 1; i, 3, 11; ii, v–viii: *beloved* recurs throughout chapters 2 and 5–8]. His bride, as was explained there, is threefold: namely the general bride, which is the universal Church; and also the particular bride, namely the soul of the just man; and the singular bride, who is the most blessed and incomparable Virgin Mary. For wisdom herself is called a bride, for the reasons already touched on. Hence we read in Proverbs too: [[Prov 7:4|Say to wisdom: Thou art my sister: and call prudence thy friend|Dic sapientiæ, Soror mea es; et prudentiam voca amicam]]. She is therefore a bride because the sincere lover, the just man, or the pure and holy rational spirit, receives her, and clasps her in the arms of love, and joins himself to her, and from union with her brings forth the fruit of the virtues. She is also the Bridegroom, because she draws the created mind to herself, and kindles it with holy love, and makes it spiritually fruitful, and from it and through it brings forth good works, according to that saying in Isaias: [[Is 26:12|thou hast wrought all our works for us|Omnia opera nostra operatus es in nobis]]. Hence the Apostle said: [[Phil 2:13|it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish|Deus est qui operatur in nobis velle et perficere]].

paras.t: Et amator factus sum formæ illius, id est pulchritudinis Sapientiæ increatæ, imo et sapientiæ infusæ, quæ est pulcherrimus mentis ornatus, increatæ menti ac Sapientiæ ejus æternæ eam conformans. At vero, quamvis pulchritudo toti supergloriosissimæ conveniat Trinitati, attamen Sapientiæ genitæ seu Verbo æterno appropriatur. Verbum namque est emanatio intellectus, ad quod pertinet repræsentare intelligentis conceptum. Ideo quidquid Patris est, repræsentatur ac plene refulget in Filio: quod ad pulchritudinis pertinet rationem. Ideo subtilissime dixit Hilarius: Æternitas est in Patre, species in imagine, id est pulchritudo in Filio, usus in munere, id est communio in Spiritu Sancto, qui est donum Patris ac Filii.
paras.en: [[8:2|and I became a lover of her beauty|Et amator factus sum formæ illius]], that is, of the beauty of the uncreated Wisdom, nay, and of infused wisdom, which is the most beautiful adornment of the mind, conforming it to the uncreated Mind and to his eternal Wisdom. But although beauty belongs to the whole most supremely glorious Trinity, yet it is appropriated [that is, attributed especially to one Person, though common to all three] to the begotten Wisdom, or the eternal Word. For a word is an emanation of the intellect, to which it belongs to represent the concept of the one who understands. Therefore whatever is the Father's is represented and shines forth fully in the Son: which belongs to the notion of beauty. Therefore Hilary said most subtly: Eternity is in the Father, form [Latin *species*, "form" or "beauty"] in the Image, that is, beauty in the Son; use in the Gift, that is, communion in the Holy Ghost, who is the gift of the Father and the Son.

paras.t: Generositatem illius, id est nobilitatem et excellentiam Sapientiæ increatæ, imo et doni sapientiæ, glorificat, id est, præclaram et summam esse manifestat, contubernium habens Dei, id est quicumque illuminatus a Deo, et per caritatem sapientiamque infusam, societatem quamdam habens cum eo, ac Creatori cohabitans per charismata gratiæ. Talis quippe sic desuper illustratus per fidem rationibus credendorum ornatam, et infusæ sapientiæ gustum, ac contemplationis acumen, novit, confitetur, magnificat Sapientiam increatam, ejusque donum ac radium, sapientiam infusam. Et talis fuit Salomon, saltem ad tempus, qui de deitate, eminentia, ac generatione æterna increatæ ac genitæ Sapientiæ, evidenter locutus est in Proverbiis; alii quoque sancti Prophetæ, et præsertim Apostoli. Potissime autem Christus secundum quod homo, plenissime adimpletus omni supero charismate suæ perfectioni non derogante, contubernalisque Patri, sicut in Apocalypsi testatur, Sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus; declaravit nobis suam deitatem, sapientiam, excellentiamque immensam, juxta illud: Deum nemo vidit unquam; unigenitus Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarravit.
paras.en: [[8:3|her nobility|Generositatem illius]], that is, the nobility and excellence of the uncreated Wisdom, nay, and of the gift of wisdom, [[8:3|She glorifieth|glorificat]], that is, shows it to be most glorious and supreme, [[8:3|by being conversant with God|contubernium habens Dei]] [Latin *contubernium*, "sharing a dwelling", "companionship"]: that is, whoever is enlightened by God and, through charity and infused wisdom, has a certain fellowship with him, and dwells with the Creator through the gifts of grace. For such a man, thus enlightened from above by a faith furnished with reasons for the things to be believed, and by the taste of infused wisdom and keenness of contemplation, knows, confesses and magnifies the uncreated Wisdom, and her gift and ray, infused wisdom. And such was Solomon, at least for a time, who spoke plainly in Proverbs of the deity, eminence and eternal generation of the uncreated and begotten Wisdom[[Prov 8:22||]] [the margin gives Prov. viii, 22–31]; and so did the other holy Prophets, and especially the Apostles. But above all Christ as man, most fully filled with every heavenly gift that does not detract from his perfection, and companion of the Father, as he testifies in the Apocalypse, [[Apoc 3:21|am set down with my Father in his throne|Sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus]], has declared to us his deity, wisdom and boundless excellence, according to that saying: [[John 1:18|No man hath seen God at any time: the only begotten Son who is in the Bosom of the Father, he hath declared him|Deum nemo vidit unquam; unigenitus Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarravit]].

paras.t: Sed et omnium Dominus dilexit illam, id est, Deus Pater dilexit ac diligit Sapientiam istam æternam, utpote Verbum suum æternum et unicum Filium, sicut in ejus baptizatione ac transfiguratione locutus est: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacui. Diligit, inquam, cum dilectione intensive immensa, videlicet tanta, quanta se ipsum. Christum vero secundum naturam assumptam, diligit plus quam totum pariter universum, quia majus bonum voluit communicavitque ei, hoc est increatum et hypostaticum esse Verbi æterni, ad quod assumpta est humanitas Christi.
paras.en: [[8:3|yea, and the Lord of all things hath loved her|Sed et omnium Dominus dilexit illam]], that is, God the Father has loved and loves this eternal Wisdom, as being his eternal Word and only Son, as he spoke at his baptism[[Matt 3:17||]] and transfiguration: [[Matt 17:5|This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased|Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacui]]. He loves him, I say, with a love intensively boundless [that is, infinite in its strength, not merely in its extent], namely as great as that with which he loves himself. But Christ according to the nature assumed he loves more than the whole universe together, because he willed and communicated to him a greater good, that is, the uncreated and hypostatic being of the eternal Word, to which the humanity of Christ was assumed.

paras.t: Doctrix est enim disciplinæ Dei, id est moralis scientiæ, per quam homines fiunt Deo placentes. Quam disciplinam Christus in Evangelio docuit copiose, dicendo: Beati pauperes spiritu, etc. Nam de plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes. Et quamvis doctrina ista non sit causa a priori, ob quam Pater diligit Christum modis jam tactis, est tamen causa a posteriori, seu signum quod diligit ipsum. Juxta quem modum Filius in Evangelio ait: Pater non reliquit me solum: quia ego quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper. Et electrix operum illius, id est, opera veraciter virtuosa ac placita Deo, approbat et eligi facit, vitiosaque reprobat, dicens: Attendite vobis a falsis prophetis, etc.; a fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos.
paras.en: [[8:4|For it is she that teacheth the knowledge of God|Doctrix est enim disciplinæ Dei]] [Latin *disciplinæ*, "discipline", "teaching"], that is, of the moral science through which men become pleasing to God. This discipline Christ taught abundantly in the Gospel, saying: [[Matt 5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit|Beati pauperes spiritu]], etc. For [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received|de plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes]]. And although this teaching is not a cause a priori, for which the Father loves Christ in the ways already touched on, yet it is a cause a posteriori, or a sign that he loves him. In which way the Son says in the Gospel: The Father [[John 8:29|hath not left me alone. For I do always the things that please him|non reliquit me solum: quia ego quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper]]. [[8:4|and is the chooser of his works|Et electrix operum illius]], that is, she approves works truly virtuous and pleasing to God and causes them to be chosen, and condemns vicious ones, saying: [[Matt 7:15|Beware of false prophets|Attendite vobis a falsis prophetis]], etc.; [[Matt 7:16|By their fruits you shall know them|a fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos]].

paras.t: Et si divitiæ appetuntur in terra, quid sapientia locupletius? quasi dicat: Quicumque cupit et amat divitias temporales, merito debet sapientiam istam appetere et amare: quia in ea est omnium bonorum, omniumque pulchrorum ac desiderabilium plenitudo immensa. Quæ in Proverbiis contestatur: Mecum sunt divitiæ et gloria. Et iterum Salomon loquitur: Quid prodest stulto habere divitias, quum sapientiam emere non possit? quia in sapientia consistit opulentia vera. Nam et vita æterna est in actu sapientiæ, qui est primæ et summæ contemplatio veritatis. Unde locutus est Isaias: Divitiæ salutis sapientia et scientia. Quæ omnia operatur. Increata namque Sapientia, omnium est creatrix, juxta quod in Evangelio legitur: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Et cuncta quotidie moderatur ac administrat et regit, quemadmodum testatur: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Quum igitur omnia operetur, constat quod omnium perfectiones in ea consistant, et ipsa universis sit ditior.
paras.en: [[8:5|And if riches be desired in life|Et si divitiæ appetuntur in terra]] [Denis's text reads *in terra*, "on earth"; a marginal note gives the reading *in vita*, "in life", which is the Vulgate's], [[8:5|what is richer than wisdom|quid sapientia locupletius]]? as if to say: Whoever desires and loves temporal riches ought by rights to desire and love this wisdom: because in her is the boundless fullness of all goods and of all things beautiful and desirable. She declares in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:18|With me are riches and glory|Mecum sunt divitiæ et gloria]]. And again Solomon says: [[Prov 17:16|What doth it avail a fool to have riches, seeing he cannot buy wisdom?|Quid prodest stulto habere divitias, quum sapientiam emere non possit?]]? because true wealth consists in wisdom. For eternal life too lies in the act of wisdom, which is the contemplation of the first and highest truth. Hence Isaias said: [[Is 33:6|riches of salvation, wisdom and knowledge|Divitiæ salutis sapientia et scientia]]. [[8:5|which maketh all things|Quæ omnia operatur]]. For the uncreated Wisdom is the creatress of all things, according to what we read in the Gospel: [[John 1:3|All things were made by him|Omnia per ipsum facta sunt]]. And daily she moderates, administers and rules all things, as he testifies: [[John 5:17|My Father worketh until now; and I work|Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor]]. Since therefore she works all things, it is clear that the perfections of all things are found in her, and that she is richer than all.

paras.t: Si autem sensus operatur, id est, si intellectus creatus, seu humana notitia, est activa diversorum effectuum, quis horum quæ sunt, magis quam illa, est artifex? tanquam dicat: Utique nullus, quoniam Sapientia increata est universorum exemplaris effectivaque causa, a qua cuncta procedunt, sicut artificiata a suo artifice. Ex quo sequitur, quod nihil potentius sapientia: ideoque, si quæratur potestas, ipsa vere omnipotens, summe est expetenda.
paras.en: [[8:6|And if sense do work|Si autem sensus operatur]], that is, if the created intellect, or human knowledge, brings about various effects, [[8:6|who is a more artful worker than she of those things that are?|quis horum quæ sunt, magis quam illa, est artifex?]]? as if to say: Surely none, since the uncreated Wisdom is the exemplar and efficient cause of all things, from which all things proceed as works of art from their craftsman. From which it follows that nothing is more powerful than wisdom; and therefore, if power is sought, she, being truly almighty, is to be sought above all.

paras.t: Et si justitiam quis diligit, id est, si quis appetit esse virtuosus. Justitia enim uno modo dicitur esse omnis seu quælibet virtus, quoniam per unamquamque virtutem homo se habet ut decet ac debet, debitumque impendit Deo obsequium: quod etiam de misericordia clarum est, quia per eam proximis subvenitur, quod a Deo præcipitur. Labores hujus magnas habent virtutes: id est, actus quibus pro sapientia obtinenda ac possidenda laboratur, annexas habent ac promerentur virtutes præcipuas, seu earum opera bona, sive profectuum incrementa, quemadmodum dictum est supra: Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus. Ipsa etiam increata Sapientia taliter laborantibus infundit virtutes, aut spirituales profectus. Propterea subditur: Sobrietatem enim, id est temperantiam, et sapientiam, id est prudentiam, docet: quia eas largitur, et qualiter utendum sit eis, inspirat; et justitiam quæ est virtus specialis, et virtutem, id est fortitudinem, quæ passionem timoris refrenat ac moderatur, et quæ ardua facit viriliter aggredi, et circa pericula mortis se strenue gerit.
paras.en: [[8:7|And if a man love justice|Et si justitiam quis diligit]], that is, if anyone desires to be virtuous. For in one sense justice is said to be every virtue, or any virtue whatever, since by each virtue a man behaves as is fitting and as he ought, and renders to God the service due to him: which is clear even of mercy, because by it our neighbours are helped, which God commands. [[8:7|her labours have great virtues|Labores hujus magnas habent virtutes]]: that is, the acts by which one labours to obtain and possess wisdom have joined to them, and merit, the chief virtues, or their good works, or increases of progress, as was said above: [[Wis 3:15|the fruit of good labours is glorious|Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus]]. The uncreated Wisdom herself also pours virtues, or spiritual progress, into those who labour so. Therefore it is added: [[8:7|for she teacheth temperance|Sobrietatem enim]] [the Latin has *sobrietatem*, "sobriety"], that is, temperance, [[8:7|and prudence|et sapientiam]] [Denis reads *sapientiam*, "wisdom", where the Vulgate has *prudentiam*], that is, prudence, she teaches: because she bestows them, and inspires how they are to be used; [[8:7|and justice|et justitiam]], which is a special virtue, [[8:7|and fortitude|et virtutem]] [Latin *virtutem*, "strength" or "virtue"], that is, fortitude, which reins in and moderates the passion of fear, and which makes one undertake hard things manfully, and bears itself bravely in the dangers of death.

paras.t: Hæ sunt quatuor cardinales virtutes. De quibus subjungitur: quibus nihil utilius est in vita hominibus: quia istæ quatuor virtutes præcipue conferunt homini ad obtinendum salutem. Verumtamen virtutes theologicæ, et etiam septem dona, sunt eis præstantiores. Sed inter virtutes morales, istæ præfulgent ac utiliores censentur. Unde et in ordine harum, cardinales (id est principales) dicuntur; vel, cardinales, quoniam aliæ virtutes morales circa ipsas versantur et reducuntur, sicut ostium in cardine vertitur. De harum quatuor virtutum cardinalium sufficientia, ratione, proprietate, et distinctione, diffuse loquitur Thomas in prima secundæ, quæstione 61.
paras.en: These are the four cardinal virtues. Of which it is added: [[8:7|which are such things as men can have nothing more profitable in life|quibus nihil utilius est in vita hominibus]]: because these four virtues especially help man to obtain salvation. Yet the theological virtues, and also the seven gifts, are more excellent than they. But among the moral virtues these shine out and are reckoned more profitable. Hence too, in the order of these, they are called cardinal (that is, principal); or cardinal, because the other moral virtues turn about them and are reduced to them, as a door turns on its hinge [Latin *cardo*, "hinge", from which *cardinalis* comes]. Of the sufficiency, nature, property and distinction of these four cardinal virtues Thomas speaks at length in the First of the Second Part, question 61.

paras.t: De quibus et Seneca in libro de Copia verborum, seu Quatuor virtutibus, pulchre tractat: Si prudentiam, inquiens, amplecteris, ubique idem eris, et prout rerum ac temporis varietas exigit, ita te illis accommodabis; nec in aliquibus te mutabis, sed magis aptabis: sicut manus eadem est, quum in palmam extenditur, et dum in pugnum restringitur. Prudentis proprium est examinare consilia, nec credulitate incauta ac facili falli. Denique fortitudinem vocat magnanimitatem. De qua scribit: Magnanimitas, quæ et fortitudo dicitur, si insit animo tuo, cum magna fiducia vives liber, intrepidus, alacer: quæ tamen si modum suum excedat, faciet virum minacem, inflatum, turbidum, inquietum, et in quascumque extollentias verborum atque factorum, neglecta honestate, festinum. Porro justitia est tacita naturæ conventio, in adjutorium multorum inventa. Justitia non nostra institutio, sed divina lex est, et vinculum societatis humanæ. Quisquis hanc sectari desideras, Deum time prius et ama, ut ameris ab eo. Amabis Deum, si eum in hoc imiteris, ut omnibus velis prodesse, nulli nocere: et tunc omnes te virum justum appellabunt, sequentur, venerabuntur ac diligent. Justus autem ut sis, non solum aliis non nocebis, sed nocentes pro viribus prohibebis. Temperantia demum a brutis te dividet, et a fœdis separabit inquinamentis, ut ratione, non passione, te regas. Hæc Seneca.
paras.en: Seneca too treats finely of them in his book On Abundance of Words, or On the Four Virtues [the work, also called *Formula vitæ honestæ*, is by Martin of Braga, though long ascribed to Seneca]: If you embrace prudence, he says, you will be the same everywhere, and as the variety of things and times requires, so you will adapt yourself to them; you will not change yourself in anything, but rather fit yourself: as the hand is the same when it is stretched out into an open palm and when it is closed into a fist. It is the mark of the prudent man to examine counsels, and not to be deceived by heedless and easy credulity. Next, he calls fortitude magnanimity. Of which he writes: If magnanimity, which is also called fortitude, is in your soul, you will live with great confidence, free, fearless, eager: yet if it exceeds its measure, it will make a man threatening, puffed up, turbulent, restless, and hasty, with no regard for what is honourable, towards every kind of vaunting in word and deed. Further, justice is a tacit agreement of nature, devised for the help of many. Justice is not an institution of ours, but a divine law, and the bond of human society. Whoever you are that desire to follow it, first fear and love God, that you may be loved by him. You will love God if you imitate him in this, that you wish to profit all and harm none: and then all will call you a just man, will follow, revere and love you. And that you may be just, you will not only not harm others, but will restrain those who do harm as far as you can. Lastly, temperance will divide you from the brutes and separate you from foul defilements, so that you govern yourself by reason, not by passion. So far Seneca.

paras.t: Et si multitudinem scientiæ, id est scientiam copiosam, desiderat quis, scit præterita, et de futuris æstimat, id est, prænoscit, et quibusdam certam, quibusdam probabilem, dat futurorum notitiam; scit versutias sermonum, id est contortas sententias, astutiasque verborum, quibus nequaquam poterit falli, et dissolutiones argumentorum. De quibus omnibus instruit suos, quibus promisit: Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri. Hinc quum quidam surrexissent de synagoga, disputantes cum beatissimo Stephano, non poterant resistere sapientiæ et Spiritui, qui loquebatur per primicerium martyrum. Signa et monstra scit, antequam fiant, id est, futura mirabilia et insolita, aliquid designantia, monstratione admirationeque digna, prænoscit. De quibus in Evangelio loquitur: Erunt signa in sole et luna. Rursus: Surget gens contra gentem, et regnum adversus regnum; et terræ motus magni erunt per loca, et pestilentiæ, et fames, terroresque de cælo, et signa magna erunt. Et apud Joelem: Dabo prodigia in cælo et in terra, sanguinem et ignem et vaporem fumi: sol convertetur in tenebras et luna in sanguinem, antequam veniat dies Domini magnus et horribilis. Et eventus temporum et seculorum, id est, quid in singulis quibusque temporibus et certis durationibus ac generationibus, fiet sive eveniet.
paras.en: [[8:8|And if a man desire much knowledge|Et si multitudinem scientiæ]], that is, abundant knowledge, [[8:8|she knoweth things past, and judgeth of things to come|desiderat quis, scit præterita, et de futuris æstimat]], that is, she knows them beforehand, and gives knowledge of things to come, certain to some, probable to others; [[8:8|she knoweth the subtilties of speeches|scit versutias sermonum]], that is, twisted sayings and cunning words, by which she can in no way be deceived, [[8:8|and the solutions of arguments|et dissolutiones argumentorum]]. In all these she instructs her own, to whom she promised: [[Luke 21:15|I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist and gainsay|Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri]]. Hence when some had risen up from the synagogue, disputing with the most blessed Stephen[[Acts 6:9||]], [[Acts 6:10|they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit that spoke|non poterant resistere sapientiæ et Spiritui, qui loquebatur]] through the first of the martyrs [Latin *primicerius*, "the first on the list", "the chief"]. [[8:8|she knoweth signs and wonders before they be done|Signa et monstra scit, antequam fiant]], that is, she knows beforehand future marvels and unwonted things, signifying something, worthy to be shown and wondered at. Of which he speaks in the Gospel: [[Luke 21:25|there shall be signs in the sun and in the moon|Erunt signa in sole et luna]]. Again: [[Luke 21:10|Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom|Surget gens contra gentem, et regnum adversus regnum]]; [[Luke 21:11|there shall be great earthquakes in divers places and pestilences and famines and terrors from heaven: and there shall be great signs|et terræ motus magni erunt per loca, et pestilentiæ, et fames, terroresque de cælo, et signa magna erunt]] [the margin gives Luke xxi, 25 only; this second quotation is Luke 21:10–11]. And in Joel: [[Joel 2:30|I will shew wonders in heaven; and in earth, blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke|Dabo prodigia in cælo et in terra, sanguinem et ignem et vaporem fumi]]: [[Joel 2:31|The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood: before the great and dreadful day of the Lord doth come|sol convertetur in tenebras et luna in sanguinem, antequam veniat dies Domini magnus et horribilis]]. [[8:8|and the events of times and ages|Et eventus temporum et seculorum]], that is, what will be done or happen in each and every time, and in fixed durations and generations.

paras.t: Proposui ergo hanc Sapientiam increatam adducere mihi ad convivandum, id est, gratiosam ejus præsentiam, inhabitationem, adventum, decrevi promereri ac adipisci, orando et alia bona agendo, ut spiritualiter epuler secum, et ipsa mecum, delectando in ea, et per ejus contemplationem, cultum, amorem, me reficiendo: quoniam ipsa in Apocalypsi testatur: Ego sto ante ostium, et pulso: si quis aperuerit mihi januam, intrabo ad illum, et cœnabo cum eo, et ipse mecum. Sciens quoniam mecum communicabit de bonis, id est, dona gratiæ suæ mihi distribuet, et spiritualiter me ditabit: quia quanto quis frequentius et affectuosius ipsam contemplatur, et ei se applicat, tanto plus crescit in donis ipsius; et erit allocutio cogitationis et tædii mei, id est, sua inspiratione et illustratione cogitationes meas diriget et purgabit, meaque tædia consolabitur et excludet: quoniam ejus irradiatio mundat, exhilarat, ac dirigit mentem, et vana atque phantastica ejicit tædia.
paras.en: [[8:9|I purposed, therefore, to take her|Proposui ergo hanc]], the uncreated Wisdom, [[8:9|to me to live with me|adducere mihi ad convivandum]] [Denis reads *convivandum*, "to feast with", where the Vulgate has *convivendum*, "to live with"; his gloss follows his reading]: that is, I resolved to merit and obtain her gracious presence, indwelling and coming, by praying and doing other good works, that I might feast with her spiritually, and she with me, by delighting in her and refreshing myself through contemplating, worshipping and loving her: for she testifies in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:20|I stand at the gate and knock|Ego sto ante ostium, et pulso]]: if any man [[Apoc 3:20|open to me the door, I will come in to him and will sup with him: and he with me|aperuerit mihi januam, intrabo ad illum, et cœnabo cum eo, et ipse mecum]]. [[8:9|knowing that she will communicate to me of her good things|Sciens quoniam mecum communicabit de bonis]], that is, she will distribute to me the gifts of her grace and will enrich me spiritually: because the more often and the more lovingly one contemplates her and applies oneself to her, the more one grows in her gifts; [[8:9|and will be a comfort in my cares and grief|et erit allocutio cogitationis et tædii mei]] [Latin *allocutio*, "a speaking to", "consolation"], that is, by her inspiration and enlightening she will direct and purify my thoughts, and will console and drive away my wearinesses: for her shining cleanses, gladdens and directs the mind, and casts out vain and fanciful wearinesses.

paras.t: Habebo propter hanc claritatem ad turbas, id est, magnæ reputationis ac famæ ero inter homines, propter sapientiam mihi infusam a Sapientia increata; et honorem apud seniores: quia eos qui in sapientia clare præfulgent, reputant honorandos.
paras.en: [[8:10|For her sake I shall have glory among the multitude|Habebo propter hanc claritatem ad turbas]], that is, I shall be of great repute and fame among men, because of the wisdom infused into me by the uncreated Wisdom; [[8:10|and honour with the ancients|et honorem apud seniores]]: because they deem those who shine out brightly in wisdom worthy of honour.

paras.t: Juvenis et acutus inveniar in judicio, id est vigorosus et subtilis ad judicandum de causis etiam arduis; et in conspectu potentium admirabilis ero, et facies principum mirabuntur me: id est, principes signa admirationis de eminentia sapientiæ meæ ostendent in vultu suo, se invicem ac me cum apparatu attonito intuendo.
paras.en: [[8:10|though I be young|Juvenis]], [[8:11|And I shall be found of a quick conceit in judgment|et acutus inveniar in judicio]], that is, vigorous and subtle in judging even difficult cases; [[8:11|and shall be admired in the sight of the mighty, and the faces of princes shall wonder at me|et in conspectu potentium admirabilis ero, et facies principum mirabuntur me]]: that is, princes will show in their faces signs of wonder at the eminence of my wisdom, looking at one another and at me with an astonished air.

paras.t: Tacentem me sustinebunt, id est, patienter ferent et præstolabuntur, quousque loqui incipiam, aut verbum interruptum resumam; et loquentem me respicient, verba sapientiæ meæ diligentissime auscultando, meamque facundiam ac peritiam admirando; et sermocinante me plura, manus ori suo imponent, id est, loqui non præsument, verba mea interrumpendo.
paras.en: [[8:12|They shall wait for me when I hold my peace|Tacentem me sustinebunt]], that is, they will bear it patiently and wait until I begin to speak, or take up again a word broken off; [[8:12|and they shall look upon me when I speak|et loquentem me respicient]], listening most attentively to the words of my wisdom, and admiring my eloquence and skill; [[8:12|and if I talk much, they shall lay their hands on their mouth|et sermocinante me plura, manus ori suo imponent]], that is, they will not presume to speak by interrupting my words.

paras.t: Propterea habebo per hanc, immortalitatem, id est, increatæ Sapientiæ ero conjunctus in vita hac, per caritatem vitamque gratiæ, et in futuro, per vitam gloriæ; et memoriam æternam his, qui post me futuri sunt, relinquam, id est, in sæculo isto per generationum successiones ero famosus usque in sæculi finem. Disponam, id est, regam, ordinabo, erudiam, populos: ad quorum gubernationem fit homo per sapientiæ eminentiam præcipue aptus; et nationes mihi erunt subditæ: quia tam caritative ac discrete ad subditos me habebo, quod libenter obedient mihi. Timebunt me audientes reges horrendi, id est, audiendo profunditatem verborum meorum, concipient reverentialem ac formidolosum affectum ad me: quemadmodum Nabuchodonosor rex metuendissimus, auditis verbis sancti Danielis, prostravit se, adoravitque eum. Et in multitudine bonus videbor: id est, tam sapienter et juste loquar, quod omnes audientes me, reputabunt me virtuosum; et in bello fortis: quia ad prævalendum invisibilibus ac visibilibus præcipue valet sapientia: quæ facit hominem ordinate procedere ac divino inniti auxilio, custoditumque esse, et consideranda considerare. Hinc in Proverbiis dictum est: Cum dispositione initur bellum; et denuo, Gubernaculis tractanda sunt bella.
paras.en: [[8:13|Moreover, by the means of her I shall have immortality|Propterea habebo per hanc, immortalitatem]] [Denis's text reads *Propterea*, "therefore"; a marginal note gives *Præterea*, "moreover", the Vulgate's reading], that is, I shall be joined to the uncreated Wisdom in this life by charity and the life of grace, and in the life to come by the life of glory; [[8:13|and shall leave behind me an everlasting memory to them that come after me|et memoriam æternam his, qui post me futuri sunt, relinquam]], that is, in this world I shall be famous through the succession of generations until the end of the world. [[8:14|I shall set|Disponam]], that is, I shall rule, order and instruct, [[8:14|the people in order|populos]]: for the governing of whom a man is made especially fit by eminence in wisdom; [[8:14|and nations shall be subject to me|et nationes mihi erunt subditæ]]: because I shall bear myself so lovingly and discreetly towards my subjects that they will gladly obey me. [[8:15|Terrible kings hearing, shall be afraid of me|Timebunt me audientes reges horrendi]], that is, on hearing the depth of my words they will conceive a reverent and fearful feeling towards me: as Nabuchodonosor, a most dreaded king, on hearing the words of holy Daniel, prostrated himself and worshipped him[[Dan 2:46||]]. [[8:15|among the multitude I shall be found good|Et in multitudine bonus videbor]]: that is, I shall speak so wisely and justly that all who hear me will reckon me virtuous; [[8:15|and valiant in war|et in bello fortis]]: because wisdom avails above all for prevailing over things invisible and visible: for it makes a man proceed in good order, and lean on divine help, and be guarded, and consider what must be considered. Hence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 24:6|war is managed by due ordering|Cum dispositione initur bellum]]; and again, [[Prov 20:18|wars are to be managed by governments|Gubernaculis tractanda sunt bella]].

paras.t: Præterea omnia ista fuerunt ad litteram in Salomone completa, propter excellentiam sapientiæ ejus. Qui, ut tertio Regum et secundo Paralipomenon legitur, undique famosissimus erat: ita quod omnes reges per gyrum desiderabant vultum ejus conspicere, et verba sapientiæ ejus audire, deferebantque ei munera, et fuerunt ei subjecti. Sed et sanctus Job vir sapientissimus testatur, hæc magna ex parte completa in se, dicens: In platea parabant cathedram mihi. Principes cessabant loqui, et digitum superponebant ori suo; vocem suam cohibebant duces; auris audiens beatificabat me.
paras.en: Moreover, all these things were fulfilled to the letter in Solomon, because of the excellence of his wisdom. He, as we read in the third book of Kings and the second of Paralipomenon, was most famous everywhere[[3 Kings 4:31||]], so that all the kings round about desired to see his face and hear the words of his wisdom[[3 Kings 4:34||]][[2 Par 9:23||]], and brought him gifts[[2 Par 9:24||]], and were subject to him[[2 Par 9:26||]][[2 Par 9:22||]] [the margin gives 3 Kings iv, 31, 34; 2 Par. ix, 22–24, 26]. And holy Job too, a most wise man, testifies that these things were in great part fulfilled in himself, saying: [[Job 29:7|in the street they prepared me a chair|In platea parabant cathedram mihi]]. [[Job 29:9|The princes ceased to speak, and laid the finger on their mouth|Principes cessabant loqui, et digitum superponebant ori suo]]; [[Job 29:10|The rulers held their peace|vocem suam cohibebant duces]]; [[Job 29:11|The ear that heard me blessed me|auris audiens beatificabat me]].

paras.t: Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum illa: id est, post occupationes externas, redeundo ad cordis proprii discussionem, atque ingrediens mentis cubiculum, conscientiæ thalamum, ecclesiam, seu habitationem quietam, vacabo per contemplationem, cum grandi tranquillitate, Sapientiæ increatæ, et ab omni exteriori strepitu ac tumultu quiescam in hoc invariabili tranquillissimoque objecto, in quo solo est pax pectoris sancta ac salutaris. De quo dixit Propheta: In pace in id ipsum dormiam, et requiescam. Hinc loquitur Dominus: Sedebit populus meus in pulchritudine pacis, et in tabernaculis fiduciæ, et in requie opulenta. Non enim habet amaritudinem conversatio illius, id est, occupatio mentis in Deo per contemplationem, dilectionem, et laudem ipsius, non habet amaricationem sibi annexam directe, nec inordinatam amaricationem, nec tædium convictus illius, id est, vivifica et contemplativa unio cum Sapientia summa, non est tædiosa, sed gaudiosa. Propter quod subditur: sed lætitiam in contemplando, et gaudium spirituale in diligendo, vel lætitiam redundantem in partem sensitivam ex plenitudine gaudii existentis in superiori animæ parte, juxta illud Prophetæ: Cor meum et caro mea exsultaverunt in Deum vivum. Nempe, quum delectatio oriatur ex unione potentiæ cum objecto convenienti, sitque diffusio animi in conceptu adeptioneque boni, dum mens sincere conjungitur summo et incomparabili bono illi, habet copiosæ delectationis incitamentum, rationem, materiam, et beatitudini Dei sui congratulatur, atque ex spe beatificæ ejus fruitionis exhilaratur: et quanto spirituales deliciæ istæ plus gustantur, tanto plus appetuntur, ac complacent, et relevant mentem; corporales vero delectationes cito vertuntur in nauseam, et aggravant corpus. Ideo Sapientia loquitur: Qui edunt me, adhuc esurient. Aristoteles quoque fatetur, quod philosophia habet mirabiles delectationes sibi admixtas. Et rursus: Delectationi, inquit, quæ est in consideratione, non est tristitia contraria. Itemque: Homo contemplativus plenus est jucundis theorematibus; nec extra se expetit delectari, quia in se habet delectationis puræ materiam.
paras.en: [[8:16|When I go into my house, I shall repose myself with her|Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum illa]]: that is, after outward occupations, returning to the examination of my own heart, and entering the chamber of the mind, the bridal room of conscience, the church, or a quiet dwelling, I shall give myself by contemplation, with great tranquillity, to the uncreated Wisdom, and shall rest from all outward noise and tumult in this unchanging and most tranquil object, in which alone is the holy and saving peace of the breast. Of which the Prophet said: [[Ps 4:9|In peace in the self same I will sleep, and I will rest|In pace in id ipsum dormiam, et requiescam]]. Hence the Lord says: [[Is 32:18|my people shall sit in the beauty of peace, and in the tabernacles of confidence, and in wealthy rest|Sedebit populus meus in pulchritudine pacis, et in tabernaculis fiduciæ, et in requie opulenta]]. [[8:16|for her conversation hath no bitterness|Non enim habet amaritudinem conversatio illius]], that is, the occupation of the mind in God by contemplation, love and praise of him has no bitterness joined to it directly, nor any inordinate bitterness, [[8:16|nor her company any tediousness|nec tædium convictus illius]], that is, the life-giving and contemplative union with the highest Wisdom is not wearisome but joyful. Wherefore it is added: [[8:16|but joy|sed lætitiam]] in contemplating, [[8:16|and gladness|et gaudium]], spiritual, in loving; or a gladness overflowing into the sensitive part from the fullness of the joy that is in the higher part of the soul, according to that saying of the Prophet: [[Ps 83:3|My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God|Cor meum et caro mea exsultaverunt in Deum vivum]]. Indeed, since delight arises from the union of a power with a fitting object, and is an expansion of the soul in conceiving and attaining a good, when the mind is sincerely joined to that highest and incomparable good, it has the incentive, the reason and the matter of abundant delight, and rejoices with its God in his beatitude, and is gladdened by the hope of enjoying him in bliss; and the more these spiritual delights are tasted, the more they are desired, and please, and lift up the mind; whereas bodily delights quickly turn to nausea and weigh down the body. Therefore Wisdom says: [[Ecclus 24:29|They that eat me, shall yet hunger|Qui edunt me, adhuc esurient]]. Aristotle too confesses that philosophy has wonderful delights mingled with it. And again: To the delight, he says, that is in contemplation, no sorrow is contrary. And likewise: The contemplative man is full of pleasant theorems [that is, truths contemplated]; nor does he seek delight outside himself, because he has within himself the matter of pure delight.

paras.t: Sed his objici potest quod in Ecclesiaste habetur: In multa sapientia multa est indignatio, et qui addit scientiam, addit et dolorem; et iterum, Cor sapientium ubi tristitia. Et respondendum, quod contemplationi seu considerationi sapientiæ, bene adjungitur bona amaritudo, contritio, dolor concomitanter, ex hoc quod homo Deum contemplando reflectitur ad sui ipsius considerationem, et ad calamitatem iniquitatemque propriam intuendam, ad considerandum quoque statum hujus exsilii, ac distantiam sui a beatifica visione: et sic suis vitiis indignatur, et cum Sancto exclamat: Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est: et cum Paulo: Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?
paras.en: But against this may be objected what is found in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:18|in much wisdom there is much indignation|In multa sapientia multa est indignatio]], [[Eccles 1:18|and he that addeth knowledge, addeth also labour|et qui addit scientiam, addit et dolorem]] [Denis reads *dolorem*, "sorrow", where the Vulgate has *laborem*, "labour"]; and again, [[Eccles 7:5|The heart of the wise is where there is mourning|Cor sapientium ubi tristitia]]. And the answer is that to the contemplation or consideration of wisdom there is well joined, as a concomitant, a good bitterness, contrition and sorrow, from this: that a man, in contemplating God, is turned back to the consideration of himself, and to looking upon his own wretchedness and iniquity, and also to considering the state of this exile and his distance from the beatific vision: and so he is indignant at his vices, and cries out with the Saint [that is, the Psalmist]: [[Ps 119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!|Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]] and with Paul: [[Rom 7:24|Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?|Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?]]

paras.t: Hæc cogitans apud me, id est in me: juxta quem modum fertur, Verbum erat apud Deum; et commemorans, id est frequenter revolvens, in corde meo, quoniam immortalitas est in cogitatione sapientiæ, id est, quod homo contemplationi sapientiæ immorando, immortalitatem gloriæ promeretur, et ipsa contemplatio, quæ hic inchoatur, in futuro perficitur ac perpetuatur: prout Christus in Evangelio dixit, Maria optimam partem elegit, quæ non auferetur ab ea; et in amicitia illius delectatio bona, id est, quod virtuosa sit delectatio quæ in dilectione Sapientiæ increatæ consistit: quam diligere sanctum est, et quæ quanto ferventius puriusque amatur, tanto amplius diligentem delectat. Nulla etenim virtus, nulla forma tam delectabiliter operatur, ut caritas. Et in operibus manuum illius, honestas sine defectione, id est, quod in operibus et creaturis, seu effectibus justis et sanctis, sit Sapientiæ æternalis indeficiens honestas, et irreprehensibilis probitas: quia nil reprehensibile ab ea procedit; sed, sicut ait Psalmista, Justus Dominus in omnibus viis suis, et sanctus in omnibus operibus suis. Unde iterum protestatur: Delectasti me, Domine, in factura tua: et in operibus manuum tuarum exsultabo. Et in certamine loquelæ illius, id est, quod in conflictu seu disceptatione sapientialium verborum ac Scripturarum, a Sapientia increata procedentium, sit sapientia, id est instructio doctrinalis: quia dum sapientes inter se caritative et sapientialiter disputant ac conferunt de Scripturis, et contra perfidorum errores ac hæreses arguunt, instruunt audientes. Unde ait Apostolus: Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad corripiendum in justitia. De episcopo quoque loquens: Potens sit, inquit, exhortari in doctrina sana, et eos qui contradicunt, arguere. Et præclaritas in communicatione sermonum ipsius, id est, quod magna sinceritas ac lucida veritas sit in verbis et eruditionibus, quibus Sapientia erudit suos, et quæ communicat suis fidelibus, sicut in Proverbiis contestatur: Justi sunt omnes sermones mei, et non est in eis pravum quid, neque perversum.
paras.en: [[8:17|Thinking these things with myself|Hæc cogitans apud me]], that is, within me [Latin *apud me*, "with me"]: in which sense it is said, [[John 1:1|the Word was with God|Verbum erat apud Deum]]; [[8:17|and pondering them|et commemorans]], that is, often turning them over, [[8:17|in my heart, that to be allied to wisdom is immortality|in corde meo, quoniam immortalitas est in cogitatione sapientiæ]] [Denis reads *in cogitatione sapientiæ*, "in the thought of wisdom", where the Vulgate has *in cognatione*, "in kinship with wisdom", which the Douay-Rheims renders "to be allied to wisdom"; his gloss follows his reading], that is, that a man, by dwelling in the contemplation of wisdom, merits the immortality of glory, and that contemplation itself, which is begun here, is perfected and made everlasting in the life to come: as Christ said in the Gospel, [[Luke 10:42|Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her|Maria optimam partem elegit, quæ non auferetur ab ea]]; [[8:18|And that there is great delight in her friendship|in amicitia illius delectatio bona]], that is, that the delight which consists in the love of the uncreated Wisdom is virtuous: to love whom is holy, and who, the more fervently and purely she is loved, the more she delights the one who loves her. For no virtue, no form, works so delightfully as charity. [[8:18|and inexhaustible riches in the works of her hands|Et in operibus manuum illius, honestas sine defectione]] [Latin *honestas sine defectione*, "unfailing honourableness", where the Douay-Rheims has "inexhaustible riches"], that is, that in the works and creatures, or the just and holy effects, of the eternal Wisdom there is an unfailing honourableness and irreproachable uprightness: because nothing blameworthy proceeds from her; but, as the Psalmist says, [[Ps 144:17|The Lord is just in all his ways: and holy in all his works|Justus Dominus in omnibus viis suis, et sanctus in omnibus operibus suis]]. Hence he declares again: [[Ps 91:5|thou hast given me, O Lord, a delight in thy doings: and in the works of thy hands I shall rejoice|Delectasti me, Domine, in factura tua: et in operibus manuum tuarum exsultabo]]. [[8:18|and in the exercise of conference with her|Et in certamine loquelæ illius]], that is, that in the contest or debate of wise words and of the Scriptures, which proceed from the uncreated Wisdom, there is [[8:18|wisdom|sit sapientia]], that is, doctrinal instruction: because when wise men dispute and confer among themselves charitably and wisely about the Scriptures, and argue against the errors and heresies of the faithless, they instruct those who hear. Hence the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 3:16|All scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct|Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad corripiendum]] [[2 Tim 3:16|in justice|in justitia]]. Speaking also of a bishop: [[Tit 1:9|that he may be able|Potens sit]], he says, [[Tit 1:9|to exhort in sound doctrine and to convince the gainsayers|exhortari in doctrina sana, et eos qui contradicunt, arguere]]. [[8:18|and glory in the communication of her words|Et præclaritas in communicatione sermonum ipsius]], that is, that there is great sincerity and shining truth in the words and teachings by which Wisdom instructs her own, and which she communicates to her faithful, as she declares in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:8|All my words are just, there is nothing wicked, nor perverse|Justi sunt omnes sermones mei, et non est in eis pravum quid, neque perversum]].

paras.t: Circuibam quærens, id est, undique investigans, cuncta occurrentia consideravi, ut mihi illam assumerem, id est, Sapientiam invenirem, et inventam, ut sponsam brachiis pii purique amoris amplecterer. In cunctis etenim rebus creatis Sapientia prima relucet, sicut artifex in opere suo. Ideo fertur in Canticis: Surgam, et circuibo civitatem; per vicos et plateas quæram quem diligit anima mea. Iste est bonus circuitus, qui a Deo incipit, et terminatur ad ipsum. Est autem et pravus circuitus, qui est inordinata evagatio per creata: de qua ait Propheta, In circuitu impii ambulant.
paras.en: [[8:18|I went about seeking|Circuibam quærens]], that is, searching on every side, I considered everything I came upon, [[8:18|that I might take her to myself|ut mihi illam assumerem]], that is, that I might find Wisdom, and having found her, embrace her as a bride with the arms of a devout and pure love. For the first Wisdom shines forth in all created things, as a craftsman in his work. Therefore it is said in the Canticles: [[Cant 3:2|I will rise, and will go about the city: in the streets and the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth|Surgam, et circuibo civitatem; per vicos et plateas quæram quem diligit anima mea]]. This is the good going about, which begins from God and ends in him. But there is also a wicked going about, which is a disordered wandering among created things: of which the Prophet says, [[Ps 11:9|The wicked walk round about|In circuitu impii ambulant]].

paras.t: Puer autem eram ingeniosus, id est acuti atque capacis intellectus. Unde in libro de Civitate Dei asserit Augustinus: Ingeniosum nasci, felicitatis est; et rursus, Faciliter intelligere, et intellecta bene implere, plena felicitas est. Et sortitus sum animam bonam, id est egregiæ indolis, utpote ex naturali dispositione ad sapientiam ac virtutes fortiter inclinatam.
paras.en: [[8:19|And I was a witty child|Puer autem eram ingeniosus]] [Latin *ingeniosus*, "gifted", "of good wit"], that is, of a keen and capacious intellect. Hence Augustine asserts in the book of the City of God: To be born gifted is a matter of good fortune; and again, To understand easily, and to carry out well what is understood, is full happiness. [[8:19|and had received a good soul|Et sortitus sum animam bonam]], that is, of excellent disposition, as being strongly inclined by natural disposition to wisdom and the virtues.

paras.t: Et quum essem magis bonus, id est melior factus, proficiendo in virtutibus atque ingenitam inclinationem assidue actuando, veni ad corpus incoinquinatum, id est mundum; et corpus meum in puritate, puta in castitate conjugali, servavi, et rationi subjeci, mundans me ab omni inquinamento animæ et corporis. Salomon enim per multos annos fuit vir virtuosus, justus, ac continens, quamvis in senectute ad extremam fœditatem dilapsus sit.
paras.en: [[8:20|And whereas I was more good|Et quum essem magis bonus]], that is, having become better, by advancing in the virtues and constantly putting my inborn inclination into act, [[8:20|I came to a body undefiled|veni ad corpus incoinquinatum]], that is, clean; and I kept my body in purity, namely in conjugal chastity, and subjected it to reason, cleansing myself from all defilement of soul and body. For Solomon was for many years a virtuous, just and continent man, although in his old age he fell into the utmost foulness.

paras.t: Et ut scivi, id est, statim postquam cognovi, quoniam aliter non possem esse continens a vitiis et concupiscentiis, nisi Deus det gratiam continendi: quia non est volentis, neque currentis, sed Dei miserentis, qui ait, Sine me nihil potestis facere. Et hoc ipsum erat sapientiæ, id est actus seu consideratio sapientiæ infusæ, et donum ac inspiratio et illuminatio Sapientiæ increatæ, scire cujus esset hoc donum. Unde ait Apostolus: Non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis. Adii Dominum, id est, Deum ubique præsentem mente accessi, dirigendo cor meum in ipsum: juxta illud, Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini; et deprecatus sum illum, et dixi ex totis præcordiis meis, id est intimis affectibus mentis, seu cum tota attentione intellectus, affectioneque integra voluntatis: secundum illud, Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo.
paras.en: [[8:21|And as I knew|Et ut scivi]], that is, as soon as I came to know, [[8:21|that I could not otherwise be continent|quoniam aliter non possem esse continens]] from vices and concupiscences, [[8:21|except God gave it|nisi Deus det]] the grace of continence [Denis's text adds *a vitiis et concupiscentiis* and *gratiam continendi*, words not in the Vulgate]: because [[Rom 9:16|it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy|non est volentis, neque currentis, sed Dei miserentis]], who says, [[John 15:5|without me you can do nothing|Sine me nihil potestis facere]]. [[8:21|and this also was a point of wisdom|Et hoc ipsum erat sapientiæ]], that is, an act or consideration of infused wisdom, and a gift, inspiration and enlightening of the uncreated Wisdom, [[8:21|to know whose gift it was|scire cujus esset hoc donum]]. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 2:12|we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is of God: that we may know the things that are given us from God|Non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis]]. [[8:21|I went to the Lord|Adii Dominum]], that is, I approached in mind God who is present everywhere, directing my heart towards him: according to that saying, [[Ps 33:6|Come ye to him and be enlightened|Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini]]; [[8:21|and besought him|et deprecatus sum illum]], [[8:21|and said with my whole heart|et dixi ex totis præcordiis meis]], that is, with the inmost affections of the mind, or with the whole attention of the intellect and the entire affection of the will: according to that saying, [[Ps 110:1|I will praise thee, O Lord, with my whole heart|Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo]][[Ps 137:1||]] [the margin gives Ps. cx, 1 and cxxxvii, 1, which both begin with these words].
